kinds.title: Minnesota statutes
kinds.intro: Laws passed by the Minnesota Legislature. They set who is eligible, what services exist, who pays and who oversees the work.

kinds.title: Minnesota rules
kinds.intro: Rules adopted by state agencies under authority from statute. They carry the force of law and fill in how a statute is carried out.

kinds.title: Community-Based Services Manual
kinds.intro: The policy manual the Disability Services Division and the Aging and Adult Services Division publish for lead agencies that administer home and community-based services.

kinds.title: Federally approved waiver plans
kinds.intro: The waiver plans the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services approved for Minnesota, and the announcements of their approval.

kinds.title: Department of Human Services policies
kinds.intro: Policies, protocols, manuals and guidance the Department of Human Services publishes outside the Community-Based Services Manual.

kinds.title: Bulletins
kinds.intro: Numbered bulletins and dated announcements the Department of Human Services sends to lead agencies and providers.

kinds.title: Federal rules

policies.title: Annual reporting by providers that pay subminimum wages (Minnesota Statutes 256B.4906)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Following the Task Force on Eliminating Subminimum Wages, the 2023 Legislature established annual reporting for specified home and community-based services providers holding a federal certificate or state permit to pay subminimum wages, under Minnesota Statutes 256B.4906 and Laws 2023, chapter 61, article 1, section 22. The reporting scope depends on the credentials and individuals described in the statute, rather than covering all providers. The Department publishes findings on its Employment First dashboards; the report for August 1, 2023 to June 30, 2024 was posted in 2025. Individually identifiable records submitted under this requirement are private.
requires: The specified home and community-based services providers holding a federal certificate or state permit as of August 1, 2023 must report annually about individuals currently paid subminimum wages or paid those wages by the provider as of that date.
The Department publishes the subminimum wage data report on the Employment First dashboards; the first report covers August 1, 2023 to June 30, 2024.
The requirement comes from Laws 2023, chapter 61, article 1, section 22 and Minnesota Statutes 256B.4906.
equityCheck: Use the published findings to examine reported patterns by provider, lead agency and demographic category where the dashboard presents them. Check the period, definitions and limits before drawing conclusions about who is affected.

In authorized planning work with a person who receives services, discuss whether their support plan includes a path to competitive, integrated employment if they want one. Use the appropriate individual records and the person’s own goals; do not attempt to identify people from the public dashboard.

policies.title: Child protection: reporting maltreatment of minors (Minnesota Statutes 260E.06)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Minnesota Statutes chapter 260E governs reporting of maltreatment of minors. Section 260E.06 says which people must report when they know or have reason to believe a child is being maltreated, or was maltreated in the past three years. The Community-Based Services Manual has a child protection page that points lead agency staff to these rules.
requires: Professionals and their delegates in social services, health care, child care, education, corrections and law enforcement must report immediately when they know or have reason to believe a child is being maltreated or was maltreated in the past three years.
Reports go to the local welfare agency, the agency responsible for assessing or investigating, a police department, the county sheriff, a Tribal social services agency or a Tribal police department.
An organization may not have a policy that prevents or discourages an employee from reporting.
Any other person may report voluntarily.
A parent, guardian or caretaker who relies on spiritual means or prayer instead of medical care must report if the lack of medical care may seriously endanger the child.
equityCheck: Check that every direct support worker, case manager and provider in your area knows who must report and where, including Tribal social services and Tribal police as listed in the statute.
Check that families with limited English or disabilities can reach the county child protection intake line and that interpreters are available.
Look at whether reports and screening decisions differ by race, disability or region, and ask why.

policies.title: Choice to waive annual reassessment (Minnesota Statutes 256B.0911, subdivisions 24, 25 and 28)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Minnesota Statutes 256B.0911 requires a reassessment every year for people who get long-term services and supports. The same section lists the limited cases where a person can choose a different arrangement: a remote reassessment by video or phone, declining an assessment when the person gets only Rule 185 case management, or longer gaps between in-person visits for a person under 65 who lives in a nursing facility. The Community-Based Services Manual lists this topic under its assessment and support planning pages.
requires: Reassessments must be done every year or as federal and state law require (subdivision 22).

A remote reassessment by video or telephone may replace an in-person one only with the person's informed choice and consent, documented by the lead agency; the person may refuse a remote reassessment at any time (subdivision 24).

Limits on remote reassessments in a row before an in-person one is required: up to four for the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion and Developmental Disabilities waivers; one for Alternative Care, Essential Community Supports and the Elderly Waiver; two for personal care assistance and Community First Services and Supports (subdivision 24).

A county need not arrange an annual certified-assessor reassessment for a person who receives only Rule 185 case management; if the person makes an informed choice to decline an assessment, the person-centered service plan must still be reviewed every year (subdivision 25).

A person under 65 in a nursing facility must have an in-person assessment at least every 12 months, or at least every 36 months if the person states in writing that annual visits are not wanted (subdivision 28).

A lead agency is a county, or a Tribe or health plan under contract with the commissioner; a Tribal Nation may set its own education and experience qualifications for certified assessors (subdivisions 10 and 13).
equityCheck: Check that the choice to use a remote reassessment is explained in the person's language and format, and that saying no has no cost to the person.
Check that people in rural areas are not pushed toward remote reassessments only because assessors are far away.
Track how often informed consent for remote reassessment is documented, by county and by group, and review the gaps.

policies.title: Consumer Support Grant
policies.summary: The Consumer Support Grant is a state-funded program that gives people with functional limitations and their families a cash grant to buy and arrange their own supports instead of using certain Medical Assistance home care services. Minnesota Statutes 256.476 sets the rules. Counties choose whether to take part, and the county agency handles applications, approvals and payments.
requires: A person must be eligible for Medical Assistance or have an approved family support grant, be able to direct care or have a representative who can, have functional limitations and need ongoing community supports, and live in the person's own home or a family member's home (subdivision 3).

A person may not get the grant while receiving personal care assistance, home health aide, home care nursing, a family support grant or Alternative Care; people in institutional or congregate settings are excluded (subdivision 3).

The grant may pay for supports such as respite care, daily living assistance, adaptive aids and assistive technology, but not items paid by other sources, special education, day training and habilitation or case management (subdivisions 2 and 4).
The county board decides whether to participate; its local agency sets written procedures and criteria for grant amounts and uses (subdivisions 2 and 4).
Enrollment is limited by the annual appropriation; unspent funds return to the state each year (subdivisions 3 and 5).

The monthly grant is raised 7.5 percent for people eligible for ten or more hours per day of personal care or Community First Services and Supports who use trained direct support workers (subdivision 11).
equityCheck: Check whether your county offers the grant; if not, people there have fewer self-direction options than people in neighboring counties.
Check that the written criteria for grant amounts are shared with applicants in their language.
Review who is told about the grant and who gets it, by race and disability.

policies.title: Consumer-directed community supports
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Consumer-directed community supports is the self-directed service option under the four disability waivers, Alternative Care and the Elderly Waiver. The person gets a budget and decides what supports to buy and who to hire, with a financial management services provider handling payroll. Minnesota Statutes 256B.4911 and the federally approved waiver plans govern it; the Community-Based Services Manual and the Consumer-Directed Community Supports Policy Manual explain how lead agencies apply it.
requires: Consumer-directed community supports is governed in whole by the federally approved home and community-based services waiver plans (256B.4911, subdivision 1) and must be offered to everyone eligible for the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waivers (256B.49, subdivision 16).
Lead agencies must explain how the budget was calculated, give the formula and inform participants of their appeal rights (256B.4911, subdivision 7).

Budget exceptions of up to 30 percent are available when the support plan shows a need to increase work time, move to certain settings or build a positive behavior support plan, and for people leaving institutions or crisis settings (256B.4911, subdivisions 3 and 4).
Parents of minor children may each provide up to 40 hours per week (80 combined), a single parent up to 60 hours, and a spouse up to 60 hours per week (256B.4911, subdivision 6).
One direct care worker may serve up to three participants at once under a written shared services agreement that the lead agency authorizes (256B.4911, subdivision 5).
Only the commissioner may create consumer-directed community supports policies; lead agency handbooks do not have the force of law (256B.4911, subdivision 8).
equityCheck: Check that the option is offered to everyone eligible and that the budget explanation is given in the person's language.
Compare use of this option by race, language and county; low use in some groups can point to how it is explained.
Check that budget exception rules are applied the same way in every lead agency.

policies.title: County of financial responsibility (Minnesota Unitary Residence and Financial Responsibility Act)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Minnesota Statutes chapter 256G, the Minnesota Unitary Residence and Financial Responsibility Act, says which county pays for social services when residence decides financial responsibility. Section 256G.02 defines the county of financial responsibility, residence and excluded time. The Community-Based Services Manual has a page that applies these rules to home and community-based services.
requires: For a state resident not living in an excluded facility, the county of financial responsibility is the county where the person lives when applying (256G.02, subdivision 4).
For a person living in an excluded facility, it is the county where the person last lived in nonexcluded status before entering (256G.02, subdivision 4).
If a person already has an open social service case in one county, later services attach to the earliest open case (256G.02, subdivision 4).

Excluded time includes stays in hospitals, nursing homes, foster homes, licensed community residential settings, correctional facilities, assisted living, integrated community supports and day support services, among others (256G.02, subdivision 6).
To reside means to have an established place of abode in one state or county and not in another (256G.02, subdivision 8).
The chapter applies to all social service programs administered by the commissioner in which residence decides financial responsibility, unless modified by rule or a federal waiver.
equityCheck: Check that disputes between counties over who pays do not delay a person's services; the person should not wait while counties argue.
Check how excluded time rules affect people leaving institutions, shelters or treatment, who are often low-income or homeless.
Make sure the rules are explained to the person in plain language.

policies.title: Developmental disabilities screening (diagnosis and needs assessment under Minnesota Statutes 256B.092)
policies.summary: Before a person can get Developmental Disabilities Waiver services, intermediate care facility services or related case management, the county of financial responsibility must confirm a developmental disability or related condition and a certified assessor must assess the person's needs. Minnesota Statutes 256B.092 sets these steps; Minnesota Rules parts 9525.0004 to 9525.0036 (known as Rule 185) set the county case management duties. The Community-Based Services Manual has a page on developmental disabilities screening and a codebook for the screening document.
requires: Before services begin, the county of financial responsibility must conduct or arrange a diagnostic evaluation to find whether the person has or may have a developmental disability or related condition (256B.092, subdivision 1).
If the person is diagnosed, the county arranges a needs assessment by a certified assessor and authorizes services in the person's support plan (256B.092, subdivision 1).
Certified assessors conduct assessments and reassessments and must make referrals to decide case management eligibility (256B.092, subdivision 7).

Medical Assistance cannot pay for intermediate care facility, waiver or nursing facility services for a person with a developmental disability until the Department of Human Services authorizes the developmental disabilities screening document.

Minnesota Rules 9525.0004 to 9525.0036 cover county board case management responsibilities, case management administration and practice standards, quality assurance, host county concurrence and determination of need.
equityCheck: Check that diagnostic evaluations are available in the person's language and that cultural bias in testing is considered.
Check how long people wait for a diagnostic evaluation by county; long waits delay all other services.
Check that adults who were never screened as children are told how to ask for a screening.

policies.title: Disability Waiver Rate System (Minnesota Statutes 256B.4914)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: The Disability Waiver Rate System is the statewide method for setting payment rates for most services under the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion and Developmental Disabilities waivers. Minnesota Statutes 256B.4914 sets the formulas, the data providers must report, the share of revenue that must go to direct care staff, and the exceptions process. The Community-Based Services Manual has a page on the system for lead agencies.
requires: Rates are set by the rates management system using staffing hours, nursing hours, staffing ratios and other values, with a base wage index tied to Bureau of Labor Statistics wage data (subdivisions 4 and 5).
Wage and component values are adjusted by the Consumer Price Index every two years starting in 2026, capped at eight percent per update (subdivision 5b).
Minimum shares of revenue must go to direct care staff compensation: 66 percent for residential rates, 45 percent for day program rates, and 60 percent for unit-based rates (subdivision 10d).

Providers must submit cost data at least once every five years and labor market data by November 1 each year; the commissioner may suspend payments when required data is not received (subdivisions 10a and 10b).
Lead agencies review and approve services and values, notify people and providers of final rates, and respond to petitions to correct wrong values (subdivision 4).
The commissioner keeps an online manual available to county and Tribal agencies and will not defer to county or Tribal agencies on technical application of the framework (subdivision 17).
equityCheck: Check whether the rate framework keeps providers open in rural areas and for culturally specific providers; track closures by region.
Check that people and families get the rate notice the statute requires and can understand it.
Use the direct care compensation reports to see whether workers from communities of color are paid the required share.

policies.title: Disability Waiver Rate System exception requests
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: When the framework rate under the Disability Waiver Rate System cannot meet a person's exceptional needs, the lead agency may ask the Department of Human Services for a rate exception. Minnesota Statutes 256B.4914, subdivision 14 sets who may ask, the criteria and the deadlines. Lead agencies submit requests on the Disability Waiver Rates System Exception Request Application (form 5820).
requires: Lead agencies identify people whose exceptional needs cannot be met under the rate system; the person, an interested party or the license holder may also ask the lead agency to submit a request (subdivision 14).

Criteria: the need cannot be met through additional units; the rate is so insufficient that a discharge notice was issued; or needs, including behavioral changes, require a change in provider or services beyond the current authorization (subdivision 14).

The lead agency acts within 30 days, sends a written recommendation and forwards all requests to the commissioner; the commissioner decides within 30 days and gives written reasons for any denial to the lead agency, the person, the interested party and the license holder (subdivision 14).
Denials may be appealed under Minnesota Statutes 256.045 and 256.0451, with a possible temporary stay of discharge (subdivision 14).

Effective July 1, 2026, exceptions for certain residential services are limited: behavioral exceptions need a documented diagnosis or assessed need, community residential exceptions cannot include positive support costs, and annual renewals need continued assessed need (subdivision 14a).

Form 5820 (revised February 2025) asks for the extraordinary need, the requested rate components, the MnCHOICES rate calculation and cost documentation, and an explanation if the request reached the lead agency more than 90 days after the requested start date.
equityCheck: Compare exception request and approval rates across lead agencies; people with the same needs should have the same chance of an exception.
Check that families and small or culturally specific providers know they can ask the lead agency to submit a request.
Check that written denial reasons are sent to the person in their language.

policies.title: Early Intensive Developmental and Behavioral Intervention benefit
policies.summary: The Early Intensive Developmental and Behavioral Intervention benefit is a Medical Assistance benefit for people under 21 with autism spectrum disorder or a related condition. It covers a comprehensive multidisciplinary evaluation, treatment under an individual treatment plan, family caregiver training and progress monitoring. Minnesota Statutes 256B.0949 sets the rules; the Community-Based Services Manual has a page on the benefit for lead agencies.
requires: The person must be enrolled in Medical Assistance, be under 21, and have a medically necessary diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder or a related condition confirmed by a comprehensive multidisciplinary evaluation based on direct observation (subdivisions 2 to 5).

Covered services include the evaluation, individual and group intervention, treatment plan development and progress monitoring, family caregiver training, coordinated care conferences and travel time; four treatment approaches are approved (subdivisions 6, 7 and 13).

Services must reflect the person's and family's primary language, culture, values and preferences; providers must have a limited English proficiency plan, and the commissioner must provide culturally and linguistically diverse training (subdivisions 3a and 12).
Agencies must provide clinical supervision of at least one hour per 16 hours of direct treatment and monthly observation by a qualified supervising professional (subdivisions 15 and 16).
Fluency in a non-English language or certification by a Tribal Nation can qualify a person for level II or level III provider roles (subdivision 15).
Telehealth delivery is covered the same as in-person services, within limits on consecutive remote supervision (subdivisions 13 and 16).
equityCheck: Check that families can get a comprehensive evaluation in their language and within a reasonable distance; evaluation waits are the first barrier.
Check that providers serving immigrant and Tribal communities are enrolled and that the language and Tribal certification provider pathways are used.
Review who receives the benefit by race, language and region against who has a diagnosis.

policies.title: Electronic visit verification
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Electronic visit verification is an electronic record that confirms when and where certain in-home and community services were delivered, as required by the federal 21st Century Cures Act. Minnesota Statutes 256B.073 lists the services that must use it, the six data elements, and the choice between the free state system and an approved third-party system. The Community-Based Services Manual has electronic visit verification policy pages, and the Department of Human Services enforces compliance.
requires: Covered services include personal care assistance, Community First Services and Supports, home health, adult companion and adult day services, early intensive developmental and behavioral intervention, integrated community supports, nonemergency medical transportation and certain hourly or minute-based waiver services (256B.073, subdivision 2).

Each visit must record the type of service, the person receiving it, the date, the location, the person providing it and the start and end times, captured at the time of service by an approved method (256B.073, subdivisions 2 and 6).
Providers may use the state-provided system at no cost or an approved third-party system at their own cost; a third-party system must connect to the state data aggregator (256B.073, subdivision 4a).

Every provider of a service that requires electronic visit verification must enroll with the state-selected system even when using a third-party system; the Department of Human Services began reviewing compliance September 1, 2024.

Live-in caregivers are not exempt but may enter the required data at least once per day instead of in real time; participants in the Safe at Home address confidentiality program use telephony and the Safe at Home post office box as the location.

Third-party system provisions in the 2026 amendments take effect January 1, 2027, or on federal approval if later; for early intensive developmental and behavioral intervention the date is July 1, 2027 (256B.073, subdivision 7).
equityCheck: Check that small, rural and culturally specific providers can meet the requirement with the free state system and do not drop out of serving people.
Check that workers without smartphones or reliable cell service can use telephony or other approved methods.
Check that people in the Safe at Home program and people with privacy concerns understand what location data is recorded.

policies.title: Home and community-based services waivers rate setting and the Rate Management System (Minnesota Statutes 256B.4914)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Minnesota Statutes 256B.4914 sets how payment rates are built for most services on the four disability waivers. Rates are calculated in a web-based Rate Management System using a framework of wage data and component values set by the commissioner. The Community-Based Services Manual pages on the Rate Management System and on rates and waiver rate limits are based on this section.
requires: Covers 24 listed services, including 24-hour customized living, adult day services, day support services, employment services, individualized home supports, integrated community supports, night supervision, positive support services and transportation.

Rates are built from base wages drawn from Bureau of Labor Statistics data by occupation, plus component values such as a 6.7 percent competitive workforce factor, an 11 percent supervisory span of control ratio, a 23.6 percent employee-related cost ratio and a 13.25 percent general administrative support ratio for many services.
Rates are set by the Rate Management System; lead agencies enter values and providers may petition the lead agency to correct values entered by mistake.
On January 1, 2026, and every two years after, the commissioner updates wage indexes and component values by the change in the consumer price index, with any increase capped at 8 percent.
Rate exceptions are available for people with exceptional or complex needs.

Several limits take effect January 1, 2027, or on federal approval, such as a maximum of eight hours per day for day support services and a 30-consecutive-day limit for in-home respite; the section defines lead agency to include a Tribal agency that administers waivered services.
equityCheck: Check whether rate exception requests are made and approved at the same rate for people in every county and every community, and whether families know they can ask.

Look at whether values entered in the Rate Management System (such as staffing ratios and hours) are set consistently for people with similar needs regardless of where they live or who their case manager is.
Ask whether providers serving rural areas or culturally specific communities can operate at the framework rates, and whether people in those areas are losing choice of provider.
Watch the January 2027 limits on day support hours and in-home respite days for people who have no other daytime support or family caregiver relief.

policies.title: Laws of Minnesota 2021, First Special Session chapter 7, article 13, section 73, Waiver Reimagine Phase II
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This uncodified session law directs the Department of Human Services to carry out the second phase of Waiver Reimagine, which restructures the four disability waivers. As amended in 2025, it sets a two-waiver structure and an individualized budget method. The full text of the 2021 chapter is long; the amended section text appears in Laws 2025, First Special Session chapter 9, article 2, section 56.
requires: Creates a two-waiver structure for people who need nursing facility, hospital, neurobehavioral hospital or intermediate care facility levels of care, starting January 1, 2027 or upon federal approval, whichever is later.
Requires an individualized budget methodology for waiver services.
Creates a budget exception for self-directed home care nursing for people who meet specific criteria, with conditions and an annual review.
Requires an online support planning and budget-tracking tool by July 1, 2026.
A separate 2025 law created the Advisory Task Force on Waiver Reimagine (Minnesota Statutes section 256B.4907), which must report to the legislature by January 15, 2027.
equityCheck: When individual budgets start, compare budget amounts for people with similar needs across counties, Tribal Nations and groups.
Check that budget exception processes are explained in plain language and other languages, so people who need more support can ask for it.
Make sure the online planning tool is accessible and that people without internet access have another way to see and track their budget.

policies.title: Laws of Minnesota 2025, chapter 38 (H.F. 2115), human services policy act
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This 2025 session law changes many human services statutes. Article 1, Aging and Disability Services, changes day services, positive support staff qualifications, case manager training, residential support criteria and limits on paid support by parents and spouses. Other articles cover the Department of Health, Direct Care and Treatment, behavioral health and the Office of Inspector General.
requires: Adds a baccalaureate-degree option for positive support analysts (Minnesota Statutes 245D.091) and bars license holders from requiring a guardian or conservator as a condition of service (245D.10).

Revises day services definitions and the duties of the commissioner, lead agencies and vendors (Minnesota Statutes 252.41 to 252.46); day training and habilitation rate changes take effect January 1, 2026.
Requires informed decision-making training and an annual competency evaluation for home and community-based waiver case managers, effective August 1, 2025 (256B.092 and 256B.49).

Adds criteria for residential support services: generally complex behavioral health or medical needs and a finding that other residential options are inappropriate (256B.092, subd. 11a and 256B.49, subd. 29).

Limits Medicaid payment for personal assistance by a parent to a minor child or by a spouse to 40 hours in a seven-day period per parent, and 80 hours combined, across the Alternative Care program and the disability and elderly waivers (256B.4911).
Requires Medical Assistance providers to give the State Medical Review Team access to electronic health records.
equityCheck: The parent and spouse hour limits fall hardest on families who cannot find outside workers, including rural families and families who need a worker who speaks their language; document unmet need when the cap binds.
When applying the new residential support criteria, check that people are not kept out of needed residential services because other options exist only on paper.
Confirm case managers have completed informed decision-making training before they guide people through choices.

source.title: Laws of Minnesota 2025, chapter 38

relatedSources.title: Minnesota Statutes 256B.4911 Consumer-Directed Community Supports

policies.title: Laws of Minnesota 2025, First Special Session chapter 9 (H.F. 3), human services budget act
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This 2025 special session budget law funds and changes aging and disability services. Article 2, Disability Services, changes assessments, case management, rate setting, licensing support and consumer-directed services, creates the Advisory Task Force on Waiver Reimagine and amends the Waiver Reimagine Phase II law. Effective dates vary by section and many depend on federal approval.
requires: Allows up to four consecutive remote reassessments for the Developmental Disabilities, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion and Brain Injury waivers if followed by an in-person reassessment, and lets adults under 65 attest to unchanged needs for up to two consecutive reassessments (256B.0911), effective January 1, 2026 or upon federal approval.

Requires an assessment to begin within 20 working days, lets lead agencies contract with hospitals when they miss timelines, and requires a public dashboard of assessment completions by lead agency updated at least twice a year.

Adds service authorization controls: increases above a prior service agreement plus legislated rate changes require manual approval and documentation (256B.092, subd. 3b and 256B.49, subd. 17a), until Waiver Reimagine is fully implemented.

Creates the Advisory Task Force on Waiver Reimagine (256B.4907) with a report due January 15, 2027, and amends the Waiver Reimagine Phase II law to set a two-waiver structure starting January 1, 2027 or upon federal approval.

Changes the Disability Waiver Rate System (256B.4914): splits night supervision into awake and asleep, caps a single inflation update at 8 percent, limits residential rate exceptions starting July 1, 2026, and makes waiver payments subject to sanctions and recovery.

Raises the enhanced rate for personal care assistance and community first services and supports from 107.5 to 112.5 percent for people needing 10 or more hours a day, effective January 1, 2026 or upon federal approval, and allows out-of-home respite for children in unlicensed residences under set conditions (245D.13).
Creates a Long-Term Services and Supports Advisory Council with recommendations due December 1, 2026, and savings provisions that could reduce competitive workforce factors if savings fall short.
equityCheck: Remote reassessments save travel but can miss needs; make sure people with limited phone or internet access, or who need an interpreter, are offered an in-person visit.
Use the assessment dashboard to compare wait times across lead agencies and ask why some areas lag.
Watch the new limits on residential rate exceptions for people with high behavioral needs, who may lose access if providers cannot be paid for their support.
Share information about the Waiver Reimagine task force and its public meetings with people and families who are often left out of policy input.

policies.title: Laws of Minnesota 2026, chapter 121 (S.F. 4476), human services policy and finance act
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This 2026 omnibus law was approved May 27, 2026. Article 1 creates continuity of care and complex transition rules for people in residential and customized living services. Other articles change assisted living and home care licensing, case management contacts, chapter 245A licensing, provider enrollment and program integrity, and targeted case management payment. Effective dates vary by section.
requires: New Minnesota Statutes 256B.045 and 256B.046 set duties for providers, lead agencies and the commissioner when a person's residential service (community residential, family residential, integrated community supports or customized living) faces a serious operational event or administrative action; complex transitions get a plan, 14-day planning timelines, status meetings every 14 days and a public dashboard.
Managed care and county-based purchasing plans must follow the transition rules and honor existing authorizations when clinically appropriate (256B.69, subd. 38).
Housing support capacity-building grants start July 1, 2026, with at least one grant outside the seven-county metro area.

Creates an 'early and often' licensor and compliance team for new home and community-based services licenses, with a technical assistance visit at three months and unannounced follow-up visits during the first 18 months (245A.042, subd. 7).

Creates a provider support and technical assistance team (256.01, subd. 46), risk-based preenrollment assessment (256B.0437), new enrollment and compliance program requirements (256B.044), high-risk provider training and enhanced prepayment review (effective January 1, 2027).

Sets cost-based fee-for-service rates for county targeted case management (256B.076) and requires monthly contacts for adult and children's mental health case management, with limits on telephone-only contacts.

Directs the Department of Health to develop a licensing category for settings with five or fewer residents serving people on the Brain Injury, Community Access for Disability Inclusion and Elderly waivers, with draft legislation due January 1, 2028.
equityCheck: When a residential provider closes or loses a license, check that every affected person gets a transition plan on the timeline, including people whose families are hard to reach or who have no family.
Use the public complex-transition dashboard to see whether some regions or groups wait longer for a new placement.
New provider enrollment and prepayment review rules can slow small and culturally specific providers; watch for gaps in the providers people want to use.

policies.title: Laws of Minnesota 2026, chapter 95 (S.F. 476), health and human services omnibus act
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This 2026 omnibus law covers Direct Care and Treatment, the Department of Health, aging and disability services, behavioral health, housing supports and vulnerable adult protection. Article 4, Aging and Disability Services Policy, changes foster care and community residential setting moratorium rules, positive support staff qualifications, Tribal Nation roles in assessment and case management, and ends housing stabilization services. Effective dates vary by section.
requires: Bars new initial licenses for child foster care, certain adult foster care not at the license holder's primary residence, community residential settings and certain children's residential treatment, with exceptions and a state-level resource needs determination process (245A.03, subds. 7b to 7d).

Lets license holders delay annual direct support staff training by up to 90 calendar days (245D.09, subd. 5), effective August 1, 2026, and updates positive support professional and analyst qualifications (245D.091).

Lets a Tribal Nation set its own education and experience qualifications for MnCHOICES assessors and determine targeted case management eligibility, effective January 1, 2027 or upon federal approval (256B.0911, subd. 13 and 256B.0924).

Adds lead agency duties to support informed choice, including information about Tribal Nation services and coordination with Tribal human services agencies, and affirms Tribal sovereignty (256B.4905, subd. 2a).
Requires targeted case management providers that also deliver a person's services to disclose the conflict of interest, get informed consent and offer alternatives.
Repeals the housing stabilization services statute (256B.051) and removes related background study requirements; replaces compliance duties with recuperative care duties.

Adds documentation and supervision standards for early intensive developmental and behavioral intervention, and lets the commissioner reject or re-verify deficient cost reports under the Disability Waiver Rate System (effective January 1, 2027).

Restrictions on a person's protection-related rights under chapter 245D must be documented, reviewed at least every six months and approved in writing; adds rights for minors receiving 245D services (245D.04).
equityCheck: The end of housing stabilization services affects people who relied on it to find and keep housing; check that each person has another support in place.
Lead agencies must now tell people about Tribal Nation services; confirm this is part of every informed choice conversation for American Indian people.
When case management and service delivery come from the same provider, verify the conflict-of-interest notice and consent are in the file.
Review restrictions on rights every six months as the law requires and look for patterns in who has restrictions.

policies.title: Licensing moratorium on corporate foster care and community residential settings (Minnesota Statutes 245A.03)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Minnesota Statutes 245A.03 bars the Department of Human Services from issuing new licenses for adult foster care at a home that is not the license holder's primary residence and for new community residential settings, with limited exceptions. The statute also sets a needs determination process and lets the commissioner impose a temporary moratorium when growth exceeds need. The Community-Based Services Manual has a page on the moratorium for lead agencies.
requires: No initial license may be issued for adult foster care at a location that will not be the license holder's primary residence, or for new community residential settings; capacity may be reduced when a resident moves out (subdivision 7b).

Exceptions the commissioner may approve include non-primary-residence foster care where at least 80 percent of residents are 55 or older, licenses needed for facility closures or community transitions, licenses for people needing hospital-level care, and certain customized living recipients until June 30, 2027 (subdivision 7c).

The commissioner determines the need for new foster care homes and community residential settings, considering local capacity and county board recommendations; applicants must say whether the location is the primary residence (subdivision 7d).

The commissioner may impose a discretionary moratorium of up to 24 months on new applications and added services when growth exceeds need, with 30 days' notice to legislative committees (subdivision 7a).
Reductions in licensed capacity require written notice, and the license holder may ask for reconsideration within 20 calendar days (subdivision 7d).
equityCheck: Check that the needs determination looks at capacity in rural counties and on or near Tribal lands, not only statewide totals.
Check that exceptions for people leaving institutions are used for people of every background, and track who is waiting for a setting.

policies.title: Medical Assistance spenddown for people with excess income (Minnesota Statutes 256B.056, subdivisions 5 and 5c)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Minnesota Statutes 256B.056 sets Medical Assistance eligibility rules. Subdivisions 5 and 5c explain the spenddown, which lets a person whose income is above the limit qualify by using medical expenses to bring countable income down to the standard. Waiver services require Medical Assistance, so the spenddown matters for people with disabilities whose income is over the limit. The Community-Based Services Manual spenddown page is based on these rules.
requires: A person with excess income qualifies when incurred medical expenses are more than the excess; those expenses are deducted to bring income down to the standard.

For people who are aged, blind or disabled, the excess income standard was 81 percent of the federal poverty guidelines; effective July 1, 2022, it is the standard in subdivision 4, paragraph (a), which allows income up to 100 percent of the guidelines.
The person chooses a one-month or a six-month budget period for deducting medical expenses.
A person on a one-month spenddown may pay the monthly amount in advance to stay continuously eligible; payment is due on or before the 20th of the month.

Room and board costs above the Medical Assistance room and board rate (81 percent of the poverty guideline for one person less the personal needs allowance) count as remedial care and may be used to meet a spenddown.
Income standards are adjusted each July 1 for the federal poverty guideline update, and spenddown enrollees have income reviewed every six months.
equityCheck: Check that people with income just over the limit, including workers with disabilities and people with Social Security income, are told about the spenddown and the advance-payment option in plain language.
Confirm the choice between a one-month and six-month budget period was explained and that the person picked what works for their income pattern.
Look at whether people lose waiver eligibility at six-month reviews because paperwork or notices were not in their language or format.
Compare spenddown use and churn by county and community to see where people are falling off Medical Assistance.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 245.825 Aversive and Deprivation Procedures; Licensed Facilities and Services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This statute directs the commissioner of human services to adopt rules on aversive and deprivation procedures in licensed facilities and services for people with developmental disabilities. It bans certain procedures outright and limits others to those the commissioner authorizes and monitors.
requires: The rules may not encourage or require aversive or deprivation procedures.
No procedure may restrict a person's normal access to nutritious food, drinking water, adequate ventilation, necessary medical care, ordinary hygiene, normal sleep or necessary clothing.
Faradic shock may not be used without a court order, and anyone receiving it must have a plan to reduce and end its use from the start.
People may not be denied ordinary access to legal counsel and next of kin.

The commissioner may designate a county case manager to authorize controlled procedures after review by the interdisciplinary team and internal review committee; use must be reported to the commissioner.
equityCheck: Any plan that limits food, sleep, clothing, hygiene or contact with family or a lawyer is prohibited; raise it at once.
Check that the person and their representative understand any approved procedure and how it will be reduced over time.
Review which people and settings have controlled procedures approved, and look for patterns by group.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 245.8251 Rules for Positive Support Strategies and Prohibitions and Limits on Restrictive Interventions
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This statute required the commissioner of human services to adopt the Positive Supports Rule by August 31, 2015. It applies the chapter 245D limits on emergency manual restraint and restrictive interventions to licensed facilities serving people with developmental disabilities, and it requires data reporting and an external review committee.
requires: The rules apply to facilities and services licensed under chapter 245D and to licensed facilities serving people with a developmental disability or related condition; child care is excluded.

Licensed facilities must report data on emergency manual restraint incidents and positive support transition plans in the format and frequency the commissioner sets; reports go to the commissioner and the Office of Ombudsman for Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities.
The commissioner must identify data elements with stakeholder input.
The rules must create an external program review committee, appointed by the commissioner, to monitor implementation and recommend policy changes.
equityCheck: Use the reported restraint data to compare providers and settings; ask what is behind high numbers.
Check that positive support transition plans are in place where required and are moving toward fewer restrictions.
Make sure people and families know they can contact the Ombudsman about restraint or restrictive interventions.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 245.91 to 245.97 Office of Ombudsman for Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: These sections create the Office of Ombudsman for Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities, an independent office appointed by the governor. The ombudsman takes complaints, reviews agency and provider actions, has access to facilities and records, and makes recommendations to promote the highest attainable standards of treatment, competence, efficiency and justice for people receiving services for mental illness, developmental disability or substance use disorder.
requires: The ombudsman may gather information about the decisions and acts of any agency, facility or program serving these people, including state divisions, county social service agencies, licensed residential and nonresidential programs and acute care inpatient facilities (245.91).
Anyone may file a complaint; there is no complaint fee; a client may not be punished or have treatment worsened for complaining, and the complainant's identity may be kept confidential (245.94).
The ombudsman gives priority to unusual deaths or injuries, emergency manual restraint reports and actions that may be unlawful, unfair, abusive or rights-violating.
Agencies, facilities and programs must notify the ombudsman within 24 hours of a client's death or serious injury, and emergency manual restraint must be reported under section 245D.061.

The ombudsman may enter and view premises, subpoena witnesses and documents, and gather client records (with consent where the client can give it); providers must respond to the ombudsman's recommendations and explain any they decline.
equityCheck: Give every person and family the Ombudsman's contact information at intake and whenever a restriction, restraint or serious incident occurs.
Check that complaint materials are available in the person's language and in accessible formats.
Look at whether complaints from some communities or settings are rare; that can mean people do not know they can complain.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 245A.042 Home and Community-Based Services; Additional Standards and Procedures
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This statute requires programs that provide certain home and community-based services to people with disabilities or people age 65 and older to be licensed under chapter 245A and to comply with chapters 245A and 245D, health care program rules and the federal waiver plan provider standards. Recent amendments add compliance education, an early licensing support team and limits on placing small residential settings next to each other.
requires: Applicants and license holders must show and keep verified compliance with chapters 245A and 245D, applicable health care program rules, and the provider standards in the federal waiver plans or the Alternative Care program (subd. 1).

The commissioner must offer licensing compliance education to providers licensed under both chapters 245A and 245D, and must give a list of legal resources to a license holder facing enforcement (subds. 5 and 6).

An early and often licensor and compliance team must help applicants, visit three months after an initial license takes effect, and make three unscheduled visits between months six and eighteen; it may issue a review report with recommendations (subd. 7).

Starting July 1, 2026, the commissioner may not authorize services in or license certain new small residential settings unless they meet heightened standards, and new settings may not sit on the same or an adjoining property as listed existing settings (subd. 8).
equityCheck: Colocation limits are meant to keep homes from becoming clusters; check that people are living in ordinary neighborhoods with access to community life.
Compliance education and the early support team can help small and culturally specific providers succeed; make sure they know about these supports.
Watch for regions where licensing delays leave people without a provider.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 245A.11 Special Conditions for Residential Programs
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This statute sets special rules for licensed residential programs. It protects the right of small programs to be in ordinary neighborhoods, limits the number of people in adult foster care and community residential settings, allows alternate overnight supervision with monitoring technology under strict conditions, and lists the rights of adult foster care residents.
requires: State policy is that zoning rules should not keep people from the benefits of normal residential neighborhoods; programs for six or fewer people are a permitted single-family use.

Adult foster care and community residential settings are limited to four beds, with a fifth bed allowed if everyone is 55 or older and has no serious and persistent mental illness or developmental disability, and variances up to five or six beds in listed situations such as emergency crisis services and disability respite (subd. 2a).

The commissioner may waive the requirement for a caregiver to be present overnight when the county recommends it, residents give informed consent and the plan is in each resident's plan; monitoring-technology licenses require written policies, response options within set times, posted notice and detailed informed consent, and a resident may not be removed for refusing electronic monitoring (subds. 7 to 7b).
Residents may choose roommates and each bedroom door must have a lock unless there is a documented health, safety or well-being reason (subd. 9).

Adult foster care residents must receive their rights at admission, including private phone use, uncensored mail, freedom to come and go, visitors, personal possessions, food access, cultural and religious observance, freedom from maltreatment and bias, and access to a grievance process; a right may be restricted only when necessary for safety, documented in the abuse prevention plan, least restrictive and reviewed to reduce the restriction (subd. 10).
Elderly Waiver customized living services may be terminated only for listed reasons with at least 30 days written notice that includes appeal rights (subd. 11).
equityCheck: Check that any restriction of a resident's rights is documented, necessary and reviewed, and look for homes where many residents have restrictions.
Confirm residents were told their rights in their own language and know how to file a grievance.
When overnight monitoring technology replaces staff, confirm each resident truly consented and understands the risks.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 245A.65 Maltreatment of Vulnerable Adults (license holder duties)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This statute sets what license holders that serve vulnerable adults must do to prevent and respond to maltreatment. It requires written policies, orientation for people served and for mandated reporters, internal reviews after a report, and program and individual abuse prevention plans.
requires: License holders must have written policies on suspected or alleged maltreatment, orient people served and mandated reporters to them, and post the policies and the common entry point phone number in a prominent place (subd. 1).
Each new person must be oriented to the reporting procedures within 24 hours of admission (up to 72 hours if a later orientation would benefit the person).

When the facility has reason to know a maltreatment report was made, it must complete an internal review within 30 calendar days and document a corrective action plan, available to the commissioner on request.

Each program must keep a program abuse prevention plan that assesses the people served, the building and the surrounding area, reviewed at least yearly, and an individual abuse prevention plan for each person, developed at the start of services and reviewed yearly (subd. 2).
Each new mandated reporter must receive orientation within 72 hours of first direct contact and yearly after that (subd. 3).
equityCheck: Check that the person's individual abuse prevention plan reflects their real vulnerabilities, including isolation, language barriers and dependence on a single caregiver.
Confirm reporting information was given to the person in a way they understand and that they know they can report without the provider's help.
Review internal reviews and corrective actions across providers to see whether the same issues recur.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 245D.03 Applicability and Effect (which services chapter 245D covers)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This statute says which home and community-based services must be licensed under chapter 245D. It divides them into basic support services, which provide assistance and supervision, and intensive support services, which add training, habilitation or treatment. It is the list the 2026 licensing moratorium refers to.
requires: Chapter 245D governs home and community-based services for people with disabilities and people age 65 and older.

Basic support services include in-home and out-of-home respite, adult companion services, 24-hour emergency assistance, personal emergency response, night supervision, homemaker services, individual community living support and individualized home supports without training.

Intensive support services include positive support, crisis respite and specialist services; semi-independent living and individualized home supports with training or family training; community residential services, family residential services, residential services for more than four people with developmental disabilities including intermediate care facilities, and life sharing; day support, day training and habilitation and prevocational services; employment exploration, development and support; and integrated community supports.

Some settings are exempt or partly exempt, such as foster care homes that provide no 245D services, homemaker providers licensed under chapter 144A, and intermediate care facility providers for listed sections.
The commissioner may grant variances except for listed sections, and providers may apply for program certification under section 245D.33.
equityCheck: Use this list to confirm a provider holds the right license for every service on a person's plan.
Employment and community living services are licensed services; check that they are offered, not only residential and day services.
Where a service type has no licensed provider nearby, document the gap and use the lead agency exception process during the moratorium.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 252.27 Children's Services; Parental Contribution
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This statute says who pays when a child with a developmental disability, physical disability or mental illness receives 24-hour care outside the home, including respite, in a facility licensed by the commissioner. It sets the county of financial responsibility and the parental contribution counties may collect.
requires: Costs are paid by the county of financial responsibility under chapter 256G; if the parents live outside Minnesota, the responsible agency in the child's home state pays first, then the parents if able, then the commissioner.

Parents or guardians are responsible for the county's cost of care up to the income and resources attributed to the child, excluding a clothing and personal needs allowance; payments go to the county that paid for the services.
A county may require full payment from parents who live outside Minnesota.
A county is not liable for services to the extent the child is eligible for health insurance benefits under the listed chapters.
Several subdivisions that set a separate parental fee schedule were repealed in 2024.
equityCheck: Explain any parental contribution clearly before placement so families are not surprised by bills.
Check that families with limited English or limited income understand the exceptions and can ask for review.
Look at whether out-of-home placements for children with disabilities are more common in some communities and what in-home supports were offered first.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 252.275 Semi-Independent Living Services for Persons with Developmental Disabilities
policies.summary: This statute creates a statewide program of semi-independent living services for adults with developmental disabilities so they can live as independently as possible in the community. The commissioner reimburses county boards for the services and for one-time living allowances.
requires: Eligible people are 18 or older, cannot function independently without these services, and are not at risk of placement in an intermediate care facility without less restrictive services.

Services include training and assistance in money management, meal preparation, shopping, personal hygiene and other skills needed to live in the community; skills should be taught in the settings where they are used, with community participation and choice in daily life (subd. 1a).
The commissioner reimburses county boards at 85 percent of eligible costs within caps, and may pay a one-time living allowance to secure and furnish a home when other public funds are not available.
Allocations are made by calendar year with a guaranteed county floor and quarterly reallocation of unspent funds; counties must report as the commissioner requires.
The commissioner may recover, suspend or withhold payments when a county or provider does not comply.
equityCheck: Check that people who are not on a waiver are told about this program as a way to get skills support.
Ask whether services are available in the person's language and whether they reach people in rural counties.
Compare county use of the allocation and ask why some counties leave funds unspent.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 252.28 Commissioner of Human Services; Duties (rules and licensing for developmental disability facilities)
policies.summary: This statute gives the commissioner of human services duties for residential and day facilities and services for people with developmental disabilities. It requires uniform rules and licensing standards, limits the concentration of residential facilities, and caps the size of new waiver-funded residential programs.
requires: The commissioner must set uniform rules and program standards for each type of residential and day facility or service and grant licenses under chapter 245A.

No new license may be granted if it would substantially contribute to an excessive concentration of community residential facilities in a town, city or county; the commissioner must consider population, land use, available services and existing facilities.

No new license may be granted for a residential program providing home and community-based waiver services to more than four people at one site, except in an emergency, and such emergency licenses are capped at 24 months.
The commissioner may not approve a determination of need that would result in two or more licenses for the same residential program at the same location.

The commissioner must adopt rules for decertifying intermediate care facility beds, encourage voluntary decertification and may not recommend involuntary decertification until appropriate services are available for affected residents.
equityCheck: The four-person limit supports small, home-like settings; check that larger settings are used only in true emergencies and for no longer than allowed.
Concentration limits are meant to keep people in ordinary neighborhoods; look at whether homes cluster in some communities.
When beds are decertified, confirm each resident has a planned community placement that fits their needs.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 252.282 Local System Needs Planning for Intermediate Care Facilities for Persons with Developmental Disabilities
programs: Intermediate Care Facilities for Persons with Developmental Disabilities
policies.summary: This statute requires host counties to plan for the service needs of people with developmental disabilities who live in intermediate care facilities. Counties gather consumer preferences and data, recommend closures, relocations or downsizing to the commissioner, and the commissioner contracts with providers for two-year periods.
requires: Host counties must run a planning process for each intermediate care facility, repeated by July 1 every two years and more often if needs change significantly.
Planning must use individual service plans, the community social services plan, waiting lists, licensing and survey results and maltreatment reports.

Counties submit recommendations to the commissioner on the same two-year schedule; certain closures, relocations and downsizings must be submitted by July 1 before the contract year or at least 90 days before the change.
The commissioner must ensure ongoing systemic review of these facilities and contract with providers for two-year periods.
The statute does not apply to semi-independent living services or residential-based habilitation funded as home and community-based services.
equityCheck: Make sure the preferences of residents themselves, not only providers and families, are gathered in the planning process, with interpreters where needed.
When a facility closes or downsizes, check that each resident gets a real choice of community options.
Compare planning outcomes across counties to see where people stay in facilities longer.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 252.291 Limitation on Determination of Need (intermediate care facility moratorium)
programs: Intermediate Care Facilities for Persons with Developmental Disabilities
policies.summary: This statute limits new intermediate care facilities for people with developmental disabilities and increases in their capacity. It caps the total number of certified beds, sets narrow exceptions, and gives the commissioner duties to plan for community alternatives and monitor the moratorium's effects.
requires: The commissioner must deny determinations of need and refuse licenses for new intermediate care facilities or capacity increases, with listed exceptions; total certified beds in community facilities and state hospitals are capped at 7,000.

A new community facility for six or fewer people may be approved only through an approved request for proposal, for identified people with serious behavioral or physical or sensory impairments whose needs cannot be met by alternatives or existing facilities.

The commissioner must set county utilization targets, define services including respite care, provide technical assistance, set up client tracking and develop a biennial state plan with bed quotas, alternatives and decertification targets.
The commissioner must monitor the moratorium's effects by geographic area and report to the legislature each year.
Specific exceptions exist for named replacement projects in Ramsey and Nicollet counties.
equityCheck: The moratorium exists to move services into the community; when a facility placement is proposed, confirm that community options were actually tried.
Check geographic data on facility use so people in some regions are not more likely to be placed in facilities.
Ask whether people in facilities are told about community options each year.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 252.32 Family Support Program (Family Support Grant)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This statute creates the Family Support Grant, a county-run program of cash or voucher grants for families raising a child with a disability at home. The grant pays for items and services related to the child's disability that help the family delay or prevent out-of-home placement.
requires: The dependent must be under 25 and certified as a person with a disability; families receiving certain waiver services, personal care assistance or a consumer support grant are not eligible; families with adjusted gross income of $60,000 or more (adjusted yearly for inflation) are ineligible unless they show extreme hardship.
Grants may be monthly or lump-sum, as cash, voucher or direct county payment to a vendor; the maximum is $250 per dependent per month or $3,000 per state fiscal year, subject to available funds.

Purchases must be over and above normal caregiving costs, directly related to the disability, provided in the least restrictive environment and not covered by other public or private funds; allowable items include adaptive or one-on-one swimming lessons for children under 12 at higher drowning risk.

Counties must submit a management plan, determine eligibility, approve items, issue grants, notify families of appeal rights, report quarterly (including denied and waitlisted families) and coordinate with other programs.
Denials, suspensions or terminations may be appealed under Minnesota Statutes section 256.045; each county has a guaranteed floor of 95 percent of its prior-year allocation.
equityCheck: Check that families who speak languages other than English know about the grant and can apply without an advocate.
Review waitlists and denials by county and group, and ask why some counties leave funds unspent.
Make sure the income limit and hardship exception are explained, since families just over the limit may still qualify.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 252.41 to 252.46 Day Services for Adults with Disabilities
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: These sections govern day services for adults with disabilities, including day support, prevocational, structured day, adult day and day training and habilitation services. They define the services, set service principles, and assign duties to the commissioner, lead agency boards and vendors, and give the commissioner authority to set day training and habilitation rates.
requires: Day services are supervision, training, assistance, support, facility-based work-related activities or community-integrated activities designed under the person's support plan to help the person reach the highest possible level of independence, productivity and community integration; they must be provided by a licensed vendor (252.41).

Service principles: services should fit the person's age in the least restrictive setting, people whose plans authorize work should take part alongside people without disabilities and be paid comparable wages, and services should be in settings the public uses and follow everyday patterns of community life (252.42).
The commissioner must determine need for day services, adopt rules, make interagency agreements, monitor cost and effectiveness and give technical help to lead agencies and vendors (252.43).
The lead agency board must authorize day services according to the support plan, ensure transportation is provided or arranged efficiently, and monitor cost and effectiveness (252.44).

Vendors must deliver the type and amount of service authorized in the support plan, design services to meet assigned outcomes, provide or arrange transportation, and comply with state and federal law (252.45).
The commissioner sets rates for all day training and habilitation services and related transportation, after consulting community partners (252.46).
equityCheck: Ask whether the person was offered employment exploration and community-integrated options before facility-based day services.
Check that people who work through day services are paid comparable wages as the principles require.
Look at whether people in rural areas have transportation to day services and whether day options reflect the person's culture and interests.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 252.41 to 252.46 Day Services for Adults with Disabilities

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 252.50 State-Operated Programs
policies.summary: This statute keeps two provisions on funding for state-operated community programs for people with developmental disabilities. Most of its former subdivisions were moved to chapter 246C or repealed in 2024 and 2025. The remaining parts let the commissioner use enhanced waiver funds and amend the waiver to serve people in regional treatment centers.
requires: Within appropriations, the commissioner may use enhanced waivered services funds under the Developmental Disabilities Waiver to move people to state-operated community programs and to private facilities (subd. 2a).

The commissioner may amend the Medical Assistance home and community-based waiver and develop special waiver procedures to target services to people currently in state regional treatment centers (subd. 3).
Subdivisions on state-operated services organization were renumbered into chapter 246C and sections 246.585 to 246.65.
equityCheck: When enhanced funds are used to move a person from a regional treatment center, check that private and community options were offered alongside state-operated ones.
Confirm the person's preferred location, near family and community, was considered.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 252.50 State-Operated Programs

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 252.54 Statewide Disability Employment Technical Assistance Center
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This 2023 statute directs the commissioner to create a statewide technical assistance center that helps programs, people and families support people with disabilities in finding meaningful, competitive employment in integrated settings.
requires: The center helps provider businesses change their models so people keep access to employment and day services.
It provides training on new, promising and emerging practices and keeps a clearinghouse of high-quality materials.
It gives direct technical assistance to programs to encourage innovation and progress.
It builds partnerships and mentorship among programs, people and families to help people move into competitive, integrated jobs.
equityCheck: Ask whether providers in your area have used the center's help to add employment services, especially in rural areas.
Check that materials and training reach families and self-advocates in languages other than English.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 252.55 Lead Agency Employment First Capacity Building Grants
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This 2023 statute creates a grant program to strengthen lead agencies' ability to help people with disabilities consider, explore and keep competitive, integrated employment.
requires: Grants may add resources and staff to help people and families understand employment options and navigate services.
Grants may pilot and evaluate new approaches to help people with disabilities and their families reach competitive, integrated employment.
Other activities may be funded with the commissioner's approval.
equityCheck: Check whether your lead agency has applied for or used these grants and whether the help reaches people with the most significant disabilities.
Look at employment outcomes by county, race and disability type to decide where capacity building is most needed.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 256.021 Vulnerable Adult Maltreatment Review Panel
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This statute creates a state panel that reviews how lead investigative agencies resolved reports of maltreatment of vulnerable adults when a vulnerable adult or interested person asks for a review. The panel meets quarterly and can require an agency to reconsider its finding.
requires: Panel members include the commissioners of human services and health or designees, the ombudsmen for long-term care and for mental health and developmental disabilities or designees, a Board on Aging member and a county human services administrators representative.
The panel considers review requests under section 626.557, subdivision 9d at its next quarterly meeting and reviews the investigation memorandum and other data.

Within 30 days the panel tells the agency and requester whether it agrees with the disposition or whether the agency must reconsider; if reconsideration is required, the agency must respond within 30 days with a detailed rationale.
Panel data created or received during a review are private data on individuals.
equityCheck: Tell people and families who disagree with a maltreatment finding that they can ask for a panel review, and help them make the request.
Check whether review requests come from all communities or only from people with advocates.
