policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 256.045 Administrative and Judicial Review of Human Services Matters (appeals and fair hearings)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This statute gives people the right to a state fair hearing when a county, Tribal Nation, health plan or the department denies, reduces or ends services or makes other listed decisions. It sets deadlines, hearing rules, case management appeal steps, continued services during appeal and review in district court.
requires: A person may appeal when assistance, medical care or social services are denied, reduced, terminated or incorrectly paid, and in other listed situations such as maltreatment findings, service termination notices and waiver or rate exception denials (subd. 3).
A written hearing request is due within 30 days of written notice, or within 90 days with good cause, which the appellant must show.

Hearings may be by telephone or video, but must be in person if a party or witness has a disability that would impair taking part by video; parties get at least five days notice, may be represented by anyone they choose, may see the case file and cross-examine witnesses, and may be reimbursed for transportation, child care and other reasonable costs (subd. 4).

For case management disputes, the person must first request a conciliation conference with the county, then may request a hearing if the county does not act within 30 days or within 90 days after the conference; a temporary order may prevent discharge from a residential or day program (subd. 4a).
Ordered assistance or services must continue while an appeal is pending, except in limited cases, and the agency may recover payments if the person is later found ineligible (subd. 10).

The human services judge recommends an order based on all relevant evidence; a party may seek reconsideration within 30 days and may appeal to district court within 30 days of the order (subds. 5 and 7).
equityCheck: Every notice of action must explain appeal rights and the 30-day deadline in plain language and in the person's language; check that this happens.
Offer an in-person hearing and an interpreter when the person's disability or language would make a phone or video hearing unfair.
Track appeal rates by county and group; very low appeal rates can mean people do not know how to appeal.
Remind people that services usually continue during an appeal if they appeal in time.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 256.045 Administrative and Judicial Review of Human Services Matters

relatedSources.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Appeals

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 256.477 Self-Advocacy Grants
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This statute directs the commissioner to fund a statewide self-advocacy network for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities and to fund subgrants for outreach to people living or working in institutional settings. The grant recipient must be governed by people with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
requires: The statewide self-advocacy network informs people of their rights in areas such as employment, housing, transportation and voting, and educates the public about civil and human rights.
The network funds and supports local self-advocacy groups, connects them, trains a statewide peer-to-peer mentor network, holds outreach events and conferences and runs an annual leadership program.

Subgrants fund outreach to people in institutional settings about community options, with peer-led skill training in six regions on housing, employment, education, transportation, state reform initiatives including the Olmstead Plan and federal home and community-based services rules, and informed choice.
A grant recipient may use part of the grant for administration and operating costs as the commissioner sets.
equityCheck: Connect people you serve, especially people in facilities and segregated settings, with the self-advocacy network and peer training.
Check that self-advocacy outreach reaches rural regions, Tribal Nations and communities whose first language is not English.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 256.477 Self-Advocacy Grants

relatedSources.title: Minnesota Statutes 256.4772 Minnesota Inclusion Initiative Grant

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes 256.4772 Minnesota Inclusion Initiative Grant
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This 2021 statute creates a grant program that funds projects by self-advocacy groups to increase community inclusion of people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. A fiscal host and an advisory committee of self-advocates, advocacy organizations and department staff run the program.
requires: The commissioner contracts with a public or private fiscal host, chosen through a request for proposals, to manage the money and set grant guidelines.
The fiscal host forms an advisory committee of self-advocates, nonprofit advocacy organizations and department staff to review applications and award grants.

Projects must have person-centered goals and address barriers to inclusion, such as workforce participation, transportation, voting access, accessible housing, accessibility under the Americans with Disabilities Act, collaboration among groups and public education on civil and human rights.
Grant recipients report to the advisory committee, which reports activities and outcomes to the commissioner.
equityCheck: Share grant opportunities with self-advocacy groups in Greater Minnesota and in communities of color and immigrant communities, not only established metro groups.
Look at where funded projects are located and who they reach.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 256.4772 Minnesota Inclusion Initiative Grant

relatedSources.title: Minnesota Statutes 256.477 Self-Advocacy Grants

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes chapter 245A, Human Services Licensing
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Chapter 245A is the Human Services Licensing Act. It says who must be licensed, how to apply, what records and systems are required, and how the Department of Human Services issues correction orders, conditional licenses, sanctions and hearings. It includes added standards for home and community-based services licenses and rules on maltreatment of vulnerable adults and minors.
requires: Section 245A.03 says who must be licensed and holds the licensing moratorium provisions for foster care and community residential settings.
Section 245A.042 sets additional standards and procedures for home and community-based services licenses.
Sections 245A.06 to 245A.08 cover correction orders, conditional licenses, sanctions and hearings.
Section 245A.16 sets standards for county and private agencies that perform licensing functions.
Section 245A.65 covers maltreatment of vulnerable adults, and section 245A.211 prohibits prone restraint.
Sections 245A.70 to 245A.75 cover remote adult day services.
equityCheck: Check whether licensing requirements are explained in ways small and culturally specific providers can follow.
Ask whether sanctions and conditional licenses fall unevenly on providers serving particular communities.
Use licensing data by county to see where licensed capacity is thin.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, chapter 245A, Human Services Licensing

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes chapter 245C, Human Services Background Studies
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Chapter 245C sets the background study rules for people who work in licensed programs and in home and community-based services. It says who must be studied, when, what information is checked, which crimes or conduct disqualify a person, and how a person can ask for reconsideration, a set-aside or a variance.
requires: Sections 245C.03 and 245C.04 say which individuals must have a background study and when it must occur.
Section 245C.12 covers background studies for Tribal organizations; section 245C.34 covers adoption and child foster care studies for Tribal organizations.
Sections 245C.14 to 245C.16 cover disqualification, disqualifying crimes or conduct and the person's risk of harm.
Sections 245C.18 and 245C.19 require removing a disqualified person from direct contact and ending affiliation when notified.
Sections 245C.21 to 245C.30 allow reconsideration, set-asides, variances and hearings.
equityCheck: Check that workers who are disqualified understand how to ask for reconsideration or a set-aside, in their language.
Ask whether disqualifications fall more heavily on workers from communities with higher rates of past criminal justice contact and whether risk of harm reviews are used.
Watch for background study delays that keep self-directed participants from hiring the worker they chose.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, chapter 245C, Human Services Background Studies

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D, Home and Community-Based Services Standards
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Chapter 245D sets the licensing standards for providers of home and community-based services. It covers service recipient rights, health services and psychotropic medication use, protection standards and emergency use of manual restraints, service planning and delivery, staffing, records, policies, integrated community supports and facility standards for community residential and day services settings.
requires: Section 245D.04 lists service recipient rights, and section 245D.06 sets protection standards with section 245D.061 on emergency use of manual restraints.
Sections 245D.07 and 245D.071 require service planning and delivery, with added requirements for intensive support services.
Section 245D.09 sets staffing and training standards, and section 245D.095 sets record requirements.
Section 245D.12 covers integrated community supports and section 245D.13 covers out-of-home respite for children.
Sections 245D.21 to 245D.31 set facility standards for community residential settings and day services, including remote overnight supervision in section 245D.261.
equityCheck: Check that rights notices and service plans are given in the person's language and in accessible formats.
Review emergency manual restraint reports by provider and population for patterns.
Ask whether staff training includes cultural responsiveness and communication supports.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, chapter 245D, Home and Community-Based Services Standards

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes chapter 252, Services for Persons with Developmental Disabilities
programs: intermediate care facilities for persons with developmental disabilities
policies.summary: Chapter 252 holds state laws on services for people with developmental disabilities. Current sections cover semi-independent living services, the family support program, intermediate care facility planning and downsizing, day services principles, lead agency board responsibilities, vendor duties and payment rates, state-operated programs, and employment technical assistance and Employment First capacity grants.
requires: Section 252.275 governs semi-independent living services and section 252.32 governs the family support program.

Sections 252.28 and 252.282 set commissioner duties and local system needs planning for intermediate care facilities; sections 252.291 to 252.295 cover need determination, conversion, emergency relocation, downsizing and a licensing exception.
Sections 252.41 to 252.46 set definitions, service principles, commissioner duties, lead agency board responsibilities, vendor duties and payment rates for day services.
Section 252.54 creates the statewide disability employment technical assistance center and section 252.55 creates lead agency Employment First capacity building grants.
equityCheck: Check that family support and semi-independent living options are explained to families in their language.
Ask whether Employment First capacity grants reach counties and regions with the fewest employment options.
Look at who is placed in facilities versus community settings by region and race.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, chapter 252, Services for Persons with Developmental Disabilities

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes chapter 252A, Developmental Disability Protection (public guardianship)
programs: Public guardianship for persons with developmental disabilities
policies.summary: Chapter 252A sets up public guardianship for adults with developmental disabilities when no other suitable guardian is available. It covers nominating the commissioner of the Department of Human Services as guardian, the comprehensive evaluation, court petitions, notice, counsel and hearings, the public guardian's powers and duties, annual review, and modification or restoration of legal capacity.
requires: Section 252A.03 covers nomination of the commissioner as guardian, and section 252A.04 requires a comprehensive evaluation.
Sections 252A.05 to 252A.101 cover petitions, filing the evaluation, notice of hearing, appointment of counsel and the hearing.
Section 252A.111 sets the powers and duties of the public guardian, and section 252A.12 says appointment is not a finding of incompetency.
Section 252A.16 requires annual review, and section 252A.19 covers modification of guardianship and restoration to legal capacity.
equityCheck: Check that less restrictive options, such as supported decision-making, were considered before public guardianship.
Ask whether the person had counsel and whether the hearing was accessible in their language and communication style.
Use the annual review to ask whether guardianship can be narrowed or ended.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, chapter 252A, Developmental Disability Protection

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes chapter 256B, Medical Assistance for Needy Persons (table of sections)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Chapter 256B is Minnesota's Medical Assistance law. Its table of sections lists about 280 sections, many repealed or renumbered, and links to the full text of each. It holds the state authority for the disability waivers, home care, personal care assistance, Community First Services and Supports, Alternative Care, Essential Community Supports and provider payment rules.
requires: Section 256B.49 is the authority for the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waivers; section 256B.092 covers the Developmental Disabilities Waiver.
Sections 256B.4905 to 256B.4914 cover the policy statement, consumer-directed community supports, providers and payment, and rate setting; section 256B.492 covers settings.
Sections 256B.0651 to 256B.0659 cover home care and personal care assistance; sections 256B.85 to 256B.851 cover Community First Services and Supports.
Sections 256B.0911 and 256B.0913 cover long-term care consultation and Alternative Care; section 256B.0922 covers Essential Community Supports.
equityCheck: Use the table of sections to find the exact section before citing a rule, and check the history line for recent changes.
When a section says a change takes effect only upon federal approval, confirm whether approval has been obtained before applying it.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, chapter 256B, Medical Assistance for Needy Persons

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes chapter 256S, Medical Assistance Elderly Waiver
policies.summary: Chapter 256S is the state law for the Elderly Waiver. It covers administration by Tribes, eligibility, assessments, case management, support plans, covered services such as adult day services and individual community living supports, termination of services, rates, monthly case mix budget caps and customized living policy and rates.
requires: Section 256S.03 covers administration by Tribes; sections 256S.05 to 256S.10 cover eligibility, assessments, case management administration, provider standards, activities and support plans.
Sections 256S.12 to 256S.14 cover adult day services, individual community living supports and termination of services.
Sections 256S.15 to 256S.19 cover service rates, authorization, excluded costs and monthly case mix budget caps, with section 256S.191 on budget and rate exceptions for high-need participants.
Sections 256S.20 to 256S.205 cover customized living policy, rates and limits; sections 256S.21 to 256S.215 cover rate setting.
equityCheck: Check that people turning 65 on a disability waiver are told how their services and budget may change under the Elderly Waiver.
Ask whether the budget exception for high-need participants was considered.
Compare customized living and in-home service access across regions.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, chapter 256S, Medical Assistance Elderly Waiver

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 245A.03, Who Must Be Licensed (licensing moratorium and temporary moratorium authority)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Section 245A.03 says who needs a Department of Human Services license and contains the moratorium on new foster care and community residential settings. In 2026 the old moratorium in subdivision 7 was repealed and replaced by subdivisions 7b to 7d. Subdivision 7a lets the commissioner declare a temporary moratorium of up to 24 months when license applications grow faster than needed capacity.
requires: Subdivision 7a allows a discretionary temporary moratorium on initial licenses or added services for up to 24 months, targeted by region or service, with 30 days' notice to legislative committees and posted exception criteria.

Subdivision 7b bars initial licenses for child foster care, adult foster care at a location that is not the license holder's primary residence, community residential settings and certain children's residential treatment, with listed exemptions.
Counties must immediately tell the licensing division when an adult resident moves out of a non-primary-residence foster home or community residential setting.
Subdivision 7c lists exceptions, including one available until June 30, 2027, for customized living settings operating on or before June 30, 2026.
equityCheck: Check whether moratorium exceptions are used to add capacity in regions and communities that lack it, not only where providers already are.
Ask how a temporary moratorium would affect people on waiting lists in your county before supporting it.
Track whether people moving out of settings are reported so capacity is reused fairly.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 245A.03, Who Must Be Licensed

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256.4776, Parent-to-Parent Peer Support
policies.summary: This law requires the commissioner of the Department of Human Services to give a grant to a Minnesota member of Parent to Parent USA. The grant pays for a statewide peer support program that matches parents of children with disabilities or special health care needs with trained support parents.
requires: The grant goes to a program that runs statewide and serves diverse cultures and geographic areas.
The program must reach out to parents of newly identified children and parents facing changes in care.
Support parents and parent staff must complete Parent to Parent USA training.
Grant money may be used only for the peer support program.
The grantee must report to the commissioner by January 15 each year with measurable outcomes, such as families served and support parents trained.
equityCheck: Check whether outreach reaches families in every region, including rural areas and Tribal communities, not only the metro area.
Ask what languages and cultural communities the support parents represent and whether interpreters are available.
Look at the annual report data to see which families were served and who may be missing.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256.4776, Parent-to-Parent Peer Support

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256.478, Transition to Community Initiative
policies.summary: This law sets up grants that help people move to or stay in the least restrictive community setting when Medical Assistance or other funding cannot pay for what they need. It covers people who are not eligible for Medical Assistance and people who need goods, supports or services that Medical Assistance does not cover.
requires: Grantees must use person-centered planning and informed choice, with accessible written information.
A person must show that current services cannot meet needs that could be met in the community with support.
The person must also meet one of four criteria, such as meeting waiver criteria under sections 256B.092 or 256B.49, or facing a delayed discharge from a hospital, residential or secure facility.
Grant funds may expand access to home and community-based services, support families and reduce emergency department use.
The program is evaluated on outcomes such as faster discharges, housing stability and living in the least restrictive setting.
equityCheck: Check that people who are not eligible for Medical Assistance, including people with immigration or income barriers, learn about this option.
Make sure written information is offered in the person's language and in accessible formats.
Review who receives grants by region and by facility to see whether some communities are left out.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256.478, Transition to Community Initiative

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256.4825, Report Regarding Programs and Services for People with Disabilities
policies.summary: This law lets three disability organizations send an annual report to the Legislature by January 15 on how well state disability policies and goals are being met. It names employment, transportation, housing, education, quality assurance, consumer direction, access and health as areas to cover.
requires: The report may be submitted by the Minnesota State Council on Disability, the Minnesota Consortium for Citizens with Disabilities and The Arc of Minnesota.
The report must describe existing state policies and goals for disability programs and include data showing whether they are being met.
The commissioner of the Department of Human Services, the Direct Care and Treatment executive board and other state agencies must cooperate and share existing published information.
equityCheck: When sharing data for this report, check whether it can be broken down by race, language, disability type and region.
Ask whether the measures reflect outcomes for people who are often left out, such as people in rural areas or people who do not speak English.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256.4825, Report Regarding Programs and Services for People with Disabilities

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256.975, Minnesota Board on Aging
policies.summary: This law creates the Minnesota Board on Aging and sets its duties. For disability services, the key parts are the Senior LinkAge Line, which partners with the Disability Hub, and the rules for screening people before they are admitted to a Medical Assistance-certified nursing facility.
requires: The Senior LinkAge Line gives long-term care options counseling and is the designated Aging and Disability Resource Center, working with the Disability Hub.
People must be screened before admission to a Medicaid-certified nursing facility; people with a mental illness or developmental disability need added evaluation by qualified professionals.
A person under 65 who was screened only by phone must be referred for an in-person assessment.
The Department of Human Services funds the Disability Hub for follow-up with people under 60 after screening.
Nursing facilities must tell residents about their right to long-term care consultation, and hospitals must refer at-risk older adults.

The law allows assessments by a county, Tribe or managed care organization under contract with the Department of Human Services, and calls for a Tribal-based service system for Native American elders.
equityCheck: Check that people under 65 who enter a nursing facility get the in-person assessment and the community options they are entitled to.
Ask whether options counseling is offered in the person's language and in accessible formats.
Look at referral data by county and region to see where follow-up after screening is weak.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256.975, Minnesota Board on Aging

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.057, subdivision 9, Employed Persons with Disabilities
programs: Medical Assistance for Employed Persons with Disabilities
policies.summary: This subdivision lets a working person with a disability keep Medical Assistance even when earnings or assets would otherwise make them ineligible. The person pays a monthly premium based on income and family size. County agencies decide eligibility and premiums.
requires: The person must be employed with more than $65 in earned income (or receive unemployment or family and medical leave benefits that began while enrolled) and meet the disability definition apart from earnings or assets.

Everyone pays a premium of at least $35, on a sliding scale from 1 percent of income at 100 percent of poverty to 7.5 percent at 300 percent or more, plus 0.5 percent of unearned income; American Indians as defined in federal rule are exempt from the premium.
A person who loses a job through no fault of their own, or is temporarily unable to work for medical reasons, may keep coverage up to four months.
Enrollees must report income and household changes within 30 days; missed premiums can end coverage unless there is good cause.
The commissioner pays the Medicare Part B premium for enrollees with income at or below 200 percent of poverty.
equityCheck: Check that people learn about this option before they turn down work or extra hours out of fear of losing coverage.
Make sure premium notices and change-reporting rules are explained in plain language and in the person's language.
Watch for people dropped for nonpayment and ask whether a good cause review or installment plan was offered.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.057, Eligibility Requirements for Special Categories

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0651, Home Care Services
policies.summary: This law defines Medical Assistance home care services and lists which ones are covered and which are not. It also gives the commissioner of the Department of Human Services the job of approving services, overseeing providers and running quality assurance.
requires: Covered services include nursing, home care nursing, home health, personal care assistance, supervision by a qualified professional and face-to-face assessments by county public health nurses.
Services in nursing facilities, hospitals or intermediate care facilities, services covered by Medicare or other insurance, and services already in a residential daily rate are generally not covered.
The commissioner decides medical necessity, cost-effectiveness and the amount, scope and duration of services.
Providers that do not take Medicare must refer dual-eligible recipients to Medicare providers when Medicare should pay.
The commissioner must run ongoing quality assurance, may demand proof of provider standards and can suspend or end enrollment.
equityCheck: Check whether home care providers are available in the person's area and in the person's language.
Ask whether cost-effectiveness decisions account for the person's access to informal support, which differs by family and culture.
Review consumer survey results and complaints by region and population.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0651, Home Care Services

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0652, Authorization and Review of Home Care Services
policies.summary: This law sets how Medical Assistance home care services are authorized and reviewed. It gives timelines, limits for each type of service, rules for temporary and foster care settings, and the right to keep services during an appeal.
requires: Authorization must be issued within 30 days after a complete request, assessment and service plan.
Authorizations last no more than 12 months; reassessment requests are due at least 60 days before they end, and amounts carry over when a person changes providers or health plans.
Personal care assistance amounts depend on a home care rating with added time for critical dependencies, complex health needs and behaviors.
Temporary services may be approved for up to 45 days; each year a person may get two face-to-face assessments, one service update and up to nine skilled nurse visits without authorization.
A person who appeals a reduction may usually keep services during the appeal, and notices must explain the reduction and its reasons.
Exceptions to prior authorization exist for emergencies, retroactive eligibility, third-party denials, agency errors and temporary disenrollment from managed care.
equityCheck: Check that reduction notices are clear, timely and in the person's language so the right to appeal is real.
Watch for delays past the 30-day authorization timeline and whether they fall more on some counties or communities.
Ask whether the home care rating captured behaviors and health needs fairly, including for people whose first language is not English.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0652, Authorization and Review of Home Care Services

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0654, Home Care Nursing
policies.summary: This law covers home care nursing, which is ongoing hourly nursing in the home ordered by a physician, advanced practice registered nurse or physician assistant. It sets assessment, care plan and authorization rules, allows shared nursing for two people, and lets certain family members be paid under hardship criteria.
requires: Services need a registered nurse assessment on a state form, a practitioner order, a care plan reviewed at least every 60 days and commissioner authorization.
One nurse may serve two people in the same setting if the agency offers the option and the person agrees; the person can withdraw at any time.

Parents of minors, family foster parents, spouses and legal guardians may be paid for extraordinary nursing care under hardship criteria, limited to the lesser of 50 percent of approved hours or 8 hours a day, up to 40 hours a week.
Payment is barred if the caregiver fails a background check, the care is unsafe or orders are not followed.
Rates are adjusted each year to track the federal home health market basket index.
equityCheck: Check that families know about the hardship option and that it is explained in their language.
Ask whether nursing agencies serve the person's area, especially in rural and Tribal communities, before shared care is proposed as the only option.
Make sure the choice to share a nurse is truly voluntary and not pushed because of staffing shortages.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0654, Home Care Nursing

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0658, Housing Access Grants
policies.summary: This law lets the commissioner of the Department of Human Services award competitive grants to public and private agencies that help people with disabilities find and keep housing. The grants pay for hands-on help such as viewing units, filling out applications and setting up a home.
requires: Grants are awarded through a competitive process to public and private agencies.
An individual with a disability includes people who are aged, blind or disabled under Social Security Act criteria and people in certain General Assistance categories.

Allowed uses include checking housing suitability, visiting units with the person, completing applications and leases, meeting landlords, applying for rental assistance, budgeting and getting furniture and household goods.
equityCheck: Check whether grantees serve every region of the state and whether rural areas have a provider.
Ask whether help is offered in the person's language and whether landlords in the area are accessible to people with disabilities.
Look at who gets served by race, disability type and age to see who is missing.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0658, Housing Access Grants

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0659, Personal Care Assistance Program
policies.summary: This law is the main rule for the personal care assistance program under Medical Assistance. It says who is eligible, how needs are assessed, what personal care assistants and qualified professionals must do, and what provider agencies must have in place. It also sets rules for shared services, flexible use of hours and the enhanced rate for people with high needs.
requires: Assessments must be in person, usually by a county or contracted public health nurse, at least once a year or after a significant change, and within 30 days of a request.
Eligibility is based on dependency in activities of daily living, complex health-related needs or behavior that needs help at least four times a week, with special limits for children.
Each person gets a service plan and a care plan; agencies must make a reasonable effort to honor a request for a same-gender assistant.
Personal care assistants must work through an enrolled agency, pass a background study, complete training and keep daily time sheets; a 310-hour monthly cap applies.
Up to three recipients may share an assistant; hours can be used flexibly within six-month spans; an enhanced rate applies for people needing ten or more hours a day.
Agencies must carry surety and fidelity bonds and insurance, and a terminated agency is barred from re-enrolling for two years.
equityCheck: Check that assessments happen within 30 days in every county and that interpreters are used when needed.
Ask whether the person was told about the choice option and same-gender preference in their language.
Watch for behavior-based needs being under-counted for people whose communication differs from the assessor's expectations.
Review access to agencies in rural and Tribal areas, where fewer enrolled providers may exist.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0659, Personal Care Assistance Program

relatedSources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.85, Community First Services and Supports

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0711, Quality Self-Directed Services Workforce
policies.summary: This law protects a participant's right to choose their own individual provider in self-directed programs and sets the commissioner's duties toward that workforce. It ties pay, benefits, orientation, training and a public registry to the state's bargaining duties with the workers' exclusive representative.
requires: Covered programs must let participants and their representatives choose individual providers, even where section 256B.0659 says otherwise.
Participants who do not choose or cannot use an individual provider may get similar services from agency employees.
The commissioner may set pay, payment terms and benefits, require orientation within three months of hire, provide training and keep a public registry of individual providers.
These powers are subject to the state's duty to meet and negotiate under chapter 179A and any agreement with the exclusive representative.
The commissioner must produce a monthly list of individual providers paid in the prior six months, with limits on its contents and sharing.
equityCheck: Check that participants know they can hire their own provider, including a family member or someone from their own community or language group.
Ask whether the registry and training reach workers in rural areas and in languages other than English.
Watch for people steered to agency services because self-direction was not explained.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0711, Quality Self-Directed Services Workforce

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.073, Electronic Visit Verification
programs: Early Intensive Developmental and Behavioral Intervention
policies.summary: This law sets up electronic visit verification for Medical Assistance services, as required by the federal 21st Century Cures Act. Providers must record visits electronically using the free state system or an approved third-party system, and claims that cannot be matched to visit data may face action.
requires: The commissioner must make the system administratively and financially reasonable, protect access to services, prevent fraud, and offer training and a free state-provided system.
Providers may use the state system or an approved third-party system connected to the data aggregator; providers who cannot connect must use the state system.
Providers must enroll, keep accurate records and a current worker list, give the commissioner and managed care organizations access, and train workers.
Visits must be recorded at the time of service with start and end times; manual visits do not comply until confirmed under commissioner processes.
Third-party vendor responsibilities apply starting January 1, 2027, or upon federal approval, with July 1, 2027, for early intensive developmental and behavioral intervention.
equityCheck: Check that workers without smartphones or reliable internet, including in rural areas, have a way to record visits.
Ask whether training and system instructions are available in the languages workers speak.
Watch for claim denials that fall on small or self-directed employers because of system access problems.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.073, Electronic Visit Verification

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0911, Long-Term Care Consultation Services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This law is the authority for long-term care consultation and the MnCHOICES assessment. It defines lead agencies, which include counties, Tribes and health plans under contract, and sets assessor certification, assessment timelines, remote reassessment rules, support planning, informed choice, the person's right to decide and a public dashboard of assessment timeliness.
requires: A lead agency is a county that administers these services, or a Tribe or health plan under contract with the commissioner; lead agencies must use MnCHOICES certified assessors and have enough of them to meet timelines.
Certified assessors must meet education or licensure requirements and recertify every three years; a Tribal Nation may set its own qualifications for its certified assessors.
An assessment must begin within 20 working days of a request and is generally in person; the assessment summary and support plan must be completed within 60 days of the visit.
Reassessments are usually yearly; remote reassessments by video or phone are allowed within program limits, with informed consent, and the person may refuse at any time.

At reassessment, assessors must offer people in certain residential or day settings the option of alternative housing, employment services or self-directed services; the person makes the final decision on placement, living arrangements, day versus employment services and self-direction.
Providers and others with a financial interest generally may not take part in the assessment; the commissioner publishes assessment completion data by lead agency at least twice a year.
equityCheck: Check that interpreters and communication supports were used in the assessment and that the person's own goals were recorded.
Ask whether a remote reassessment was the person's informed choice and not the agency's convenience.
Use the public dashboard to compare assessment timeliness across lead agencies.
Confirm that alternatives to residential and day settings were offered at every reassessment.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0911, Long-Term Care Consultation Services

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0913, Alternative Care Program
policies.summary: This law governs Alternative Care, a state-funded program of home and community-based services for people 65 and older who need nursing facility level of care but are not yet eligible for Medical Assistance. Counties and contracted Tribes act as lead agencies, authorize services and manage a yearly allocation.
requires: A person must be 65 or older, need nursing facility level of care, be a United States citizen or national, and would qualify for Medical Assistance within 135 days of nursing facility admission.

Covered services include adult day services, home care, personal care, case management, respite, home-delivered meals, transportation, nursing, consumer-directed community supports and interpreter services; assisted living and adult foster care are excluded.
Monthly costs are generally capped at 75 percent of the limit under section 256S.18, and discretionary services cannot exceed 25 percent of a lead agency's base allocation.
Case managers must reassess at least every 12 months and give ten days' written notice before a denial, termination or reduction.
Clients pay fees from zero to 30 percent of service costs based on income and assets; the commissioner may waive fees in some cases.
The commissioner may contract with federally recognized Tribes with a reservation in Minnesota to serve as lead agencies, and Tribal governments under contract handle prior authorization.
equityCheck: Check that interpreter services are authorized when needed and that notices are in the person's language.
Ask whether the client fee was calculated correctly and whether a waiver was considered for people in hardship.
Compare allocations and spending across lead agencies to see whether rural or Tribal areas have less access.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0913, Alternative Care Program

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0914, Conflicts of Interest Related to Medicaid Expenditures
policies.summary: This law sets conflict-of-interest rules for state officials, employees and contractors who handle large Medicaid or MinnesotaCare purchases of more than $10,000,000. It restricts sharing bid information, taking jobs with contractors and representing contractors after leaving state service, and sets penalties.
requires: Officials may not disclose or obtain bid or source selection information before a contract is awarded unless the law allows it.
An official contacted about outside employment during a procurement must report it in writing and either reject the offer or step out of the procurement.
Former officials face one-year, two-year and permanent limits on working for or representing contractors on matters they handled.
The commissioner, or the governor for the commissioner, may waive some limits with written public-interest findings.
Violations can bring criminal penalties, civil penalties, contract cancellation and suspension or debarment.
equityCheck: When large contracts shape who delivers services, check that the process was open and that community-based and culturally specific vendors could compete.
Ask whether procurement decisions were documented so the public can see who benefited.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0914, Conflicts of Interest Related to Medicaid Expenditures

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0916, Expansion of Home and Community-Based Services
policies.summary: This law sets how the Department of Human Services gives Developmental Disabilities Waiver funding to counties and county partnerships, how unused resources are reassigned, and how waiting list and financial data are reported. Several subdivisions are set to be repealed when federal approval is obtained, but the text is still printed as law.
requires: Counties submit a request and plan for waiver funding that names who will be served and their priorities; partnerships get priority.
The commissioner monitors use, reassigns unused resources and gives priority to people in unstable living situations and children at risk of out-of-home placement.
Financial information is posted at least monthly and waiting list information quarterly on the department website, with an annual report by December 1.
Counties and Tribal agencies that overspend their allocation must submit a corrective action plan; recoupment happens only if statewide spending exceeds the appropriation.
Counties and Tribal agencies that spend less than 97 percent of their allocation while keeping a waiting list must submit a corrective action plan.
Legal representatives may be paid for certain support services under an agreed health and safety plan.
equityCheck: Compare waiting list and spending data across counties and Tribal agencies to find where people wait longest.
Check whether priority rules for unstable living situations are applied the same way for every family.
Ask whether an agency that underspends is leaving people on a waiting list who could be served.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0916, Expansion of Home and Community-Based Services

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0918, Employee Scholarship Costs
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
intermediate care facilities for persons with developmental disabilities
policies.summary: This law lets the commissioner of the Department of Human Services fund employee scholarships through a small rate increase for selected providers of waiver, home care and day training services. Scholarships pay for nursing and other health care education that leads to career advancement or work in long-term care and disability services.
requires: Scholarship recipients must average at least 20 hours of work a week; executive managers without direct care duties, registered nurses and therapists are not eligible.
Providers apply through a request for proposals; selection considers provider size, the share of eligible employees and paraprofessional retention.
Selected providers received a rate increase of up to 0.3 percent for the first rate period and must repay unused funds.
Providers must report spending and recipient details on a schedule set by the commissioner or repay all funds.
The commissioner reports to the Legislature each year on how the funds were used.
equityCheck: Check whether scholarship funds reach small and culturally specific providers, not only large ones.
Ask whether direct support workers from immigrant and rural communities know about and can use the scholarships.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0918, Employee Scholarship Costs

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0919, Adult Foster Care and Family Adult Day Care
policies.summary: This law sets capacity limits for adult foster care homes that serve adults 60 and older who do not have a serious and persistent mental illness or a developmental disability. It also lets a county certify a relative to provide adult foster care to a family member 65 or older under the Elderly Waiver when the family would face financial hardship.
requires: An adult foster care license holder may serve up to five adults age 60 or older who do not have a serious and persistent mental illness or a developmental disability.
The same license holder may also provide family adult day care without a separate license, with a combined cap of five adults.
A county may certify a relative who is exempt from licensure to provide adult foster care to a related person 65 or older and be paid under chapter 256S if the relative would face financial hardship.
equityCheck: Check that families who want to care for an older relative at home know about county certification.
Ask whether hardship is judged the same way for every family, including families with low or irregular income.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0919, Adult Foster Care and Family Adult Day Care

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.092, Services for Persons with Developmental Disabilities
policies.summary: This law is the main state rule for services to people with developmental disabilities, including the Developmental Disabilities Waiver. It sets county duties for diagnosis and assessment, case management standards, the written support plan, informed choice, authorization limits, residential support criteria and the federal waiver authority.
requires: The county of financial responsibility must arrange a diagnostic evaluation, inform the person about case management, arrange a needs assessment and authorize services in the support plan.

Case managers must develop the support plan, explain options, help with appeals, coordinate and monitor services with at least one face-to-face visit a year, and complete 20 hours of training a year including an informed choice curriculum.
Every waiver recipient gets a written, person-centered support plan signed by the person and the county that covers needs, preferences, informed choice, goals, service amounts and appeal rights.
Only case managers or certified assessors may authorize or end services; technology requests must be decided within 30 business days with a written reason for any denial.
Residential support services are limited to people with complex behavioral health or medical needs after other options are considered, with exceptions.

Starting January 1, 2028, after two or more admissions in a year to an emergency room, psychiatric unit or institution, a mental health or behavioral professional must consult within 30 days of discharge.
equityCheck: Check that the support plan was explained in the person's language and that the person signed with real understanding.
Ask whether independent living and self-direction were offered before a provider-controlled setting.
Review waiting list priorities and residential criteria for patterns by race, region or disability type.
Make sure appeal and conciliation rights under section 256.045 are given every time services are reduced or denied.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.092, Services for Persons with Developmental Disabilities

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0922, Essential Community Supports
policies.summary: This law creates Essential Community Supports, a small benefit of up to $400 a month for people 65 and older who do not meet nursing facility level of care and are not eligible for Medical Assistance. It also covers people who lose eligibility because of the revised nursing facility level of care.
requires: A person must be 65 or older, not eligible for Medical Assistance, found through a community assessment not to need nursing facility level of care, financially eligible for Alternative Care and in need of at least one listed service.
Listed services include adult day services, caregiver support, homemaker support, chores, a personal emergency response device, home-delivered meals and community living assistance.
Service coordination is available up to $600 per 12-month period, and people must be reassessed at least once a year.
Starting January 1, 2027, or upon federal approval if later, weekly unit limits apply to chore and homemaker services and one unit a month to personal emergency response systems.
equityCheck: Check that people who lose waiver eligibility after a level of care change are told about this benefit and about case management help.
Ask whether listed services, such as home-delivered meals, are available in the person's area and match cultural food needs.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0922, Essential Community Supports

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0924, Targeted Case Management Services
programs: Targeted case management for vulnerable adults and adults with developmental disabilities
policies.summary: This law covers Medical Assistance targeted case management for adults who are vulnerable, have a developmental disability or a related condition and do not get home and community-based waiver services, and for adults experiencing homelessness. Counties and Tribal agencies decide eligibility and may provide or contract for the service.
requires: A county or Tribal agency must find the person is 18 or older, receives Medical Assistance, has significant functional limitations and needs coordination to live in an integrated community setting.

For people with developmental disabilities, services follow section 256B.092; for others, services include assessment, a written plan reviewed at least yearly, referrals, monitoring, advocacy and face-to-face contact at least twice a year.
Providers must meet capacity, coordination, record-keeping and conflict-of-interest disclosure standards and meet performance outcomes for access, quality and satisfaction.

Individuals certified by a federally recognized Tribal government in Minnesota may serve as case managers; Tribal agencies may decide eligibility under Tribal codes consistent with adult protection law.
The commissioner sets up the program and performance measures in consultation with county boards and Tribal Nations; the Tribe provides the nonfederal share for services it delivers.
equityCheck: Check that adults experiencing homelessness and adults with related conditions are not turned away because they do not fit a familiar category.
Ask whether face-to-face contacts happen in a place and language the person chooses.
Compare access, quality and satisfaction outcomes across counties and Tribal agencies.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0924, Targeted Case Management Services

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0926, Admission Review Team; Intermediate Care Facilities
programs: intermediate care facilities for persons with developmental disabilities
policies.summary: This law requires an admission review team before a person with a developmental disability is admitted to a community intermediate care facility. The team checks that the provider can meet the person's needs in the individual service plan and weighs the person's and family's preferences.
requires: Before admission, a review team must confirm the provider can meet the person's needs under the plan required by section 256B.092.
The team follows federal rule 42 C.F.R. 483.440 on membership; the county may set up the team, and if not, the provider does and invites a county representative.
The team considers the person's and guardian's or family's preferences, the provider's criteria, bed and day service availability and whether admission avoids a more restrictive setting.
When several people apply, the team decides who is served first and documents its reasons; emergency admissions must be reviewed within 14 days.
Providers must give the team written admission, level of care and discharge criteria and a description of services and staffing.
equityCheck: Check that the person's own preference was heard, with interpreters or communication support if needed.
Ask whether community alternatives were offered before the facility admission.
Review documented reasons for who was admitted first to see whether they are fair and consistent.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0926, Admission Review Team; Intermediate Care Facilities

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.093, Services for Persons with Traumatic Brain Injuries
policies.summary: This law requires the Department of Human Services to run a statewide traumatic brain injury program with an advisory committee. The program provides administrative case management and consultation for Medical Assistance recipients with brain injuries, coordinates the Brain Injury Waiver and gives training and technical help to case managers and providers.
requires: The commissioner must keep a statewide program, supervise related policies and maintain an advisory committee of 10 to 30 members.
Medical Assistance recipients with traumatic or certain acquired brain injuries who are at risk of institutionalization are eligible for administrative case management and consultation.

Program duties include recommending approval of out-of-state placements, coordinating the Brain Injury Waiver, supporting admissions and discharges at specialized facilities, advising on home care authorization and identifying people with brain injury in nursing facilities and hospitals.
The program works with counties and others to build local capacity, including supportive housing, and gives information and referral to people who are not eligible for Medical Assistance.
Traumatic brain injury is defined as a sudden insult or damage to the brain that is not degenerative or congenital.
equityCheck: Check whether people with brain injury in rural nursing facilities and hospitals are being identified and offered community options.
Ask whether information and referral are available in the person's language and in formats that work for cognitive disabilities.
Look at who receives out-of-state placements and whether in-state options were fully explored.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.093, Services for Persons with Traumatic Brain Injuries

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0949, Early Intensive Developmental and Behavioral Intervention Benefit
programs: Early Intensive Developmental and Behavioral Intervention
policies.summary: This law creates the Medical Assistance benefit for early intensive developmental and behavioral intervention for people with autism spectrum disorder or a related condition. It sets eligibility, the comprehensive multidisciplinary evaluation, the individual treatment plan, approved treatment methods, provider qualifications and agency duties.
requires: A person must be enrolled in Medical Assistance, have a qualifying diagnosis under current diagnostic criteria and meet medical necessity criteria.
A comprehensive multidisciplinary evaluation with direct observation decides medical necessity and must document the family's treatment preferences and describe available methods.
The individual treatment plan must be person-centered, with goals and discharge criteria; progress is reviewed at least every six months.
Approved methods include applied behavior analysis, DIR/Floortime, the Early Start Denver Model and relationship development intervention.

Services must reflect the person's and family's primary language, culture, values and preferences; providers must have a limited English proficiency plan, and the commissioner must offer multilingual provider training.
Tribal Nation certification is recognized as an alternative qualification for certain providers; billing limits take effect July 1, 2027, or upon federal approval.
equityCheck: Check that the family's preferred treatment method and cultural values are documented, not only the provider's preferred method.
Ask whether rights information and training were given in the family's language.
Look at wait times and provider availability by region, especially in rural and Tribal areas, and whether shortage exceptions were used.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.0949, Early Intensive Developmental and Behavioral Intervention Benefit

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.097, Regional and Systems Improvement for Minnesotans Who Have Disabilities
policies.summary: This law keeps regional quality councils that work to include people with disabilities, improve person-centered outcomes and track quality of life. Councils must include people with disabilities, families, providers, advocates, lead agency staff and state staff, with an emphasis on people with lived experience from diverse racial and cultural backgrounds.
requires: The commissioner maintains the regional quality councils; subdivisions 1 to 6 are repealed and subdivisions 7 to 10 are in force.
Membership must reflect the community, with emphasis on people with lived experience from diverse racial and cultural backgrounds.

Councils identify barriers to home and community-based services, promote informed decision-making and self-direction, analyze quality and critical incident data and report life safety concerns to the licensing division.
Councils resolve complaints, provide training, make recommendations to decision-makers and report to legislative committees every two years.
Council work must be informed and directed by the needs and desires of people with disabilities in the region.
equityCheck: Check whether the council in your region has members from the racial, cultural and language communities it serves.
Ask what the council's data shows about barriers by county and population, and whether it reaches rural areas.
Use council reports when reviewing where services are hard to reach.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.097, Regional and Systems Improvement for Minnesotans Who Have Disabilities

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.49, Home and Community-Based Service Waivers for Persons with Disabilities
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This law is the state authority for the Brain Injury Waiver, Community Alternative Care Waiver and Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver for people under 65. It sets waiting list priorities, informed choice, case management duties, assessment and support planning, service rules, cost limits, allocations, the customized living moratorium and residential support criteria.
requires: People likely to need nursing facility or hospital care must be told about home and community-based alternatives and allowed to choose.

Case managers must help with support plans, options, providers, appeals and monitoring, complete at least 20 hours of training a year including employment support training, and pass an informed-choice competency evaluation.
Certified assessors determine level of care; each person gets a written support plan, and counties must offer a meeting before denying, reducing or ending services.
Consumer-directed community supports must be offered to all eligible people; technology requests must be decided within 30 business days.

Average per-person spending may not exceed institutional costs; counties and Tribal agencies must spend at least 97 percent of allocations while keeping waiting lists or submit corrective action plans.

New customized living settings of four or fewer people in single-family homes are generally barred for the Brain Injury and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waivers; residential support is limited to people with complex behavioral health or medical needs.
equityCheck: Check that the person was offered self-direction and technology before staffed services were proposed.
Ask whether the support plan meeting and notices were in the person's language and accessible format.
Compare waiting list, allocation use and corrective action plans across counties and Tribal agencies.
Look at residential support authorizations for patterns by race, region or disability type.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.49, Home and Community-Based Service Waivers for Persons with Disabilities

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.4905, Home and Community-Based Services Policy Statement
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This law states Minnesota's policy of informed choice for people with disabilities who use waiver services. It sets presumptions that people can work in competitive integrated employment, live outside provider-controlled settings, direct their own services and use assistive technology or remote supports, and requires that these choices be offered before other options.
requires: Lead agencies must give complete information in culturally and linguistically appropriate ways and help people access services that fit their preferences and needs.
Informed decision-making must include accommodations, personal goals, cultural needs, presenting all options, visiting alternatives, meeting peers, transition plans and ample time to decide.

Working-age recipients must be offered the chance to work and earn a competitive wage before being offered only day services, and an informed choice about work or postsecondary education at least yearly.
Adults must be offered the chance to live as independently as possible in a non-provider-controlled setting before a provider-controlled setting, and may make that choice at least yearly.
Each recipient must be offered self-direction before non-self-directed services, and assistive technology or remote support before services that use direct support staff are offered or reauthorized.

For members of or people affiliated with a federally recognized Tribal Nation in Minnesota, informed choice includes the right to receive services administered or provided by their Tribe; lead agencies must inform people of Tribal services, coordinate with Tribal human services agencies and make timely referrals, and the law states it does not limit Tribal sovereignty.
equityCheck: Check that the informed choice conversation was documented in the person's language and that all options, not only the familiar ones, were presented.
Ask whether peers and site visits were offered before a decision on work, housing or self-direction.
For a person affiliated with a Tribal Nation, confirm that Tribal services were explained and that coordination with the Tribal agency took place.
Review how often employment, independent living, self-direction and technology are chosen by county and population.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.4905, Home and Community-Based Services Policy Statement

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.4906, Subminimum Wages in Home and Community-Based Services Reporting
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This law requires home and community-based services providers that held a federal certificate or state permit to pay subminimum wages as of August 1, 2023, to report each year on the people paid those wages. The commissioner of the Department of Human Services analyzes the data to track employment and community life outcomes.
requires: Providers under sections 256B.092 or 256B.49 that held a federal section 14(c) certificate or a state permit under section 177.28 as of August 1, 2023, must report.
Reports include each person's name, date of birth, identified race and ethnicity, disability type and employment and community life measures set by the commissioner.
Reports are due each year on a date the commissioner sets with at least 30 days' notice; the commissioner may delay Medical Assistance payment until data is submitted.
Individually identifiable data is private data under section 13.02; the commissioner analyzes the data each year.
equityCheck: Use the race, ethnicity and disability data to see who is still paid subminimum wages and in which regions.
Check whether people paid subminimum wages were offered informed choice about competitive employment at least yearly.
Protect the privacy of individual data when sharing findings.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.4906, Subminimum Wages in Home and Community-Based Services Reporting

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.4907, Advisory Task Force on Waiver Reimagine
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This 2025 law creates a 15-member advisory task force on Waiver Reimagine, the plan to restructure Minnesota's four disability waivers. The task force includes people who receive waiver services, county assessment staff, advocates, providers and state agencies, must seek public input, and reports to the Legislature by January 15, 2027.
requires: Members include four legislators, four people under 65 who receive disability waiver services, county assessment staff, the Department of Human Services, the Minnesota Council on Disability, advocacy and family groups, providers, the Ombudsman's office, the Olmstead Implementation Office and the Minnesota Disability Law Center; the governor must ensure greater Minnesota representation.
The task force must meet at least quarterly under the open meeting law, with the first meeting by November 30, 2025.

Duties cover consolidating four waivers into two, individualized budgets not tied to service location, rate and budget exception criteria, assessments including MnCHOICES, covered services, service planning and supports to live in one's own home.
The task force must seek public input from counties, recipients, families, providers, agencies and advocates and hold meetings accessible to remote participants.
A report is due to legislative committees by January 15, 2027; the task force does not expire.
equityCheck: Check whether people from rural areas, Tribal Nations and communities of color are among those giving input.
Ask how proposed individual budgets would affect people with high needs or few local providers.
Share county-level data on waiting lists and service gaps with the task force process.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.4907, Advisory Task Force on Waiver Reimagine

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.4911, Consumer-Directed Community Supports
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This law governs consumer-directed community supports, the self-directed option under the disability and elderly waivers. It says the federally approved waiver plans control the service, sets budget exceptions, shared services rules, limits on paying parents and spouses, and requires lead agencies to explain budgets and appeal rights. Only the commissioner may set consumer-directed community supports policy.
requires: The service is governed entirely by the federally approved waiver plans.

The commissioner must provide up to 30 percent more funds in listed cases, such as more work time, a move to certain settings or a positive behavior support plan, and a budget exception for people leaving institutions who are not offered services within 60 days.
Up to three people may share a direct care worker with a shared services plan, one financial management services provider and lead agency authorization; a person may withdraw at any time.
A parent may provide up to 40 hours per week when more than one parent serves (80 combined), a sole parent up to 60 hours, and a spouse up to 60 hours.
When authorizing a budget, the lead agency must give an accessible explanation of the calculation, the budget formula and appeal rights.
Lead agency handbooks and guidance have no force of law and receive no deference in state fair hearings.
equityCheck: Check that the budget explanation was given in the person's language and that appeal rights were explained.
Ask whether the person knows they can hire family or community members as workers, including under the parent and spouse rules.
Watch for county guidance that adds limits the commissioner has not set.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.4911, Consumer-Directed Community Supports

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.4912, Home and Community-Based Waivers; Providers and Payment
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This law sets provider enrollment, training, insurance, data reporting, payment, documentation and billing rules for disability waiver services. It requires annual workforce data from providers, a direct support professional survey, public labor market reports, and, starting in 2027, unit limits for some services and a ban on using Medical Assistance payments for housing costs.
requires: Providers must have a provider agreement, pass background studies under chapter 245C, complete one-time enrollment training and billing training within six months, and show liability insurance when asked.
Providers must report annual workforce data such as staff counts, wages, hours, turnover and vacancies; chapter 245D providers also report emergency manual restraint use.
Payment methods must be transparent and equitable and cover supervision, staff pay and administration.
Services are paid only when provided under the approved waiver plan with required documentation, and payments can be recovered for noncompliance.
Starting January 1, 2027, or upon federal approval, unit caps apply to some services, such as assistive technology at $10,000 a year.
Providers may not use Medical Assistance payments for housing costs unless room and board is in a federally approved waiver.
equityCheck: Use the workforce and labor market data to check staffing shortages by region and their effect on access.
Ask whether enrollment and training steps are a barrier for small or culturally specific providers.
Check that unit caps do not leave people with high technology or emergency response needs without options.
