policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.4914, Home and Community-Based Services Waivers; Rate Setting
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This law creates the disability waiver rates system used to set payment rates for Developmental Disabilities, Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waiver services. Rates are built from wage data and component values in a web-based system, updated for inflation every two years, with exceptions for people with exceptional needs and rules on how much providers must spend on direct care staff.
requires: Rates are set in the rates management system using component values; lead agencies and providers supply the data, and providers may ask to correct mistaken values.
Each service type has its own framework: residential support, day services, unit-based services with and without programming, and respite.
Wage values come from Bureau of Labor Statistics data and are updated with the Consumer Price Index every two years starting January 1, 2026, with each update capped at 8 percent.
Rate exceptions are allowed for people with exceptional or complex needs.
Providers must spend at least 66 percent of residential rates, 45 percent of day rates and 60 percent of unit-based rates on direct care staff pay and related costs.
Providers must submit cost data at least every five years and labor market data by November 1 each year; a lead agency includes a Tribal agency that administers waiver services.
equityCheck: Check that rate exceptions are requested for people whose needs are not captured by the standard frameworks, including people with communication or cultural support needs.
Ask whether day service and night supervision limits starting in 2027 leave rural areas with fewer options.
Review whether direct care spending rules are met by the providers serving your county.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.4914, Home and Community-Based Services Waivers; Rate Setting

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.492, Home and Community-Based Settings for People with Disabilities
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This law says where disability waiver services may be delivered and protects a person's control over their own home. Settings must meet federal home and community-based settings rules and must not have institutional qualities. It defines community-living settings, limits provider control of leases, and generally bars new integrated community supports settings.
requires: Waiver settings must meet federal Medicaid rules and the approved waiver and transition plans, and must not restrict meals, sleep, visitors or privacy; any individual restriction must be documented, least restrictive and time-limited.
A community-living setting is a home the person or family owns or rents and controls by lease; homes owned by the service provider or in which the provider has a financial interest do not qualify.

People in community-living settings may not be required to receive or share services, may choose their providers and housemates, must have a lockable unit with living, sleeping, bathing and cooking areas, and must be able to come and go and access the community.
Leases follow chapter 504B, landlords may not charge waiver recipients different rent, and a provider may cosign a lease only with a transition plan to transfer it within two years.

The commissioner generally may not approve new integrated community supports settings; exceptions require a lead agency request to meet a person's disability-related needs, with priority for regions lacking capacity.
equityCheck: Check that the person understands their lease rights and control over visitors, meals and daily routine, in their language.
Ask whether housing options exist in the person's home community so they are not moved far from family or culture.
When a provider cosigns a lease, confirm the transition plan and timeline are in place.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.492, Home and Community-Based Settings for People with Disabilities

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.501, Rates for Community-Based Services for Persons with Disabilities
programs: intermediate care facilities for persons with developmental disabilities
policies.summary: This law governs how the Department of Human Services sets payment rates for intermediate care facilities for persons with developmental disabilities and some waivered services. It covers cost containment, property and capital limits, day services, crisis services and respite access through short-term facility stays.
requires: The commissioner sets rate procedures and rules for intermediate care facilities, including cost containment, property limits, accounting standards and appeal procedures.

Day services must meet active treatment requirements, and a residential provider may deliver day services only if the person or legal representative is offered a choice of providers and agrees in writing.
Counties must screen people on request and place them on or off the waiver so they can use short-term facility care for respite.
Medical Assistance pays for community crisis services for facility residents, with residential crisis stays limited to 21 days unless extended and up to 18 therapeutic leave days.
Capital, lease and preopening cost limits apply to new facilities.
equityCheck: Check that the choice of a separate day service provider was offered and documented.
Ask whether crisis services are reachable for facilities in rural areas.
Make sure respite through a short-term stay was explained as an option to families who need it.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.501, Rates for Community-Based Services for Persons with Disabilities

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.85, Community First Services and Supports
policies.summary: This law creates Community First Services and Supports, the participant-controlled Medical Assistance benefit that replaces the personal care assistance program. It sets eligibility, assessment, the service delivery plan, the agency-provider and budget models, support worker and consultation provider rules, participant rights and responsibilities and lead agency duties.
requires: A person must be on Medical Assistance, Alternative Care, certain waivers or have services in an individualized education program, and need help with at least one activity of daily living or have Level I behavior.
A certified assessor conducts a face-to-face assessment at least yearly; results are sent in writing within ten business days with appeal rights, and services are authorized within 40 days.
Each participant has a person-centered service delivery plan approved by the lead agency or case manager; participants have a free choice between the agency-provider and budget models.

Support workers must pass a background study, complete standardized training and a certification test, and are capped at 310 hours a month; an enhanced rate applies for people needing ten or more hours a day.
Consultation services are required and must be independent of the financial management services provider, the lead agency and the participant's agency-provider.

Participants have rights to information, to refuse or end services, to have worker preferences considered, to records, grievances and privacy, and to be free from maltreatment and retaliation; a parent or spouse working as a support worker faces hour limits.
equityCheck: Check that both service models were explained in the person's language and that the budget model was not withheld because it seems harder to manage.
Ask whether worker training and certification are available in languages other than English so people can hire from their own community.
Watch the 40-day authorization timeline by county and population.
Confirm the person was given written rights at the start and each year.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.8502, Community First Services and Supports; Definitions
policies.summary: This section defines the terms used in the Community First Services and Supports law and its payment rate law. It explains activities of daily living, dependency, complex health-related needs, the agency-provider and budget models, consultation services, financial management services, support workers, shared services and medication assistance.
requires: Activities of daily living are dressing, grooming, bathing, eating, transfers, mobility, positioning and toileting; four of these are critical activities of daily living.
Dependency means the person needs hands-on help or supervision, with a special rule for children.
Services may be delivered through an agency-provider model or a budget model with a financial management services provider.
Medication assistance includes reminders and organizing medications but not deciding doses or times or giving injections.
Shared services allow one worker to serve two or three participants; lead agency has the meaning in section 256B.0911.
equityCheck: Use the definitions to check that behavior and complex health needs are counted the same way for every person, including people with limited English.
Make sure participants understand both service models in plain language before choosing.

source.title: Minnesota Statutes 2026, section 256B.8502, Community First Services and Supports; Definitions

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.851, Community First Services and Supports; Payment Rates
policies.summary: This law sets the payment rate method for Community First Services and Supports and personal care assistance services. Rates are built from a base wage index, a competitive workforce factor, component values and worker retention components, with cost reporting and periodic reports to the Legislature.
requires: Base wages come from Minnesota-specific median wage data; the initial competitive workforce factor is 4.7 percent for personal care and Community First Services and Supports services.
Component values cover benefits, taxes, administration and absence, plus worker retention components based on cumulative hours and, from 2027, completion of a specified orientation.
Rate adjustments outside the cost components, including those needed for collective bargaining agreements, must be applied as changes to the components.
Agencies must submit cost data at least every three years; the commissioner may suspend payment for missing data and must validate a random sample.
The commissioner reports to the Legislature every two years on whether rates cover costs and on the long-term effects of the method, starting August 1, 2028.
equityCheck: Check whether the retention components reward workers who serve rural and non-English-speaking participants, where turnover may be higher.
Ask whether budget model participants were told how retention components change their authorized amount.

policies.title: Minnesota Statutes section 626.557, Reporting of Maltreatment of Vulnerable Adults
policies.summary: This law, part of the Vulnerable Adults Act, requires mandated reporters to report suspected maltreatment of a vulnerable adult right away to the common entry point. It sets how reports are screened and investigated, protects reporters, and gives counties adult protective services duties under supervision of the Department of Human Services.
requires: Mandated reporters must immediately report suspected maltreatment or an unexplained injury to the common entry point; anyone may report voluntarily.

Facilities may have internal reporting but remain responsible for external reports, must give the reporter written notice within two working days and may not retaliate; adverse action within 90 days of a report is presumed retaliatory.
The common entry point operates 24 hours a day, refers suspected crimes to law enforcement right away and sends reports to the lead investigative agency within two working days.
Lead agencies must issue final dispositions within 60 calendar days and give notice if the deadline is missed; requests for reconsideration are generally due within 15 calendar days.
Counties handle intake and screening, generally within seven calendar days, assessments and investigations, and may seek protective interventions including court orders.
Facilities must keep abuse prevention plans; investigative data is confidential, and data may be shared with a Tribal agency when pertinent and necessary.
equityCheck: Check that people receiving services and their families know how to report in their language and that interpreters are used in interviews.
Watch for reports from people with communication disabilities being screened out too quickly.
Review timeliness of county screening and lead agency dispositions by county.
Make sure reporters from direct care staff, who are often from immigrant communities, are protected from retaliation.

policies.title: Public guardianship of adults with developmental disabilities (Minnesota Statutes chapter 252A)
policies.summary: Chapter 252A lets the commissioner of the Department of Human Services be appointed by a court as public guardian for an adult with a developmental disability who cannot make personal decisions or meet basic needs even with support. The law says public guardianship is the most restrictive form of guardianship and may be used only after less restrictive options have been tried. The Community-Based Services Manual public guardianship page is based on this chapter.
requires: A person must be 18 or older, have a developmental disability diagnosis, lack enough capacity to make personal decisions, and be unable to meet basic needs even with support (section 252A.02).

Less restrictive options such as supported decision making and community services must be tried first and found not enough; the court must find no less restrictive alternative exists (sections 252A.01 and 252A.101).

The local agency prepares a comprehensive evaluation (medical report, psychological report and case manager report) within 90 days of the court order; the commissioner must accept or reject a nomination in writing within 20 working days of receiving it (sections 252A.03 and 252A.04).
The court appoints a lawyer for the person before the hearing (section 252A.09).

The public guardian must visit the person at least twice a year, use the least restrictive approach consistent with safety, and seek input from the nearest relative; appointment is not a finding of incompetency and does not take away the right to vote (sections 252A.111 and 252A.12).

The commissioner must review each person's progress every year and must petition the court to restore capacity or narrow the order when full guardianship is no longer needed; the person or any interested person may also petition to end or change it (sections 252A.16 and 252A.19).
equityCheck: Before any nomination, document which less restrictive options were offered, including supported decision making, and who explained them to the person in their own language.
Check whether people from some communities or counties are nominated for public guardianship more often than others, and whether private guardians or family were sought first.
Confirm the person had a lawyer, understood the hearing, and knows they can ask the court to end or narrow the guardianship.
Make sure the yearly review looks at the person's own goals and asks whether capacity can be restored, not just whether services are in place.

policies.title: Relocation service coordination targeted case management (Minnesota Statutes 256B.0621)
programs: Relocation service coordination targeted case management
Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Minnesota Statutes 256B.0621 makes relocation targeted case management a Medical Assistance service for people living in an institution who choose to move to the community. It says who can provide the service, what it includes and how long it can be paid for. The Community-Based Services Manual page on relocation service coordination is based on this section.
requires: A person must be on Medical Assistance, living in an institution, and choosing to move to the community.
The service may be paid for during the last 180 consecutive days of the institutional stay, or the federal Medicaid limit if that is shorter.

County providers must be enrolled Medical Assistance providers with legal authority to provide public welfare, or a federally recognized Indian Tribe; private vendors must be certified by the commissioner, have a bachelor's degree or qualifying license or equivalent training plus two years of experience, and have no financial interest in out-of-home residential services for the people they serve.

Services include assessment, a written individual service plan, routine contact, referral coordination, monitoring, documentation, travel to visits and coordination with the institution's discharge planner.
A county case manager must visit the person within 20 working days of a request; if the county or Tribe does not provide the service, the person may use another certified provider.
Providers must coordinate with Tribes, and Tribes must cooperate with certified providers; providers may be credentialed by an American Indian Tribe under section 256B.02.
equityCheck: Check that people in nursing facilities, hospitals and intermediate care facilities are told about their right to move and to get relocation case management, in their language and with help for people who have guardians.
Track how many days people wait for the first visit after asking, and compare across counties and facilities.
Confirm the person was offered a choice between the county and a certified private vendor where both exist.
Look at who moves out and who stays by race, age, disability and region, and ask whether the 180-day limit is being used to start planning early enough.

policies.title: Semi-independent living services for persons with developmental disabilities (Minnesota Statutes 252.275)
policies.summary: Minnesota Statutes 252.275 sets up the state semi-independent living services program for adults with developmental disabilities who are not on a waiver. The commissioner of the Department of Human Services funds county boards, which pay for training and help so a person can live in the community instead of an intermediate care facility. The Community-Based Services Manual page on semi-independent living services is based on this section.
requires: A person must be 18 or older, be unable to function on their own without these services, and not be at risk of placement in an intermediate care facility for persons with developmental disabilities if less restrictive services are provided.

Services include training and help with managing money, preparing meals, shopping, personal appearance and hygiene, and other activities needed to live in the community; services must teach skills, support decision making and community participation, and follow the routines of peers of the same age.
A one-time living allowance of up to $1,500 per state fiscal year may be paid to help a person get and furnish a home when no other public funds are available.
The commissioner reimburses county boards for 85 percent of eligible costs up to the county allocation; counties may pay providers directly or give the person a voucher or cash.
The cost of services for a person is capped at the state share of the average Medical Assistance cost of intermediate care facility services.

The commissioner sets allocations by calendar year, reviews county spending each quarter, may move unspent money to counties that have used their full allocation, and may recover or withhold payment for noncompliance.
equityCheck: Check that adults who are not on a waiver, including people new to the county and people with limited English, are told about semi-independent living services as an option.
Compare how much of the county allocation is used and who receives it by race, language and part of the county, and look for people who were not offered the living allowance.
Confirm skills training fits the person's culture and community, not a standard checklist.
In counties with few providers, ask whether vouchers or cash payment to the person were offered so the person can choose their own helper.

policies.title: Targeted case management for vulnerable adults and adults with developmental disabilities (Minnesota Statutes 256B.0924)
programs: Vulnerable adult and developmental disability targeted case management
policies.summary: Minnesota Statutes 256B.0924 makes targeted case management a Medical Assistance service for adults who are vulnerable adults, adults with developmental disabilities or related conditions who are not on a waiver, and adults without a permanent home. It says who is eligible, what the case manager must do, who may provide the service and how it is paid. The Community-Based Services Manual page on this case management is based on this section.
requires: The person must be 18 or older, on Medical Assistance, have significant functional limitations, and need help coordinating services to live in an integrated community setting, as determined by a county or Tribal agency.

Case management for adults with developmental disabilities follows Minnesota Statutes 256B.092; for other adults it includes assessing need, writing and reviewing a personal service plan, coordinating referrals, monitoring services, advocating for the person and keeping records.

Providers may be county boards, vendors under contract with a county, or vendors under contract with a Tribal government; a person certified by a federally recognized Tribe in Minnesota may serve as a case manager.

Face-to-face monitoring is required at least twice a year, contact standards in section 256B.094 apply, and the personal service plan must be reviewed and updated at least once a year and whenever the person's situation changes.
For people living in a nursing facility, intermediate care facility or hospital, payment is limited to the last 180 days of the stay or the federal limit.

Tribal provisions stated in the section: Tribal agencies may determine eligibility, Tribal vendors are paid under Indian Health Service rules or a negotiated monthly rate, the Tribe provides the nonfederal share for Tribal agency services, and the commissioner consults Tribal Nations on program design and performance measures. Some 2026 amendments take effect only on federal approval.
equityCheck: Check that adults with a related condition who are not on a waiver, and adults without a permanent home, are being found and offered this case management, not only people already known to adult protection.

Confirm the twice-yearly face-to-face visits actually happen for people in rural areas and for people who move often, and that interactive video is used only where the law allows and the person agrees.
Look at caseload data by race, language and county for differences in how often plans are updated and how quickly referrals are made.
Make sure the person had a choice of provider where more than one exists and knows they can ask for a different case manager.

policies.title: Minnesota Rules 9525.0004 to 9525.0036, Case Management Services to Persons with Developmental Disabilities (Rule 185)
policies.summary: These rules set the standards county boards and case managers must meet when providing case management to people with developmental disabilities. They cover who gets a case manager, how fast, what the assessment and individual service plan must include, informed choice of providers and how often the case manager must check on services.
requires: The county board must designate a case manager within 10 working days of an application and make sure a diagnostic assessment is done within 35 working days; it must give people a written description of available services so they can make an informed choice (9525.0012).

The county may not buy case management from a provider that has a financial interest in the person's other services; a county that wants to provide both case management and residential or day services needs commissioner approval with conflict-of-interest safeguards (9525.0012).
Case managers need a bachelor's degree and one year of experience (or supervised aides with 40 hours of training) and at least 20 hours of training each year.

The case manager must assess or arrange assessment of basic needs, health and safety, social skills, communication, self-care, home living, community use, employment, education and legal representation, and lead an individual service plan that is developed or revised at least once a year and signed by the person or legal representative (9525.0024).

The case manager must help the team make informed choices by identifying service types, funding, comparative costs, locations and provider capacity, and must note in the plan when no appropriate provider is found.

The case manager must make a monitoring visit at least twice a year to check that services match the plan, providers are meeting their duties, and the person's health, safety and rights are protected.
equityCheck: Check that the 10-day and 35-day timelines are met for everyone, including people who applied through an interpreter or who have no family to push the process.
Confirm the person was offered a real choice of providers, with comparative information, rather than the one provider the county uses most.
Monitoring visits are a chance to ask about rights, cultural needs and satisfaction directly; make sure the person is asked, not only the provider.

policies.title: Minnesota Rules 9525.0900 to 9525.1020, Grants for Semi-Independent Living Services
policies.summary: These rules set out how the Department of Human Services awards and administers grants to county boards for semi-independent living services. These services teach adults with developmental disabilities skills such as managing money, preparing meals, shopping and personal care so they can live in the community.
requires: The program is authorized by Minnesota Statutes section 252.275 and aims to help people live as independently as possible and to reduce unnecessary use of intermediate care facilities and home and community-based services (9525.0910).

Semi-independent living services are training and assistance in managing money, preparing meals, shopping, personal appearance and hygiene and other community living activities; a unit of service is one hour delivered under the person's individual program plan (9525.0900).
A living allowance (cash or voucher) may be provided when other public funds are not available so an eligible person can secure housing.
Providers must meet part 9525.0930 and Minnesota Statutes chapter 245B (now chapter 245D) standards; county boards contract with providers and receive base and targeted allocations.
The rules cover eligibility (9525.0920), provider approval, residential location standards, reimbursement, allocations, reporting, variances, repayment of funds and penalties.
equityCheck: Check that people who are not on a waiver but could use these services are told about them; the program is funded separately from the waivers.
Ask whether training is offered in the person's language and in the setting where the skill is used, as the statute expects.
Compare county allocations and use to see where services are scarce.

policies.title: Minnesota Rules 9525.1200 to 9525.1330, Training and Habilitation Reimbursement Procedures for Intermediate Care Facilities
programs: Intermediate Care Facilities for Persons with Developmental Disabilities
policies.summary: These rules set the procedures for Medical Assistance payment of day training and habilitation services for people with developmental disabilities who live in intermediate care facilities. They say which providers the commissioner may approve and what agreements and records are needed.
requires: The rules apply to county boards that administer or recommend rates for these services and to day service providers the county selects; they do not apply to services provided by state hospitals (9525.1200).

To be approved, a day service provider must hold a day training and habilitation license, hold a current need determination, not be controlled by the same entity that runs the person's intermediate care facility, and have written agreements with each facility and the county (9525.1230).

An approved provider must make at least 195 full days of reimbursable service available each calendar year and have service and transportation rates proposed by the county board and approved by the commissioner.
Providers must comply with federal standards in 42 CFR 483.410(d) and 483.440.
The rules also cover client eligibility, agreements, reimbursable services, billing, required records, penalties and appeals.
equityCheck: Check that people in intermediate care facilities are offered community-integrated day options, including employment, and not only facility-based activities.
Confirm the day provider is independent of the residential provider so the person has a real choice.
Look at whether people in rural facilities have the same day options as people in metro facilities.

policies.title: Minnesota Rules 9525.1800 to 9525.1930, Funding and Administration of Home and Community-Based Services
policies.summary: These rules govern how county boards administer Medical Assistance funds for home and community-based services for people with developmental disabilities under the Developmental Disabilities Waiver. They define the services, set eligibility and provider contract rules, and cover allocations, records and penalties.
requires: The rules apply to county boards that administer waiver funds, to providers that contract with county boards and to their subcontractors, and stay in effect only while the federal waiver is in effect (9525.1810).

Home and community-based services are defined as services for people with developmental disabilities authorized under the federal Medicaid waiver; defined services include residential-based habilitation, day training and habilitation, respite care, homemaker services, in-home family support and adaptive modifications and equipment (9525.1800).
Adaptive modifications and equipment are reimbursable only for people with physical disabilities, sensory deficits or behavior problems, and only if approved under the waiver plan.
The rules cover eligibility, parental contribution fees, provider reimbursement, contracts, county proposals, allocations, state-county agreements, county funding, records, penalties and appeals.
Later parts 9525.2000 to 9525.2140 are repealed.
equityCheck: Many detailed waiver policies now live in the Community-Based Services Manual and statute; use the rule for county duties but check the manual for current service definitions.
Check that adaptive equipment and home modifications are authorized based on need and are reachable for people who rent or live in rural areas.

policies.title: Minnesota Rules 9525.3010 to 9525.3100, Public Guardianship of Persons with Developmental Disabilities
policies.summary: These rules carry out Minnesota Statutes chapter 252A, which lets the commissioner serve as public guardian for adults with developmental disabilities who have no qualified private guardian. The commissioner delegates most duties to county boards. The rules set standards so that a person's rights are limited only as much as clearly necessary.
requires: The rules apply to county boards that provide public guardianship to people with developmental disabilities; they exclude people with related conditions as defined in Minnesota Statutes section 252.27 (9525.3010).

The purposes are to protect people who cannot fully meet their own needs, to avoid restricting a person's decision-making beyond what is clearly necessary, and to help people get services they are entitled to.
A guardian may use only the powers needed to meet the ward's demonstrated needs, and may limit civil rights and personal freedoms only as far as needed for necessary care and services (9525.3030).

County staff acting as public guardian may consent to aversive or deprivation procedures only when all rule and federal requirements are met, must withdraw consent when the procedure is not in the ward's best interest, and must review data and document the review quarterly (9525.3045).

The rules also cover who is subject to guardianship, appointment, nondelegated consent, monitoring, county responsibility, contracting, modification or termination, death of a ward, training and review.
equityCheck: Ask first whether the person could use supported decision-making or a limited guardianship instead of full public guardianship.
Check that the person under guardianship is still asked about their own preferences in planning and that the guardian's decisions reflect them.

policies.title: Minnesota Rules 9555.9600 to 9555.9730, Adult Day Care Center or Adult Day Services Center Licensure
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: These rules set licensing standards for adult day care and adult day services centers, which serve functionally impaired adults for less than 24 hours a day outside their homes. Adult day services are a waiver and Alternative Care service, so these standards apply to providers that lead agencies authorize.
requires: A center that regularly provides adult day care (more than 30 cumulative days in 12 months) must be licensed under Minnesota Statutes chapter 245A; a unit inside a nursing home, hospital or boarding care home must be licensed separately if it serves six or more non-residents at a time (9555.9610).
Licensed capacity is the maximum number of participants allowed on the premises at one time, and the license may include a variance from specific provisions (9555.9600).

A center must keep a written record for each participant with an application, medical report, service agreement, monthly progress notes, needs assessment and care plan, a signed participants' rights statement, incident reports and an individual abuse prevention plan (9555.9660).
Participants, guardians or caregivers must be told in writing of their right to contest the accuracy of their records.
The rules also cover policy and program information, personnel, participants' rights, staffing, service planning, safety and physical plant.
equityCheck: Check that the center's program and food reflect the cultures and languages of the people it serves, and that participants' rights are explained in a language the person understands.
Ask whether transportation to the center is arranged so people in outlying areas can attend.
Confirm the center offers community-integrated activities, not only activities inside the building.

policies.title: Minnesota Rules chapter 2960, parts 2960.3000 to 2960.3340, Foster Family Settings, Foster Residence Settings and Treatment Foster Care
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: These rules set the minimum licensing standards for foster family homes, foster residence settings and treatment foster care for children. Children on the disability waivers who live in foster care, including children served by state-operated intensive therapeutic homes, live in settings licensed under these parts.
requires: The goal is that a foster child experiences a safe and healthy family life; license holders must work with the placing agency on the case plan and include the child in daily family life (2960.3000).

A foster home may have no more than six foster children and no more than eight children in total, with at least one adult for every five children; no more than four foster children at a time if any have severe or profound developmental disabilities, severe emotional disturbance or rely on medical technology (2960.3030).
Capacity must also be set case by case based on the license holder's ability to supervise, training and experience, the home's structure, emergency response and the children's needs.

Nonrelative foster parents must complete at least six hours of orientation before a child is placed, and all foster parents must complete at least 12 hours of training each year; foster parents caring for children who rely on medical equipment must meet Minnesota Statutes section 245A.155 (2960.3070).
Each home has a statement of intended use covering the number and ages of children and whether it provides emergency shelter, treatment foster care or medically fragile care.
Parts 2960.3200 to 2960.3340 add requirements for foster residence settings and treatment foster care, including admission, treatment, discharge and training.
equityCheck: Check that a child with a disability is placed in a home that can meet their needs and keeps them connected to family, culture and language.
Confirm the four-child limit is applied when children have significant disabilities, so support is not spread too thin.
Look at whether children with disabilities from some communities are placed farther from home or stay longer in foster care.

policies.title: Minnesota Rules chapter 9544, Positive Support Strategies and Restrictive Interventions (Positive Supports Rule)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: The Positive Supports Rule sets standards for how licensed providers support people whose behavior is challenging. It requires person-centered positive support strategies, bans a long list of harmful procedures, limits emergency manual restraint, and requires staff training and reporting. It took effect August 31, 2015 and replaced the earlier Rule 40.
requires: Applies to home and community-based services providers licensed under Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D serving people with disabilities or people age 65 and older, and to other chapter 245A licensed providers serving people with developmental disabilities or related conditions (9544.0010).

Positive support strategies must be written into the person's plan, based on an assessment of strengths, needs and preferences, be person-centered and least restrictive, and be reviewed with the person at least every six months (9544.0030); a functional behavior assessment by a qualified professional is required when an intervention is developed or changed (9544.0040).

Prohibited procedures (9544.0060) include prone restraint, metal handcuffs, faradic shock, demeaning or threatening speech, withholding equipment such as wheelchairs or hearing aids, painful techniques, sensory deprivation and restraint used for staff convenience or punishment.

Emergency manual restraint is allowed only under chapter 245D; records must be kept at least five years, and a positive support transition plan is required after three incidents in 90 days or four in 180 days (9544.0070).

Staff need at least eight hours of core training before taking on duties, extra training for those who develop strategies, and four hours of refresher training each year; competence must be shown through testing or observed skills (9544.0090).

Providers must report emergency manual restraint, related medical emergencies, 911 calls, crisis respite use and certain as-needed medication use to the commissioner on the behavior intervention report form (9544.0110); an external program review committee reviews requests and provider capacity (9544.0130).
equityCheck: Ask whether behavior is being read through the person's culture, communication style and trauma history before it is labeled a target behavior.
Check that the functional behavior assessment and plan were explained to the person and family in their language and that they agreed.
Review restraint and incident reports by provider, setting and group; repeated incidents point to unmet needs, not a 'difficult' person.
Confirm the six-month review actually happens and that strategies are becoming less restrictive over time.

policies.title: Minnesota Rules chapter 9555, parts 9555.5050 to 9555.6265, Adult Foster Care Services and Licensure of Adult Foster Homes (Rule 203)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: These rules set standards for adult foster care, where a functionally impaired adult receives food, lodging, protection, supervision and household services in a licensed home. They cover how local agencies develop and license homes, assessment of residents, services, training, resident records and protection from maltreatment and discrimination.
requires: Adult foster care means food, lodging, protection, supervision and household services for a functionally impaired adult in a residence, and may include personal care, living skills help, medication assistance and safeguarding of cash (9555.5105).

The service parts (9555.5105 to 9555.5705) exist to make sure people who live in or are considering an adult foster home get an assessment of their need for foster care and are told about available services (9555.5305).

Operators and caregivers must complete the local agency orientation before the first resident is placed; caregivers with up to five years of experience need 12 hours of training a year and those with six or more years need 6 hours (9555.6185).

Operators must protect residents from maltreatment under the Vulnerable Adults Act and must follow the nondiscrimination rules for public accommodations in Minnesota Statutes section 363A.11 (9555.6195).

The licensure parts (9555.6105 to 9555.6265) cover the application process, licensing study, negative licensing actions, capacity, individual resident placement agreements, physical environment, food, sanitation, resident records and safeguards for resident cash.
Capacity and resident rights for adult foster care are also set in Minnesota Statutes section 245A.11.
equityCheck: Confirm the person chose the home and was offered other options, including their own home with supports.
Ask whether the home can meet the person's cultural, language, dietary and religious needs.
Check that resident rights, including the right to come and go and have visitors, are explained in a way the person understands and are not restricted without documentation.

policies.title: Positive support strategies and restrictive interventions (Minnesota Rules chapter 9544)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Minnesota Rules chapter 9544, the positive supports rule, sets standards for how licensed home and community-based services providers support people whose behavior may put them or others at risk. Its stated goal is to end all use of aversive and deprivation procedures. It lists what is prohibited, what is allowed, how emergencies must be handled, and what training, records and reports are required. The Department of Human Services positive supports pages and the Community-Based Services Manual positive supports page are based on this chapter.
requires: Applies to home and community-based services providers under Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D serving people with a disability or people 65 and older, and to other chapter 245A licensed providers serving people with a developmental disability or related condition (part 9544.0010).

Prohibits prone restraint, faradic shock, punishment, mechanical restraint, chemical restraint and manual restraint except in an emergency, among a list of prohibited items; seclusion is prohibited when medically contraindicated or done without monitoring (part 9544.0060).

Allows only positive verbal correction focused on the behavior and temporary removal of an object used to hurt self or others, with expanded support team approval, parent approval for a child, and documentation in a plan (part 9544.0050).

Emergency use of manual restraint follows Minnesota Statutes 245D.06 and 245D.061; a positive support transition plan is required after three emergency manual restraints in 90 days or four in 180 days; records are kept at least five years (part 9544.0070).
Staff must have at least eight hours of core training before taking on duties and four hours of refresher training each year; staff who develop strategies need four more hours (part 9544.0090).

Emergency manual restraint, 911 calls and as-needed medication for behavior must be reported to the commissioner on the behavior intervention report form; positive support strategies must be reviewed with the person at least every six months; an external program review committee appointed by the commissioner monitors the chapter (parts 9544.0110, 9544.0030, 9544.0120, 9544.0130).
equityCheck: Review behavior intervention reports by race, disability type, age and setting to see whether some groups experience restraint or emergency interventions more often.

Check that functional behavior assessments and positive support plans reflect the person's culture, language and communication style, and that the person and family were part of the expanded support team.
Confirm that providers in every region, including small and rural providers, meet the training hours and have access to qualified positive support professionals.
Ask whether people and families know what procedures are prohibited and how to report concerns.

policies.title: Rule 185 case management for persons with developmental disabilities (Minnesota Rules 9525.0004 to 9525.0036)
policies.summary: Minnesota Rules 9525.0004 to 9525.0036, known as Rule 185, set out how counties provide case management to people with developmental disabilities and to children under five found eligible. The rules cover county administration (part 9525.0016) and the case manager's service activities (part 9525.0024), including assessment, the individual service plan and monitoring. The Community-Based Services Manual page on Rule 185 case management is based on these rules and Minnesota Statutes 256B.092.
requires: The county must arrange a comprehensive diagnostic evaluation within 35 working days of receiving an application, and the case manager must review the diagnosis at least every three years (part 9525.0016).
The screening team must meet within 60 working days of a service request, or within five working days of an emergency admission to an intermediate care facility (part 9525.0016).

The case manager must assess, or arrange an assessment of, the person's skills and needs in ten areas such as health and safety, self-care and employment; health, safety and service-authorizing assessments may not be waived (part 9525.0024).

The individual service plan must include the person's preferences, goals and services, and must be signed by the person, legal representative and case manager at least once a year and whenever it changes (part 9525.0024).
The case manager must make a monitoring visit at least every six months to check that services match the plan and that rights, health and safety are protected (part 9525.0024).

The plan must tell the person about the right to a conciliation conference or a hearing under Minnesota Statutes 256.045; a conciliation conference must be held within 30 days of the request (parts 9525.0016 and 9525.0024).
equityCheck: Check that the diagnostic evaluation and screening deadlines are met for every applicant, and compare wait times by county, language and race.
Confirm the individual service plan was written in a way the person can understand and reflects what the person wants, not only what providers offer.
Ask whether people and families know about the conciliation conference and hearing rights, and whether notices went out in their language.
Look at whether six-month monitoring visits happen as often for people in rural counties and in settings far from the county office.

policies.title: Chore services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Chore services are help with heavy household tasks that keep a person's home safe and livable. The Community-Based Services Manual page sets who can get chore services under the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion and Developmental Disabilities waivers and under Alternative Care, Essential Community Supports and the Elderly Waiver. The lead agency approves the service and the provider.
requires: The manual lists chore services as an approval-option, direct-delivery service: the lead agency must approve it in the person's support plan before it is delivered.
The manual sets separate eligibility conditions for the aging programs (Alternative Care, Essential Community Supports, Elderly Waiver) and for the four disability waivers.

Minnesota Statutes 256B.0913 lists chore services as a covered Alternative Care service (subdivision 5), and Minnesota Statutes 256B.0922 lists chores as an Essential Community Supports service within the $400 monthly cap (subdivision 1).
Starting January 1, 2027, or on federal approval if later, Essential Community Supports chore services are limited to 24 fifteen-minute units per week (256B.0922, subdivision 3).

Starting July 1, 2027, or on federal approval if later, administrative fees for chore, transitional and transportation services under the Disability Waiver Rate System are capped at six percent (256B.4914, subdivision 22).
equityCheck: Check whether people who rent, live in shared housing or live on Tribal land are told how the eligibility conditions apply to them.
Check that chore providers exist in rural counties; if none are enrolled, note the gap and how the person's need will be met.
Review whether authorizations differ by county for people with similar needs.

policies.title: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: The Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver funds home and community-based services for children and adults with disabilities who need the level of care given in a nursing facility but choose to live in the community. The Community-Based Services Manual page describes the program; Minnesota Statutes 256B.49 is the state law behind it.
requires: A certified assessor must find at the first assessment and at each later assessment that the person needs nursing facility level of care (256B.49, subdivision 14).
People found eligible before age 65 may stay on the waiver after 65 if they still meet the other criteria (256B.49, subdivision 14).

Each person on the waiver gets case management from a qualified vendor; case managers must finish the person-centered support plan, explain service options, help find providers and monitor services (256B.49, subdivision 13).
Lead agencies must tell people who are likely to need nursing facility care about home and community-based options and let them choose (256B.49, subdivision 12).
Consumer-directed community supports must be offered to everyone eligible under the waiver (256B.49, subdivision 16).

County and Tribal agencies must spend their annual allocation and are responsible for spending above it; underspending below 97 percent while keeping a waiting list requires a corrective plan (256B.49, subdivisions 26 and 27, which the statute notes are repealed upon federal approval).
equityCheck: Check that people are told about this waiver in their own language and that disability determinations are not delayed for people without a regular doctor.
Compare enrollment and spending across counties and Tribal lead agencies for people with similar needs.
Check that the choice between institutional care and community services is offered and documented, not assumed.

policies.title: Community Alternative Care Waiver
policies.summary: The Community Alternative Care Waiver funds home and community-based services for children and adults who are chronically ill or medically fragile and need the level of care given in a hospital. The Community-Based Services Manual page describes the program and the hospital level of care test; Minnesota Statutes 256B.49 is the state law behind it.
requires: The person must be assessed through MnCHOICES as needing hospital level of care, and a medical provider must document the person's treatment, monitoring or intervention needs.

Hospital level of care means the person needs a 24-hour plan of care, including a backup plan, to reasonably ensure health and safety in the community, and would need frequent or continuous hospital care without the waiver; it does not refer to inpatient behavioral health care.
A certified assessor must confirm the level of care at the first assessment and at each later assessment (256B.49, subdivision 14).
Each person on the waiver gets case management from a qualified vendor (256B.49, subdivision 13).
Consumer-directed community supports must be offered to everyone eligible under the waiver (256B.49, subdivision 16).
equityCheck: Check that families without a regular specialist can still get the medical documentation the level of care test needs.
Check that medically fragile children in rural areas have access to the nursing and home care providers the plan relies on.
Make sure the backup plan is written with the family and in their language.

policies.title: Community First Services and Supports and personal care assistance
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes personal care assistance and the newer Community First Services and Supports program that is replacing it. Personal care assistance gives day-to-day help at home and in the community so a person can stay independent. Community First Services and Supports gives people more flexible ways to meet those same needs.
requires: The Department of Human Services started moving people from personal care assistance and the Consumer Support Grant to Community First Services and Supports in October 2024.
Community First Services and Supports replaces both personal care assistance and the Consumer Support Grant.

Until the transition is finished, policy for both personal care assistance and Community First Services and Supports lives in the Community First Services and Supports Policy Manual, which has a section on the transition.
The legal authority for personal care assistance is Minnesota Statutes 256B.0659; the authority for Community First Services and Supports is Minnesota Statutes 256B.85.
The page points lead agencies and providers to the Department of Human Services program pages and the Minnesota Health Care Programs provider-type pages for details.
equityCheck: Check that every person still on personal care assistance or the Consumer Support Grant has had the move to Community First Services and Supports explained in their language and in a format they can use, and that no one loses hours during the change.
Ask whether people in rural counties and in communities with few agencies have a real choice of Community First Services and Supports agency or budget model, not just the one agency that is left.
Look at who is choosing the self-directed budget option and who is not, and whether information and support to use it reach people with limited English, limited reading, or no representative.
Make sure a person's own family members and community members who already give care can keep doing so as paid workers under the new program where the rules allow it.

policies.title: Community First Services and Supports Policy Manual
policies.summary: Community First Services and Supports is the Medical Assistance program that replaced personal care assistance and the Consumer Support Grant. The Department of Human Services publishes a separate policy manual for it. Minnesota Statutes 256B.85 is the state law; the federal approvals are state plan amendments under sections 1915(i) and 1915(k) of the Social Security Act.
requires: A person must be eligible for Medical Assistance (or Alternative Care or certain waivers), need help with at least one activity of daily living or have Level I behavior, and get a face-to-face assessment by a certified assessor at least once a year (256B.85, subdivisions 3 and 5).
Services must be authorized within 40 calendar days of the assessment; authorized units depend on the person's home care rating (256B.85, subdivision 8).

The participant develops a person-centered service delivery plan that is reviewed at least once a year and approved by the lead agency or case manager; the plan must allow participant choice and consider cultural factors (256B.85, subdivision 6).
People choose an agency-provider model or a budget model with a financial management services provider (256B.85, subdivisions 7c to 7g and 13).
Agencies must spend at least 72.5 percent of Medicaid revenue on worker wages and benefits (256B.85, subdivision 7c).
Parent and spouse support workers have weekly hour limits (256B.85, subdivision 7b).
equityCheck: Check that people moving from personal care assistance or the Consumer Support Grant were reassessed and kept their hours; look for drops by race, language or county.
Check that budget-model information and consultation services are available in the person's language.
Check that rural participants can find enrolled agencies and financial management services providers.

policies.title: Community living assistance (Essential Community Supports)
policies.summary: Community living assistance is help that lets a person keep living in the community. It is an Essential Community Supports service under Minnesota Statutes 256B.0922. The Community-Based Services Manual page (reviewed November 22, 2024) describes the service and says the lead agency approves the provider.
requires: Covers help with basic living tasks and social skills, such as reaching community resources like transportation, employment and housing, and reminders for daily living activities.
Covers help with household management, including basic help with technology that supports community living.
The lead agency approves the provider.

Essential Community Supports serves people age 65 and older who do not meet nursing facility level of care and are not eligible for Medical Assistance, with services capped at $400 per person per month (256B.0922, subdivision 1).
equityCheck: Check that older adults who do not qualify for Medical Assistance are told about this program and not just turned away.
Check that technology help is offered in the person's language and fits the devices the person actually has.
Look at whether approved providers exist outside metro counties.

policies.title: Community residential services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Community residential services are residential supports for adults in a community residential setting licensed under Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D, where the license holder does not live. The Community-Based Services Manual page describes the waiver service; the rate is set under the Disability Waiver Rate System in Minnesota Statutes 256B.4914.
requires: A community residential setting is a residential program for adults where the license holder owns, leases or rents the facility but does not live there (245D.02, subdivision 4a).
Community residential services are an intensive support service under the home and community-based services license (245D.03, subdivision 1, paragraph (c)).

Rates are set by the Disability Waiver Rate System residential formula, and at least 66 percent of revenue for these rates must go to direct care staff compensation (256B.4914, subdivisions 6 and 10d).

Effective July 1, 2026, rate exceptions for community residential services cannot include positive support costs, and exceptions for increased community time or transportation are barred (256B.4914, subdivision 14a).
No initial license may be issued for new community residential settings under the licensing moratorium, with limited exceptions (245A.03, subdivisions 7b and 7c).
Each adult waiver recipient must be offered the chance to live in a non-provider-controlled setting before being offered a provider-controlled one (256B.4905, subdivision 8).
equityCheck: Check that the person was offered independent living options first and that the choice is written in the support plan.
Check how far the setting is from the person's family, community and cultural supports.
Check that staff can communicate in the person's language and that the person can get to religious and cultural activities.

programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: The Community-Based Services Manual is the Department of Human Services policy manual for lead agencies that administer home and community-based services, including the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion and Developmental Disabilities waivers, Alternative Care, Essential Community Supports and the Elderly Waiver. It has an A to Z index of every page and a What's new page that logs each change by date.
requires: Lead agencies use the manual as the policy source for assessment, support planning, service authorization and program rules for home and community-based services.
The What's new page lists recently updated policies; Department of Human Services weekly updates point lead agencies there for changes.
Each service page states the legal basis, who is eligible, what the service covers, provider standards and lead agency instructions.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: 24-hour emergency assistance
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines 24-hour emergency assistance, a waiver service that gives a person on-call counseling, on-call problem solving or an immediate response at home during a health or personal emergency. It covers who is eligible, what is and is not covered, and the provider license and background study rules. The service does not replace calling 911.
requires: A person is eligible if they live in their own home, do not get 24-hour supervision and would otherwise need extensive routine supervision, or if they live with a primary caregiver who would otherwise need extensive support to get help in an emergency.
Covers immediate response at home, on-call counseling and problem solving, and personal emergency response system installation, device and monitoring.
Cannot be authorized together with services that duplicate it, such as 24-hour customized living, community residential services, family residential services or integrated community supports.
When a person has an unexpected need, the lead agency may authorize the service right away but must review and update the support plan within five days.
Non-equipment providers need a 245D basic support license or a 144A home and community-based services designation, plus a background study; the service may be delivered through remote support.
The lead agency authorizes the service at the market rate within the Long-Term Services and Supports Service Rate Limits (form 3945).
equityCheck: Check that people who live alone in rural areas, or whose first language is not English, know this service exists and can reach the on-call line in a way that works for them.
If the response is remote (telephone or video), confirm the person can actually use that method; offer in-person response when they cannot.
Record who is offered this service and who is steered toward residential services instead, and look for patterns by region, race or disability type.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Adult companion services
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines adult companion services under the Elderly Waiver and the Alternative Care program. An adult companion gives non-medical care, supervision and socialization that helps an older adult work toward a therapeutic or community integration goal in their support plan. The page lists covered and non-covered activities, provider licenses, staff requirements and the rate.
requires: The companion may help with tasks such as laundry, light housekeeping, meals or shopping only while working on the person's goal; these tasks cannot be billed as separate services.
Not covered: activity fees, help with activities of daily living, hands-on nursing care, services that are only recreational, and services by relatives unless a 245D exclusion applies.
Providers need a 245D basic support license, a 144A home and community-based services designation, or be part of the federal Senior Companion Program; direct-contact staff need a background study.
Each staff member must be able to handle emergencies, follow the support plan, keep information private and have training or experience caring for people with functional limitations.
The service can be delivered through remote support when it meets the manual's remote support requirements.
The lead agency authorizes the service at the state-set 15-minute rate.
equityCheck: Ask whether the companion options offered match the person's language, culture and community; a companion who shares these can make the goal reachable.
Check that remote delivery is a real choice for the person and not the only option offered because of where they live.
Review how often the service is authorized across counties and Tribal Nations and whether some areas have no enrolled providers.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Adult corporate foster care and community residential setting closure process and procedure
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains how a licensed adult corporate foster care home or community residential setting is closed in a planned way. The Department of Human Services manages statewide capacity of these settings and may approve a closure proposed by a county, Tribal Nation, the license holder or the Department itself. The page lists what a closure proposal must contain and the notice people must receive.
requires: A closure proposal must include a closure plan, a timeline, proposed rates during the closure period and a relocation plan for every person affected.

The county corporate foster care moratorium liaison sends the proposal to the Department on the Setting Closure Proposal form, form 6021B; if someone other than the license holder starts the proposal, the license holder must be told first.

The Department weighs local need for services, per-capita use of these settings in the area, whether residents live where they choose, whether residents prefer to stay, Medical Assistance savings and the effect on people's services.

After approval, the license holder must give written notice within five working days to each county of financial responsibility, current and prospective residents and their representatives, at least 60 days before closing.
Once a closure is approved, the license holder may not admit new people to the setting.
equityCheck: Before supporting a closure, confirm each resident has been asked, in a way they understand, where and with whom they want to live, and that the relocation plan reflects their answer.
Check whether the closure removes the only culturally specific or specialized setting in a region and what that means for people who rely on it.
Look at who is affected by closures over time by region, race, language and disability, and whether some groups are moved more often than others.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Adult day services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page sets the policy for adult day services, a structured daytime program of activities, assistance, health services, supervision, exercise and meals outside the person's home. It covers in-person and remote delivery, setting location limits, and licensing. It also records the temporary adult day center licensing moratorium that began February 1, 2026.
requires: Covered services must maintain or improve the person's ability to care for themselves and include meaningful activities, help with daily living tasks, health services overseen by a registered nurse, supervision, a daily exercise program and meals or snacks.

For the Brain Injury Waiver, the Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver and the Developmental Disabilities Waiver, the lead agency may authorize adult day services only when the person chooses them, does not choose day support or employment services, and the service meets the person's outcomes.

The lead agency cannot authorize the service in a setting adjoined to or on the same property as an institution with a financial interest in it; a provider with several settings on the same property may be authorized in only one.

Remote adult day services are allowed only for people who also receive in-person services from the same provider, for up to six hours a day, with in-person attendance at least quarterly; group size is limited to eight with two-way video and one-to-one without it.
All providers must be licensed under Minnesota Statutes chapter 245A and follow Minnesota Rules 9555.9600 to 9555.9730; remote providers have added requirements.
Effective February 1, 2026, the Department of Human Services stopped accepting new adult day center license applications and cancelled pending ones, for an expected 24 months ending January 31, 2028.
equityCheck: Check that the person was told about day support and employment services, in plain language and their own language, before adult day services were chosen.
With the licensing moratorium in place, watch for areas where no adult day center exists and record what alternatives people in those areas are offered.
For remote delivery, confirm the person has the device, internet and skills needed, and that waiver funding for enabling technology was considered.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Adult foster care (Elderly Waiver)
policies.summary: Since January 1, 2022, this Community-Based Services Manual page covers adult foster care only under the Elderly Waiver. Adult foster care gives ongoing residential care, supervision, household services and living-skills help to an adult living in a licensed family foster care home or community residential setting. The page lists non-covered items, setting size and location limits, licensing options and how rates are set.
requires: Covered: protection, supervision, household services and living-skills assistance based on the support plan; not covered: room and board, items of comfort, facility upkeep and payments to the person or their family.

Services that duplicate adult foster care, such as chore, homemaker, home-delivered meals, respite, personal care assistance or individual community living supports, cannot be authorized at the same time.
A home may serve up to five adults only if all are age 55 or older and none has a serious and persistent mental illness or a developmental disability.
Since March 18, 2023, a new provider in or next to an institution cannot bill waiver services until the setting passes the federal heightened-scrutiny review.

Providers need a 245D intensive support license, a 245A foster care license under Minnesota Rules 9555, or county certification of a relative under Minnesota Statutes 256B.0919, plus a background study; emergency manual restraint is prohibited.
Rates are set with the Elderly Waiver Residential Services Rate Tool in the MnCHOICES support plan.
equityCheck: Confirm the person chose this setting after hearing about own-home and other options in a way they understood.
Check that room and board help through Housing Support was explained so cost does not quietly decide where someone lives.
Review placements by region to see whether people in some counties or Tribal areas have fewer home-like options.

source.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Adult foster care
