42 CFR 441.301(c) home and community-based settings

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Adult protection
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains adult protection under the Minnesota Vulnerable Adults Act. It defines who is a vulnerable adult, the types of maltreatment, who must report, and how counties and Tribal Nations provide adult protective services after a report to the Minnesota Adult Abuse Reporting Center.
requires: A vulnerable adult is a person 18 or older who lives in or gets services from a facility or provider licensed by the Department of Human Services or the Department of Health, receives personal care assistance or Community First Services and Supports, or has an impairment that keeps them from meeting basic needs or protecting themselves.
Maltreatment includes emotional abuse, financial exploitation, neglect, physical abuse, self-neglect and sexual abuse, as defined on the page.

Mandated reporters, including social service professionals, licensed providers and enrolled Medical Assistance providers, must report suspected maltreatment immediately to the Minnesota Adult Abuse Reporting Center online or at 1-844-880-1574.

Counties and Tribal Nations provide adult protective services in the least restrictive way, such as arranging care, seeking protective orders or guardianship, or arranging a sexual assault examination.
Lead investigative agencies are counties, the Department of Human Services licensing function and the Department of Health, depending on the alleged perpetrator's relationship to a licensed service.
equityCheck: Make sure reporting information and the brochure are given in the person's language and format, and that interpreters are used in investigations.
Check that protective responses respect the person's own choices and culture and stay least restrictive; removal or guardianship should not be the default for any group.
Track reports and outcomes by race, language, disability and region to spot under-reporting or over-intervention.

source.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Adult protection

relatedSources.title: Minnesota Statutes 626.557
Minnesota Statutes 626.5572

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Alternative Care conversion case management
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes Alternative Care conversion case management, which coordinates discharge planning so a person in a nursing facility, hospital, intermediate care facility or certified boarding care home can move to the community with Alternative Care services. It sets eligibility, covered activities, the 180-day limit and the Medicaid Management Information System steps.
requires: The person must live in a qualified setting, plan to move to the community and plan to receive Alternative Care services.
Covered activities include building and carrying out a relocation plan, coordinating referrals and communicating with the person, their representative, informal supports and providers.
The service is limited to 180 consecutive days per admission; the lead agency must close the service agreement if the person stays in the setting longer.
If the person becomes eligible for Medical Assistance, the lead agency closes Alternative Care and opens relocation service coordination targeted case management instead.
The service is paid at the pre-determined rate and is not counted against the person's Alternative Care cap.
equityCheck: Check that people whose first language is not English, and people without family advocates, are offered conversion case management as readily as others.
Watch the 180-day clock for people who face housing shortages in their area so they are not left without support when it runs out.

source.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Alternative Care conversion case management

relatedSources.title: Minnesota Statutes 256B.0913

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Alternative Care program
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page is the policy page for Alternative Care, a state program with federal 1115 demonstration approval that funds home and community-based services for people age 65 and older who need nursing facility level of care, choose to live in the community and are not yet financially eligible for Medical Assistance. It lists eligibility, covered and non-covered services, estate recovery and funding rules.
requires: To qualify a person must be a Minnesota resident and a citizen, national or qualified non-citizen, be 65 or older, be assessed by MnCHOICES to need nursing facility level of care, have a support plan that fits the case mix budget, and have income and assets that cannot pay for 135 days of nursing facility care.
A person cannot be on Alternative Care while on Medical Assistance; temporary Alternative Care may cover up to 60 days while a Medical Assistance application is pending.

Covered services include adult day services, case management, chore, consumer directed community supports, home-delivered meals, homemaker, home care nursing, respite, specialized equipment and non-medical transportation; residential placements such as customized living are not covered.
Alternative Care follows the same transfer penalty and estate claim rules as Medical Assistance; the case manager must file an estate claim referral (form 4801) when a person dies.
Since July 1, 2015, all Alternative Care funds sit in one statewide account; the Department of Human Services no longer allocates funds to individual lead agencies.
People on Alternative Care must complete the Client Disclosure Form, form 3548, at least yearly or when finances change.
equityCheck: Check that citizenship and immigration verification steps are explained in the person's language and do not delay services for eligible people.
Make sure the estate recovery information (form 5186) is given and understood before enrollment so families are not surprised later.
Compare Alternative Care use across counties and Tribal Nations to see whether older adults in some areas are routed to nursing facilities instead.

source.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Alternative Care

relatedSources.title: Minnesota Statutes 256B.0913
Alternative Care 1115 demonstration record at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Appeals
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains a person's right to a fair hearing when they disagree with a decision by the state, a county, a Tribal Nation or a health plan about their services, eligibility or payments. It covers the county and Tribal Nation duties to explain appeal rights, send notices of action and share appeal paperwork, and the conciliation conference option for people with developmental disabilities.
requires: The county or Tribal Nation must give the person their appeal rights during assessment and support planning and document that it did so.
A notice of action must be sent when an assessment or reassessment is completed and when services are denied, ended or reduced.
Since January 1, 2018, a person in a managed care organization must use the plan's appeal process before appealing to the Department of Human Services Appeals Division.
During an appeal the county or Tribal Nation must send all appeal paperwork to the person, the Appeals Division and the Aging and Adult Services or Disability Services division, and keep copies.

A person with a developmental disability or related condition may request a case management conciliation conference; they may then appeal within 90 days of the conference if it is not held within 30 days, no report is issued, or they are unhappy with the result.
equityCheck: Check that appeal rights are explained verbally and in writing in the person's language and in an accessible format, not just signed on a form.
Look at who actually files appeals; low appeal rates in a community may mean people do not know their rights or fear losing services.
Offer help preparing for the hearing, including interpreters and phone or in-person options, so people without advocates can take part.

source.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Appeals

relatedSources.title: Minnesota Statutes 256.045
Your Appeal Rights, form 1941

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Assessment and support planning overview
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page introduces the assessment and support planning section. It explains that access to most long-term services and supports starts with an assessment, and that when a person receives publicly funded services the lead agency works with them to build a person-centered support plan that reflects their needs, preferences and goals. It links to every assessment and planning page in the manual.
requires: An assessment helps the person learn which public programs could pay for services and what other options exist if they do not qualify.
The lead agency must develop a person-centered support plan with the person that supports informed decision-making about services that help them live and take part in their community.
For people on Community First Services and Supports, a consultation services provider also offers support planning help.

The section includes pages on assessment timelines, nursing facility assessment for people 64 and younger, county of residence procedures, waiving annual reassessment, Developmental Disabilities screening, initial assessment review, MnCHOICES, certified assessors, notice of action, emergency backup planning, informed choice and residential support service criteria.
equityCheck: Check that the assessment conversation happens in the person's language and preferred format, with an interpreter when needed, at a time and place that works for them.
Make sure the support plan records the person's own goals and culture, not only the services a provider has available.
Review assessment timeliness and plan quality across counties and Tribal Nations to see where people wait longer or get thinner plans.

source.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Assessment and support planning overview

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Assessment applicability and timelines
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page sets which assessment a person needs and when. It covers in-person versus remote assessments, initial assessments, how long an assessment stays valid, annual reassessments, the 65th birthday reassessment, functional needs updates for Alternative Care and the Elderly Waiver, and returning to a disability waiver after age 65.
requires: All initial assessments must be in person, completed no later than 20 business days after the request; the assessor must give the person an estimated completion timeline, and urgent requests must be expedited.

An initial assessment is valid for 365 days to establish eligibility or open a program; the lead agency must determine the outcome within 60 days of the interview, and other assessment types are valid for 60 days.
Annual reassessments are required for everyone on a waiver, Alternative Care, Community First Services and Supports or Essential Community Supports, within 60 days before the service agreement ends.

For the four disability waivers, assessments completed on or after January 1, 2026 may use remote reassessment (video or telephone) for four consecutive years, with an in-person reassessment in the fifth year; the person must be given informed choice and give informed consent, and the lead agency must document that choice.

During the person's 64th year the county or Tribal Nation must discuss service options and the effects of moving to the Elderly Waiver at 65; the 65th birthday reassessment may not happen earlier than the month before the birthday.
A functional needs update is a remote update of assessed need available only for Alternative Care and the Elderly Waiver, due within 20 calendar days of the request.
equityCheck: When offering a remote reassessment, consider interpreter needs, hearing or memory loss and recent changes in the person's life; a remote option must not be used because it is cheaper or faster for the agency.
Track assessment wait times by county and Tribal Nation against the 20-business-day rule and look for who waits longest.

Make sure the 65th birthday discussion covers services the Elderly Waiver does not offer, such as employment supports, so people are not moved into a narrower program without understanding the trade-off.

Checklist for 65th Birthday Discussion, form 8691

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Assistive technology
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines assistive technology under the Developmental Disabilities Waiver: devices or equipment that improve a person's ability to communicate, control their environment or do daily activities. It covers the assessment and equipment parts of the service, who may assess, how electronic tablets are funded, and authorization before discharge from an institution.
requires: Assistive technology assessment covers evaluating the person's need for devices, including software; equipment covers trial rental, customization, training, maintenance, repair and ongoing training for the person and caregiver.
A tablet used only for communication is funded by the state plan as durable medical equipment; a tablet used for both environmental control and communication is funded by this waiver service.

Only listed professionals may do the assessment, such as a licensed physician, a certified assistive technology professional, an occupational therapist, a registered physical therapist or a certified speech-language pathologist; direct-contact providers need a background study.
The lead agency authorizes the service at the market rate within the Long-Term Services and Supports Service Rate Limits (form 3945).
The lead agency may authorize and arrange the technology before a person leaves an institution but can bill only after discharge and waiver enrollment.
equityCheck: Check that assistive technology is discussed at assessment for everyone, including people whose communication needs are easy to overlook or who speak a language other than English.
Confirm the person and their caregiver get training in a form they can use, not only a device.
Look at how often this service is authorized by county and Tribal Nation; low use in an area may mean a shortage of qualified assessors.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Brain Injury Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page is the program page for the Brain Injury Waiver, which funds home and community-based services for children and adults with a brain injury who need the level of care of a specialized nursing facility or a neurobehavioral hospital. It lists the nine eligibility criteria and every covered service, and points to the shared waiver processes.
requires: To qualify a person must be eligible for Medical Assistance, be certified disabled, be younger than 65 when first opening to the waiver, and be assessed through MnCHOICES to need nursing facility or neurobehavioral hospital level of care.

The person must have a documented acquired or traumatic brain injury, or a degenerative or genetic disease with cognitive impairment that became symptomatic at 18 or later, with significant cognitive and behavioral impairment.

The person must have the potential to benefit from rehabilitative services, need supports beyond the Medical Assistance state plan, and need a provider with brain injury expertise or a higher amount or rate of service.

Covered services include 24-hour emergency assistance, adult day services, case management, community residential services, consumer directed community supports, customized living, day support, employment services, individualized home supports, integrated community supports, positive support services, respite, transitional services and transportation.
Assessors use the Brain Injury Waiver Eligibility and Documentation Checklist, form 3471B.
equityCheck: Check that people whose brain injury happened in another country or without medical records get help documenting the diagnosis rather than being turned away.
Make sure the choice of waiver, including the Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver, is explained so the person is not placed by habit.
Review enrollment by race, language and region against prevalence of brain injury to spot who is missing.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waiver allocations
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains how the Department of Human Services distributes allocations for the Brain Injury Waiver, the Community Alternative Care Waiver and the Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver to lead agencies. It describes the state pool, the priorities lead agencies use when awarding allocations and the factors in the Community Access for Disability Inclusion allocation formula.
requires: The Department keeps a state pool of Brain Injury Waiver allocations and Community Alternative Care Waiver conversion allocations and manages statewide distribution; lead agencies view their allocations in the Waiver Management System.

Lead agencies must prioritize eligible people in the community who would otherwise need nursing facility or hospital care, manage waiver funds to 97 percent while serving people on waiting lists, and follow the statewide priorities in Minnesota Statutes 256B.49, subdivision 11a.
Community Access for Disability Inclusion allocations use a formula based on each county's share of re-use allocations, waiting list, waiver recipients, service days and population.

Brain Injury and Community Alternative Care allocations are accessed through the S2 pool in the Waiver Management System; a lead agency without funds for an eligible person contacts the Disability Services Division response center.
equityCheck: Check whether waiting list length and time to funding differ by county or Tribal Nation, and whether the formula's population and service-day factors disadvantage smaller or rural agencies.
When a lead agency says it has no allocation, confirm the state pool request was made so a person is not denied because of where they live.
Review who moves off the waiting list first and whether the statewide priorities are applied the same way for everyone.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waiver conversion and diversion
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines a waiver conversion, which is when a person enrolls in the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care or Community Access for Disability Inclusion waiver immediately after leaving an institution where Medical Assistance paid for at least 30 days of care, and a diversion, which covers everyone else who is eligible. The distinction matters because conversion and diversion allocations are managed differently.
requires: A Brain Injury Waiver neurobehavioral conversion applies when the person enrolls immediately on discharge from a long-term care hospital where they received neurobehavioral services paid by Medical Assistance for at least 30 days; a Brain Injury Waiver nursing facility conversion applies when the person enrolls immediately on discharge from a nursing facility after at least 30 days of Medical Assistance-paid care.
A Community Alternative Care Waiver conversion applies when the person enrolls immediately on discharge from a hospital after at least 30 days of Medical Assistance-paid hospital care.

A Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver conversion applies when the person enrolls immediately on discharge from a nursing facility after at least 30 days of Medical Assistance-paid nursing facility care.
A person who meets waiver eligibility but not the conversion criteria, including people leaving other institutions or treatment facilities, is a diversion.
The page was last updated in 2011; the allocations page for these waivers explains how conversion and diversion allocations are managed.
equityCheck: Check whether people leaving hospitals or nursing facilities without 30 days of Medical Assistance-paid care wait longer for a diversion allocation than people who qualify as conversions.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Care coordination
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes care coordination for people enrolled in Minnesota Senior Health Options, Minnesota Senior Care Plus or Special Needs BasicCare. It explains the care coordinator's role, who may be one, and how the roles split when a person in managed care uses a disability waiver through a county or Tribal Nation.
requires: A care coordinator must be a social worker, licensed social worker, registered nurse, physician assistant, nurse practitioner, public health nurse or physician; for the senior programs most must also be certified assessors.

The care coordinator completes a health risk assessment, builds a person-centered support plan, helps with care transitions, links the person to services, educates about health and Medicare, and helps with grievances.

A person in managed care who asks for the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion or Developmental Disabilities waiver gets the MnCHOICES assessment, case management and waiver authorizations from the county or Tribal Nation, with fee-for-service Medical Assistance paying for waiver services.

When county or Tribal Nation staff fill both the case manager and care coordinator roles, they bill the managed care organization for health-related support and the disability waiver for disability-specific support planning.

The page states that people living on or near the White Earth, Leech Lake, Red Lake, Mille Lacs or Fond du Lac reservations may be able to choose Elderly Waiver services through the Tribal health or human services division or through the managed care organization.
equityCheck: Check that a person in managed care understands that disability waiver services come from the county or Tribal Nation, and who to call for what, so no one falls between two systems.
Make sure health education and Medicare information are given in the person's language and reading level.
Review whether people in dual-role arrangements get the same amount of support planning time as people with separate staff.

source.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Care coordination

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Caregiver living expenses
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines caregiver living expenses, which reimburse part of the rent and food of an unrelated caregiver who lives with an adult on a disability waiver and also provides an approved waiver service. It covers eligibility, approved services, exclusions and the lead agency's duties.
requires: The person must be an adult living in their own home with an unrelated live-in caregiver who provides consumer directed community supports, extended home care nursing (Community Alternative Care Waiver only), extended personal care assistance, or individualized home supports with or without training.
Reimbursement is not allowed for relatives or legally responsible individuals, in a home owned or leased by a Medical Assistance-enrolled provider, or when the caregiver owns the home.
The service cannot be combined with community residential services, out-of-home crisis respite, customized living, family residential services or integrated community supports.

The lead agency must confirm the caregiver's enrollment status if required, make sure the expenses are reasonable, document the caregiver's role outside the paid service in the support plan, and use the Caregiver Living Expenses Worksheet, form 4929.
The lead agency authorizes the service at the market rate based on the worksheet.
equityCheck: Consider whether this option is explained to people whose culture favors shared households, since it can support living arrangements outside provider-owned settings.
Check that 'reasonable expenses' are judged against local housing costs so people in high-cost or rural areas are not penalized.
Review use by region and race to see whether some communities never hear about this option.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Case management aide
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines the case management aide, a role that helps a waiver, Alternative Care or Essential Community Supports case manager with administrative tasks. It lists what an aide may and may not do, the aide's qualifications and billing limits.
requires: An aide may prepare and file case materials, contact providers to schedule services or make referrals, make administrative phone contacts, enter screening documents and service authorizations in the Medicaid Management Information System, and update support plan documentation under the case manager's oversight.
An aide cannot take on duties that need professional judgment, conduct assessments or reassessments, or develop support plans.

An aide must be a high school graduate with one year of related experience or post-secondary education, employed by an agency that provides case management, and supervised by a qualified case manager.
Neither the case manager nor the aide may have a financial interest in the person's services.

Aide services are paid at the predetermined rate, cannot be billed as case management, cannot be billed by two providers on the same day, and are not billable under Alternative Care or the Elderly Waiver when the person uses consumer directed community supports.
equityCheck: Make sure the person knows the difference between their case manager and the aide and can reach the case manager directly for decisions.
Check that aides are not the main contact for people with language or communication needs when those needs call for professional judgment.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Case management overview
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page is the section overview for case management. It describes what case managers do and lists the types of case management the Department of Human Services administers, including waiver, Alternative Care and Essential Community Supports case management, Rule 185 developmental disabilities case management, care coordination and several targeted case management programs.
requires: Case managers work with people to understand their needs, make plans to meet their needs and goals, connect them with services, track progress and follow up with others who help them.

Types include Alternative Care conversion case management, care coordination, developmental disabilities (Rule 185) case management, relocation service coordination targeted case management, vulnerable adult and developmental disability targeted case management, and waiver, Alternative Care and Essential Community Supports case management.
Child welfare and mental health targeted case management are administered separately and linked from the page.
equityCheck: Check that each person knows which type of case management they have, who their case manager is and how to reach them directly.
Compare caseloads and contact frequency across counties and Tribal Nations so people in some areas do not get less attention.

source.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Case management

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Changes to the size of setting by waiver service (fifth bed)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains when a licensed foster care or community residential setting serving people on the four disability waivers may temporarily or permanently serve a fifth person. It covers temporary capacity variances for emergencies, crisis respite and respite, and the permanent fifth bed capacity license.
requires: A temporary capacity variance lets a license holder serve up to five people for a limited time; an initial variance covers one specific person for no more than six months, and a general variance lasts the license period but any one person may stay no more than six months.

A temporary bed may be requested only in an emergency such as a natural disaster, risk of separating siblings, risk of hospital or nursing facility placement, sudden closure of the person's home or loss of the primary caregiver.

Before adding a temporary bed the license holder must authorize waiver services per person, have enough space and staff, and consult the people who already live there, their representatives and case managers.

Respite variances limit the provider to two different respite users a month and 120 respite days a year, require a separate bedroom, and require 60 days' written notice to current residents before the first placement.

A community residential setting may have a capacity of five only if everyone is age 55 or older without a serious and persistent mental illness or developmental disability; homes dually licensed as supervised living facilities on the Developmental Disabilities Waiver may serve up to six adults.
equityCheck: Confirm the people already living in the setting were asked about the added resident and that their privacy and preferences were respected, not only notified.
Watch whether emergency placements into a fifth bed become long-term for people without family advocates.
Review which regions rely on fifth-bed variances; heavy use may signal a shortage of own-home options there.

Minnesota Statutes 245A.04

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Consumer Support Grant transition to Community First Services and Supports
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page compares the Consumer Support Grant, a state-funded alternative to personal care assistance, home health aide and home care nursing, with Community First Services and Supports, which is replacing both the grant and personal care assistance. It explains eligibility, how budgets differ, what people and financial management services providers are responsible for, and the transition steps at the person's assessment.
requires: The Consumer Support Grant is a state-funded alternative to home care nursing, home health aide and personal care assistance; Community First Services and Supports will replace both personal care assistance and the grant.

To use the grant a person must be eligible for Medical Assistance, be able to direct their care or have a representative who can, have a functional limitation that requires ongoing supports, live in their own or family home, have a personal care assistance or home care nursing home care rating, and not be on Alternative Care, a waiver, Minnesota Senior Health Options or Minnesota Senior Care Plus, personal care assistance, home health aide, home care nursing or the Family Support Grant.

In the grant a person receives only the state share of funding; in Community First Services and Supports a person receives state and federal funding, works with a consultation services provider, has a worker training budget, and can use either model while on a waiver, Alternative Care or managed care; a budget model budget is about twice the grant budget, and people with the LT home care rating get more hours.

A person using the grant in place of personal care assistance moves to Community First Services and Supports at their assessment: the county or Tribal Nation assesses, the person picks a consultation services provider, and that provider explains the differences; a person using the grant in place of home care nursing cannot replace nursing hours with Community First Services and Supports and must be offered a MnCHOICES assessment to plan other services.

People who employ workers in the grant or the budget model recruit, train, schedule, supervise, set pay for and verify hours of their workers and follow the collective bargaining agreement; financial management services providers enroll workers, bill, run payroll and reimburse approved goods and services.

Covered goods and services must relate directly to the person's functional limitations, help delay or prevent out-of-home placement, relate to an assessed need and not be covered by another source; Community First Services and Supports has more restrictions on goods and services.
equityCheck: Check that people moving from the grant understand the new restrictions on goods and services before they lose access to them.
Ask whether consultation services providers are available in the person's language and region.

source.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Consumer Support Grant transition to Community First Services and Supports (page posted October 1, 2003; page reviewed May 20, 2024; page updated May 21, 2026)

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Developmental Disabilities Waiver diversion allocations
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains how the Department of Human Services distributes new Developmental Disabilities Waiver diversion allocations to lead agencies each calendar year, the factors in the allocation method, and how unused allocations are reviewed and reassigned each quarter. Lead agencies see their allocations in the Waiver Management System.
requires: The Department of Human Services distributes new waiver allocations each calendar year and reviews unused new diversion allocations every quarter, reassigning them to maximize use and address unmet needs.

Additional allocations are distributed using each county's number of people on the Developmental Disabilities Waiver waiting list, the number added to the waiver through service optimization, unused diversions in the current year and the aggregate reserve dollar amount.

The allocation method uses each county's share of total waiver recipients, waiver service days, state population, people on the waiting list, people added through service optimization, unused diversions from the prior year and projected current-year spending.
Alliance partnerships receive priority as required by Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0916.
Legal authority listed on the page: the federally approved Developmental Disabilities Waiver plan and Minnesota Statutes section 256B.092, subdivision 12 (statewide priorities).
equityCheck: Compare waiting list size and time to funding across counties and Tribal Nations, and ask whether the allocation method closes or widens those gaps.
Check how reassigned allocations reach people in counties that underuse their allocations while people elsewhere wait.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Electronic visit verification
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains electronic visit verification, the electronic system the federal 21st Century Cures Act requires providers of personal care services and home health services to use to record in-home and community visits. It describes the six data elements, Minnesota's hybrid model with a state-selected system and third-party options, the phased rollout from June 2022 to October 2023, provider training duties, and compliance enforcement that began September 1, 2024.
requires: Providers of personal care services (including personal care assistance, Community First Services and Supports and some waiver services) and home health care providers must use electronic visit verification for the state to receive full federal Medicaid matching funds, under Public Law 114-255 signed in December 2016.
The system verifies the type of service, who received it, the date, the location, who provided it, and when it began and ended.
Minnesota uses a hybrid model: providers may use the state-selected system, HHAeXchange, or a third-party system that sends data meeting state requirements to the state data aggregator.

Rollout was phased: financial management services providers for consumer-directed community supports and the Consumer Support Grant on June 20, 2022; remaining personal care service providers on November 14 and December 12, 2022; managed care organizations on June 5, 2023; home health services on October 16, 2023.

Providers, and people who receive financial management services with employer and budget authority, are responsible for training and onboarding the people they support and their direct support workers on the chosen system.

Billing does not change; the Department of Human Services uses the data in post-payment review, which may lead to takebacks when claims are not supported by visit data; effective September 1, 2024 the Department reviews usage and enforces compliance for all providers regardless of payer.
equityCheck: Ask how workers and people without smartphones, reliable internet or English fluency are supported to use the system, and whether telephone and other methods are offered.
Check that self-directed participants who act as employers got training in their language and are not penalized for system problems outside their control.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Eligibility update for home and community-based services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes the eligibility update, a follow-up activity that let a lead agency extend the time to decide program eligibility after an initial in-person assessment without doing another assessment. Lead agencies may no longer use eligibility updates for assessments completed on or after July 1, 2025; they use the initial assessment review instead. The page remains for assessments dated before that.
requires: Eligibility updates apply only to assessments with activity dates before July 1, 2025; for later assessments the lead agency must use the initial assessment review.
An eligibility update could be completed between the 60th and 90th day after the initial assessment and gave the lead agency another 60 days to establish eligibility.

It was used when a person was waiting on a disability determination, a Medical Assistance or long-term care application, a Developmental Disabilities diagnostic determination or a delayed institutional discharge.
The certified assessor who did the initial assessment completed the update, in direct communication with the person, and entered it in MnCHOICES and the Medicaid Management Information System.
It could not replace an in-person assessment, follow a reassessment, be used for someone already open to a program, or be done more than once.
equityCheck: Delays past 60 days often come from backlogs in Medical Assistance long-term care eligibility or disability determinations; check whether those backlogs fall harder on some counties, Tribal Nations or language groups.
Make sure the switch to initial assessment reviews does not leave people assessed before July 1, 2025 without a path to services.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Employment development services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines employment development services, individualized waiver services that help a person get competitive, integrated employment, become self-employed or start a microenterprise business. The service has a plan phase and a find phase, a 12-month limit, and must not duplicate services available from Vocational Rehabilitation Services, State Services for the Blind or special education.
requires: A person must be eligible for one of the four disability waivers, have employment development as an assessed need in their support plan, and not have access to the same services through Vocational Rehabilitation Services, State Services for the Blind or the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act.

Covered job development services include strengths-based assessment and discovery (the planning phase may not exceed 120 days), support during orientation for up to 30 days after a new job starts, job search help, benefits analysis, help negotiating employment terms, applications and resumes, and outreach to businesses.

Covered self-employment services include help choosing and registering a business, writing a business plan, finding start-up financing, setting up a legal structure, marketing, licenses and permits, insurance and bookkeeping; a microenterprise has five or fewer employees and the provider may not have a financial interest in it.

Services are authorized in a plan phase (work goals, a benefits plan and a job search launch) or a find phase; the whole service should end after 12 months, with reauthorization allowed for a verifiable change in employment, a health condition or life event, a provider change, or up to 60 days while waiting for a Vocational Rehabilitation Services eligibility decision.

Not covered: incentive payments to employers, wage supplements, unrelated vocational training, services funded under special education or the Rehabilitation Act, and services in facility-based or sheltered workshop settings.

Providers must enroll with Minnesota Health Care Programs, hold a chapter 245D intensive support services license, have background studies and ensure staff competency; the service is a framework service paid through the Rate Management System and the plan and find phases can be delivered through remote support.
equityCheck: Check whether the lead agency confirmed Vocational Rehabilitation Services availability without leaving the person waiting with no service.
Compare job placement outcomes across counties, Tribal Nations, race and disability type.
Ask whether self-employment was presented as an option to people whose culture or community favors it.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Employment exploration services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines employment exploration services, a waiver service that helps a person learn about competitive, integrated employment in their community so they can make an informed decision about work. It lists covered and non-covered activities, the 12-month limit, group size, remote delivery, provider standards and billing rules.
requires: To receive the service a person must be eligible for the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion or Developmental Disabilities waiver and have employment exploration as an assessed need in their support plan.

Covered activities include educational visits to businesses, career education, peer mentoring with employed people with disabilities, job shadowing and try-outs, job clubs, individualized and volunteer work experiences, benefits analysis, and planning for assistive technology and accommodations.

The service is time-limited and should end after a maximum of 12 months; the lead agency may reauthorize it only when the person has not yet made an informed decision about competitive, integrated employment, has a health condition or life event that interrupted services, or changes providers.

Group size may not exceed five people; not covered are incentive payments to employers, wage supplements, unrelated vocational training, services available under special education or the Rehabilitation Act, and services in facility-based or sheltered workshop settings.

Providers must enroll with Minnesota Health Care Programs, hold a chapter 245D intensive support services license, have background studies, ensure staff competency and report controlled procedures and restraint use on the Behavior Intervention Report Form (form 5148).

Employment exploration is a framework service paid through the Rate Management System; in-service transportation is included, travel between home and the service site is billed as waiver transportation, and the service may be delivered through remote support.
equityCheck: Check that the person met peers with disabilities who work in community jobs and visited real workplaces before deciding about work.
Review reauthorizations past 12 months for patterns that keep some groups in exploration without a path to a job.
Ask whether benefits information was explained in the person's language.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Employment overview (Employment First)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page introduces the employment section. It states that Minnesota is an Employment First state that wants everyone who wants to work in competitive, integrated jobs to be able to do so with the supports they need. It points to the federal Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, asks each lead agency to name an employment liaison, and links the three waiver employment services and the guidance documents.
requires: Minnesota is an Employment First state: the goal is that everyone who wants to work in competitive, integrated employment can do so with the supports they need.

The federal Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act increases access to employment, education, training and support services and limits the use of subminimum wages; the manual has a separate page with guidance for lead agencies.

The Department of Human Services asks each lead agency to appoint at least one staff person as its employment liaison, the main point of contact for building a coordinated system that helps people on waivers meet their employment goals.

Employment liaisons work with Vocational Rehabilitation Services and State Services for the Blind and with employment service providers, and make sure lead agency staff and contracted staff know new processes and have tools for the work.

The employment policy pages are employment exploration services, employment development services, employment support services and prevocational services; guidance pages cover employment services authorization, lead agency employment liaisons, and transportation with day and employment services.
equityCheck: Compare the share of working-age waiver recipients with competitive, integrated employment across counties, Tribal Nations, race and disability type.
Check that each lead agency has a named employment liaison and that people know how to reach that person.
Ask whether information about work and benefits was given in the person's language and in a form they could use.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Employment support services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines employment support services, individualized waiver services that help people keep paid employment in community businesses or run their own business. Services happen in integrated community settings, may be individual or in groups of up to six, and cannot be delivered in facility-based settings or in businesses owned by the person's day and employment services provider.
requires: A person must receive Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion or Developmental Disabilities waiver services and have employment support as an assessed need in their support plan.

Covered job support includes job analysis and redesign, coaching on work skills and coworker relationships, help understanding wages and benefits, transportation training, arranging accommodations and assistive technology, advocacy with the employer, building natural supports, fading schedules, and progress reporting; self-employment support covers day-to-day business operations.

Group employment support serves two to six people who share one job's tasks; coaching people who hold separate jobs at different locations is individual support with a shared coaching arrangement, not group support.

Services may not be delivered in a facility-based setting or in a business owned or operated by the organization that provides the person's day and employment services; wages and benefits must follow federal and state law.
A person can receive employment support and employment development at the same time while looking for other work, and can receive exploration services only together with group employment support.

Providers must enroll with Minnesota Health Care Programs, hold a chapter 245D intensive support services license, have background studies and ensure staff competency; the service is a framework service paid through the Rate Management System and can be delivered through remote support.
equityCheck: Check how many people are in group arrangements versus individual jobs, and whether the person chose the arrangement.
Ask whether the person's job supports include a plan to fade coaching and build natural supports at work.
Compare wages and hours of supported employees across race, disability type and region.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Environmental accessibility adaptations (home and vehicle modifications)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines environmental accessibility adaptations, physical changes to a person's primary home or vehicle that protect health and safety or let the person function more independently. It covers assessments and installations, the yearly service limits for the aging programs and for the four disability waivers, the exception process to exceed the disability waiver limit, covered and non-covered home modifications, and how work can begin before a person leaves an institution.
requires: A modification must be for the person's direct and specific benefit, necessary for health and safety or greater independence, and necessary to meet an assessed need.

Under Alternative Care and the Elderly Waiver, combined home and vehicle assessments and installations are limited each waiver year to the amount in the Long-Term Services and Supports Service Rate Limits (form 3945), adjusted each January 1 by the Consumer Price Index, within the case mix budget cap, with no exceptions.

Under the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion and Developmental Disabilities waivers, a person may receive up to $40,000 per year counted back from the service agreement end date; the lead agency may ask the Department of Human Services for an exception that allows another $40,000 drawn from the next year's budget, for a maximum of $80,000 in two years.

An exception requires that other options were explored with the person, the project is cost effective, two comparison bids are included, the work is needed in the current year, and it increases functional use of the home or community access; the lead agency uses the checklist (form 5504C) and the exception request (form 5504B).

Covered home modifications include bathroom and kitchen changes, grab bars, ramps, widened doorways, entry and exit changes tied to assessed needs, shatterproof windows, specialized electrical and plumbing for medical equipment, monitoring technology and alarm systems required by life safety codes; not covered are additions to square footage (except the separate additional square footage policy), comfort or convenience items, items not for the person's direct benefit, and the homeowner's own maintenance and code responsibilities.

The lead agency may let a provider start a modification before the person leaves an institution when discharge and waiver enrollment are expected and the change is needed to return to the community; the service is authorized after enrollment, and reimbursement for unforeseen circumstances is available if the person does not enroll.
equityCheck: Check that renters, people in Tribal housing and people in older or rural homes can use the service and that landlord permission issues are addressed.
Compare exception approvals and denials across lead agencies and communities.
Ask whether the person was told about assistive technology and specialized equipment options as well as modifications.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Essential Community Supports
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page is the program page for Essential Community Supports, community-based services for people age 65 and older who do not need nursing facility level of care, choose to live in the community and are not yet financially eligible for Medical Assistance. It lists eligibility, covered services, the monthly budget limit and the eligibility worksheets the lead agency must complete each year.
requires: A person must be 65 or older, not financially eligible for Medical Assistance, not eligible for nursing facility level of care, live in their own home or apartment, meet Alternative Care financial eligibility (income and assets cannot pay for 135 days of nursing facility care) and need one or more of the program's services to live in the community.

The program includes case management plus adult day services, chore services, community living assistance, family caregiver services, home-delivered meals, homemaker and personal emergency response systems.

Services are not covered when available through another funding source such as Medicare, Medical Assistance or long-term care insurance; Older Americans Act funding is not treated as another funding source.

There is a maximum monthly budget per person for all services, and case management is limited to a maximum yearly amount within that budget; the amounts are in the Long-Term Services and Supports Service Rate Limits document (form 3945).

The lead agency case manager helps the person complete the eligibility worksheet (form 6683, or form 6683A for a married person with a community spouse), completes the financial disclosure form (form 6826), and must reassess eligibility every year.
equityCheck: Check that older adults who do not qualify for a waiver are told about this program and about Older Americans Act services.
Ask whether the monthly budget limit meets needs in high-cost areas.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Family residential services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines family residential services, training or habilitation, ongoing residential care and supportive services for adults or children who live in a licensed family foster care home where the license holder lives. It explains how the service differs from community residential services, the size limit of four people, settings that cannot be used, collocation limits, licensing, life sharing and the move to tiered rates in 2026.
requires: The service is delivered in a licensed family foster care setting where the license holder lives in the home; community residential services, by contrast, use shift staff in a corporate setting; a life-sharing arrangement for an adult 18 or older can be supported through this service.

Covered services are individualized training, habilitation, residential care and supports in areas such as activities of daily living, communication, community participation, health care, household management, money management, positive behavior and mental health support, self-care and socialization; the service meets the habilitation requirement of the Developmental Disabilities Waiver.

Not covered: the basic foster care rate and difficulty of care rate, vehicle and facility upkeep, services paid by other sources, items of comfort, payment for full-day absences, payments to the person, room and board including Housing Support for adults, and services to the person's immediate family.

No more than four people unrelated to the principal care provider may live in the setting; exceptions are settings that continuously provided waiver services before July 1, 2000 (Brain Injury and Community Access for Disability Inclusion) or May 1, 2001 (Community Alternative Care), people age 55 or older, and emergency exceptions the Department of Human Services may approve for up to five people for no more than two years.

The lead agency may not authorize the service in a setting adjoined to or on the same property as a hospital, nursing facility, intermediate care facility or institution for mental disease, and may authorize services in only one of a provider's settings on the same or adjoining property, with exceptions tied to the 2017 and 2018 settings attestation process.

Providers must be enrolled, hold a chapter 245D intensive support services license, have background studies and report controlled procedures and restraint use on the Behavior Intervention Report Form (form 5148); services with a renewal or new start date of April 1, 2026 or later are tiered-rate services under the Disability Waiver Rate System.
equityCheck: Ask whether the person chose the home and the people they live with, and whether host families reflect the person's culture and language when the person wants that.
Review tiered-rate assignments for patterns by race, disability type or region.
Check that children in family residential settings keep contact with their own families and communities.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Guide to encouraging informed choice and discussing risk
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual guide helps support planners (case managers, care coordinators and certified assessors) decide when and how to talk with people about their right to make informed choices that may include risk. It defines informed choice, risk and maltreatment, lists the support planner's duties, gives a four-step conversation guide that can be used through the whole service cycle, and explains how to report suspected maltreatment.
requires: Person-centered practices promote independence, encourage people to make informed choices about their lives and recognize that people have the right to take risks; the support planner must support and encourage informed choice and respect the person's right to take risks.

An informed choice is based on the person's likes, dislikes and community-based experiences, the possible effects on their quality of life, and information about other available options from their support system.

The support planner must keep working assertively with a person who refuses necessary services, understand their reporting duties under the maltreatment laws, understand person-centered planning, and build a plan that meets the person's needs and wants while addressing identified risk.

When the person names a goal, the planner addresses the risk area in the support plan by managing it rather than eliminating it, offers support options even if other team members resist, balances what is important to and for the person, makes sure the person has the information to choose, and updates the plan as successes and challenges are shared.

Legal authority listed on the page: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0911, subdivision 3a, and section 626.557; mandated reporters report suspected maltreatment of a vulnerable adult to the Minnesota Adult Abuse Reporting Center by phone or online form.
equityCheck: Ask whether risk is judged the same way for people of all races, cultures and disability types, or whether some people are steered away from choices others are allowed to make.
Check that the person had community-based experiences and information in their language before the choice was called informed.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Home-delivered meals
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines a home-delivered meal as a nutritionally balanced meal delivered to the person's home. It sets separate eligibility rules for the aging programs and the four disability waivers, limits the service to one meal a day, says when meals cannot be authorized in residential and apartment settings, and lists provider food safety and nutrition standards.
requires: Under Alternative Care, Essential Community Supports and the Elderly Waiver the person must meet the overall program requirements, have an assessed need in the support plan, and the service must be the most cost-effective way to provide a balanced meal; under the four disability waivers the person must also be unable to prepare their own meals because of their disability, and the service may not substitute for parental responsibility or available informal supports.
A person may receive up to one program-funded home-delivered meal a day; the lead agency may authorize other services such as homemaker or individualized home supports to help with additional meals.

Meals are not covered when the person already receives meals through another service or funding source such as adult foster care, community residential services, family residential services, Housing Support, or customized living or integrated community supports that include three meals a day; the service may not be used only to save money on food and does not cover meals for a minor child when a responsible adult is available to cook.

In customized living or integrated community supports settings, meals may be authorized only when the setting provides fewer than three meals a day, a separate provider delivers the meals, and the case manager documents there is no duplication; the person may eat the meal in their unit or a common dining space in the building, and does not need a permanent home.
Lead agencies should authorize meals within program limits and may use Older Americans Act Title III-C meals for people 60 and older when the program cannot authorize enough meals.

Providers (hospitals, restaurants, schools and others) must enroll, follow state and local food safety rules, deliver meals in insulated containers, provide at least one-third of the daily dietary allowance set by the Food and Nutrition Board of the National Academy of Sciences, adapt meals to dietary needs and have menus approved by a licensed dietitian or nutritionist; the service is paid at the predetermined rate.
equityCheck: Ask whether meal providers can offer culturally and religiously appropriate food and whether people in rural areas have a provider at all.
Check that the one-meal-a-day limit is paired with other support when a person cannot cook.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Homemaker
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines homemaker services, help with general cleaning and household activities. There are three types: homemaker cleaning, homemaker home management and homemaker assistance with activities of daily living. The page sets eligibility, what cannot be combined with the service, who counts as a primary caregiver, remote delivery, and provider standards for each type.
requires: A person is eligible when they need support to manage general cleaning and household activities, or when the primary caregiver who normally does them cannot manage them or is temporarily absent; under the four disability waivers the primary caregiver must live at the same address and own or lease the home.

Homemaker cleaning covers light housekeeping and laundry only; home management adds incidental help with arranging transportation, meals, shopping and simple repairs; assistance with activities of daily living adds incidental help with walking, bathing, dressing, eating, grooming and toileting; in every type cleaning must be the main service and the provider monitors the person's well-being and home safety.

Homemaker does not cover training or habilitation and cannot be authorized when it duplicates chore or transitional services, when the person lives in a licensed setting, or when the person receives adult foster care, community residential services, family residential services or customized living; a person in integrated community supports may receive homemaker only from a different provider.
The person need not be present for cleaning but must be present for home management and assistance with activities of daily living; home management may be delivered through remote support.

Under the Developmental Disabilities Waiver, when a parent or unpaid caregiver provides habilitation, the lead agency may authorize homemaker or respite to free the caregiver's time, documented in the support plan; homemaker itself is not habilitation.

Homemaker cleaning is an approval-option direct-delivery service that counties and Tribal Nations may approve from non-enrolled vendors; home management and assistance with activities of daily living require enrollment and a chapter 245D basic support license or a chapter 144A license with a home and community-based services designation, unless a 245D exclusion applies; all providers need a background study.
equityCheck: Check that homemaker is not denied on the assumption that family members in the home will do the work.
Ask whether people who speak languages other than English can find approved vendors in their area.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Individual community living supports
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines individual community living supports, a bundled service for people age 65 and older on Alternative Care or the Elderly Waiver who need scheduled reminders, cues, intermittent or moderate supervision or physical assistance to stay in their own homes. It has six components, is planned on a required planning form, and may be delivered in person or through remote service delivery.
requires: The six components are active cognitive support, adaptive support, activities of daily living support, household management, health, safety and wellness, and community living engagement; the case manager or care coordinator must complete the planning form (form 3751) covering at least two components and say whether each is delivered in person or remotely.

The service is for scheduled, intermittent help; it is not the right service for constant supervision or physical help throughout a task (except bathing), which personal care assistance or Community First Services and Supports meets.

Household management may include cleaning, meals, shopping, budgeting, communication tasks and transportation when it is integral to the goals and no community or informal transportation is available; health, safety and wellness may include medication assistance and health monitoring under written instructions from a licensed health professional, but not telehealth or Medicaid-covered health monitoring.
Community living engagement helps the person reach community activities and resources and build or keep informal supports.
Under the remote support policy, the service is limited to 12 hours a day including remote delivery and requires at least one scheduled in-person visit each week.
Legal authority listed on the page: the federally approved Elderly Waiver plan, the Alternative Care 1115 demonstration, Minnesota Statutes sections 256B.0913 and 256S.13, and 42 CFR 441.725(b)(9).
equityCheck: Check that older adults who speak languages other than English can find providers for this service.
Ask whether remote delivery was the person's choice and whether they have the technology to use it.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Individualized home supports
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines individualized home supports, waiver services that give support or training in community living skills to a person who lives in their own home or their family's home. There are three options: without training, with training, and with family training. The provider may not have a financial interest in the person's housing. The page sets eligibility, the four community living categories, limits such as 16 hours a day and no overnight supervision, and which services cannot be combined with it.
requires: A person must live in their own home or their family's home, and the provider may not have any direct or indirect financial interest in the property or housing where services are delivered; the person must be on the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion or Developmental Disabilities waiver.

Individualized home supports without training gives support, assistance and supervision for adults and children when the person needs consistent help to do tasks safely or wants to keep current skills; with training gives training for adults; with family training gives training and support to the person and their family in the family's home; the with-training and with-family-training options meet the habilitation requirement of the Developmental Disabilities Waiver.

Covered services are support or training in four categories: community participation, health, safety and wellness, household management, and adaptive skills, delivered in the home or in community spaces open to the public, in person or by remote support.

Not covered: supervision when the person is not actively engaged in a covered service, supervision during primary sleeping hours, more than 16 hours a day of in-person service, housing search activities, and services that mainly deliver activities of daily living support; when the person also uses personal care assistance or Community First Services and Supports, the lead agency must tell the person they may choose a different provider and document the choice.

The service cannot be authorized with community residential services, customized living, family residential services or integrated community supports, except that a separate provider with no financial interest in the housing may deliver individualized home supports without training in the community for a person in community residential or family residential services, or with training for a person in customized living.
Individualized home supports with family training is not covered for families licensed to provide adult foster care, child foster care, family residential services or community residential services.
equityCheck: Check that the person was told they may choose a different provider for personal care or Community First Services and Supports than for individualized home supports.
Ask whether families from different cultures are offered family training in their language and in a form that fits their household.
Review the balance between training and ongoing support so people are not kept in a service that no longer builds skills.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Integrated community supports
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines integrated community supports, support and training in community living skills for a person who lives in a living unit of a provider-controlled setting such as an apartment building. The service can be delivered up to 24 hours a day. The page sets eligibility, the four community living service categories, what cannot be authorized with the service, choice of provider, roommate rules and setting requirements, including the setting capacity report.
requires: A person must meet the overall waiver service requirements, live in an approved integrated community supports setting (a setting with at least three living units where the provider owns, leases or has a financial interest in the person's unit) and have an assessed need in at least one community living category: community participation, health, safety and wellness, household management, or adaptive skills.

The service does not cover transportation, nursing, care for family members or the household, or supervision alone; it cannot be authorized with 24-hour emergency assistance, adult foster care, community residential services, customized living, caregiver living expenses, family residential services, individualized home supports, night supervision or respite.

A person who lives in an integrated community supports setting is not required to receive the service; when they do, only the provider who controls the setting may deliver it, and that provider may not deliver other home and community-based services in the setting except transportation and extended home care nursing; the person may instead choose other services from a provider that does not control the setting.

A person receiving the service may also receive chore, home-delivered meals, homemaker and personal care assistance from a different provider, and the case manager must document how the services do not duplicate each other.

When more than one person lives in a unit, the provider may not direct who lives there and must let each person choose, and must document that each person, their case manager and legal representative chose the arrangement.

Settings are provider-controlled home and community-based settings that must meet 42 CFR 441.301(c); before delivering services the provider must submit a setting capacity report (form 8062) to the Department of Human Services for each setting; the service can be delivered through remote support, and the provider must give written reports to the lead agency and the person at least once a year.

Legal authority listed on the page: the federally approved Brain Injury and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waiver plans (2021), the Community Alternative Care and Developmental Disabilities waiver plans (2023), Minnesota Statutes sections 245D.03, 245D.12 and 256B.49, subdivision 23.
equityCheck: Check that the person knows they may refuse the controlling provider's services and choose another provider while keeping their apartment.
Review leases and roommate choices to confirm the person, not the provider, made them.
Watch for buildings where most tenants are waiver recipients and ask whether the setting still meets the federal community integration standard.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Jensen Settlement Agreement
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains the Jensen Settlement Agreement. The agreement settled a 2009 lawsuit against the Department of Human Services about the use of restraint and seclusion at the former Minnesota Extended Treatment Options program. Its Comprehensive Plan of Action led to the Positive Supports Rule and to the development of Minnesota's Olmstead Plan.
requires: The United States District Court for the District of Minnesota approved the settlement agreement on December 5, 2011.

The Positive Supports Rule (Minnesota Rules chapter 9544) replaced the earlier Rule 40 and took effect in August 2015; it sets standards for positive support strategies and limits on restrictive interventions.

The Comprehensive Plan of Action that carried out the settlement had three parts: closing and replacing the Cambridge program with community-based homes and services such as Minnesota Life Bridge, modernizing Rule 40, and developing Minnesota's Olmstead Plan.
On September 4, 2020 the court found the Department of Human Services in substantial compliance with the settlement agreement, and the court's jurisdiction ended on October 25, 2020.
equityCheck: When a plan includes any restriction of a person's rights, check that positive supports were tried first and that the restriction is documented and reviewed.
Ask whether the person is living in the most integrated setting they would choose, and what supports would make a less restrictive setting possible.
Look at data on restraint and emergency interventions by setting and by group to spot where people are more likely to experience restriction.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Lead agency oversight of waiver and Alternative Care approval-option service vendors
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains how a lead agency may approve its own vendors for a set of basic waiver and Alternative Care services instead of using only Minnesota Health Care Programs-enrolled providers. It sets the checks a lead agency must do before approving a vendor and the oversight it must keep up afterward.
requires: A lead agency may choose to use only Minnesota Health Care Programs-enrolled providers, or it may approve its own vendors for the listed basic services.
The lead agency must log each approved vendor on the tracking log (form 7004A), including exclusion-list checks, licenses, background study confirmation and the date of approval.
Vendors that deliver services directly must sign the assurance statement (form 7004B), and the lead agency must re-review direct-delivery vendors at least once every five years.
Vendors providing direct-contact services must complete a Department of Human Services background study.
The lead agency is responsible for overseeing every approval-option service it authorizes and must keep records of those services for at least five years.
equityCheck: Check whether approval-option vendors are available across all parts of your service area, including rural areas and communities with few enrolled providers.
Ask whether vendors reflect the languages and cultures of the people served, and whether people were offered a real choice among options.
Review claims for duplicate or unusual charges evenly across all vendors, not only those serving certain groups.
