policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Level of care (nursing facility, hospital, neurobehavioral hospital, intermediate care facility)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains the four institutional levels of care used to decide waiver eligibility: nursing facility, hospital, neurobehavioral hospital, and intermediate care facility for persons with developmental disabilities. A person must meet the level of care tied to a waiver before the waiver can be opened.
requires: Nursing facility level of care: the person must meet one of five categories of need, such as cognitive or behavioral needs, support in at least four of eight activities of daily living, daily clinical monitoring, or living arrangement and risk factors.

Hospital level of care: the person needs skilled interventions several times a day and a 24-hour plan of care, with health changes that could cause rapid decline; a behavioral health inpatient stay does not count as hospital level of care.

Neurobehavioral hospital level of care: the person meets nursing facility criteria and also needs a formal behavioral support plan, intensive behavioral intervention and access to neurobehavioral hospital services; the person does not need to live in such a hospital.
Intermediate care facility level of care: the person has a developmental disability or related condition, needs active treatment and is unable to generalize learned skills.

The Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver and Elderly Waiver require nursing facility level of care, the Community Alternative Care Waiver requires hospital level of care, and the Brain Injury Waiver requires either specialized nursing facility or neurobehavioral hospital level of care.
equityCheck: Make sure the assessment captures needs that may be under-reported when a person or family is unfamiliar with the system or describes needs differently in their culture or language.
Check that behavioral and cognitive needs are assessed as carefully as physical needs, so people with brain injury or mental health needs are not screened out.
Review level of care denials by county and by group to see whether some communities are more often found ineligible.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Life sharing matching process and ongoing support options
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual resource page describes life sharing, where an adult on a disability waiver lives with an unrelated host individual or family. The page explains how existing waiver services are used to set up and support the arrangement and what each party does.
requires: Life sharing is open to adults age 18 or older on the Brain Injury Waiver, Community Alternative Care Waiver, Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver or Developmental Disabilities Waiver.

Three parties are involved: the person on the waiver, a life-sharing agency licensed under Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D that handles matching, support and billing, and the host individual or family.

The lead agency authorizes family residential services; the life-sharing agency holds the license and is the enrolled provider, and the host home must meet family residential services setting requirements.
A home may include no more than two adult waiver recipients living with the unrelated host family, and the lead agency must monitor this limit.
A live-in unrelated caregiver can also be supported through the caregiver living expenses service.
Minnesota Statutes section 245D.03 lists life sharing among residential supports covered by chapter 245D.
equityCheck: Check that the person chose life sharing freely and was offered other residential options, including their own home with supports.
Ask whether host families are available who share the person's language, culture or faith when that matters to the person.
Confirm the person keeps control over daily choices, visitors and privacy in the host home.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Limited English Proficiency program, interpreter and translation services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes the Department of Human Services Limited English Proficiency program. The program helps provide spoken and written language assistance to people whose limited English keeps them from getting health and human services. The page has sections on interpreter services and on translation services.
requires: Language assistance covers both spoken interpreting and written translation for people with limited English proficiency.

Minnesota Health Care Programs providers must offer spoken language interpreter services to people with limited English proficiency, whether or not the person is enrolled in Minnesota Health Care Programs.
Providers should not plan to rely on a person's family members, friends or other informal interpreters, except in an emergency.
An interpreter does not need formal certification, but self-identifying as bilingual is not enough to show competence.
The Department of Human Services strongly encourages providers to keep a written Limited English Proficiency plan (template form 4210).
equityCheck: Ask what language the person and their family prefer for speaking and for reading, and record it in the file so every contact uses it.
Check that assessments, support plans, notices and appeal rights are explained in the person's language, not only in English.
Do not use a child or other family member as the interpreter unless it is an emergency; arrange a qualified interpreter.
Look at who in your area is not reaching services; language access gaps often show up as low enrollment from specific communities.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Long-term care consultation
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes long-term care consultation, the set of activities that help people with disabilities and older adults plan, coordinate and get long-term care supports. It includes the MnCHOICES assessment used to open home and community-based programs.
requires: Any person can request and is entitled to receive long-term care consultation, regardless of age or eligibility for Minnesota Health Care Programs.
Each local long-term care consultation team must include at least one social worker and one nurse.
A certified assessor must complete the MnCHOICES assessment, and the assessment is conducted in person with the person.
The MnCHOICES assessment does not determine diagnoses, does not determine financial eligibility for Minnesota Health Care Programs and does not assess mental health targeted case management.
Long-term care consultation includes referrals, information about self-directed options and certain preadmission screenings, which can be provided in any combination.
equityCheck: Offer an interpreter and accessible formats before the assessment so the person can take part fully.
Check that assessment wait times are similar across counties, Tribal Nations and communities; the department's public dashboard shows completions by lead agency.
Make sure the person hears about self-directed options and all program choices, not only the ones most common in the area.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Market rate services (Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion and Developmental Disabilities waivers)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains the market-rate part of the Disability Waiver Rate System. Some waiver services have no state framework rate, so the lead agency works with the provider to set a rate based on the person's needs. The page lists those services and the factors used.
requires: The Disability Waiver Rate System splits waiver services into framework rates, market rates and pre-determined rates; market-rate services include 24-hour emergency assistance, assistive technology, respite, specialist services and waiver transportation.

Lead agencies work with the provider to set a market rate using the components of the person's service and support needs, such as the wages and expertise of the worker, the number of people sharing the service and administrative costs.
A rate may not include costs that Medical Assistance does not allow.
Lead agencies use the Rate Management System to calculate waiver service rates, and per-service limits are in the Long-Term Services and Supports Service Rate Limits document (form 3945).

When a person's needs cannot be met at a framework rate, the provider works with the lead agency (county or Tribal Nation), which submits an exception request to the Department of Human Services on form form 5820.
equityCheck: Compare market rates set for similar needs across people and across counties so that people in some areas or groups are not systematically under-funded.
Check that rate exceptions are requested whenever a person's assessed needs call for one, not only for people with strong advocates.
Watch for service gaps where no provider will accept the rate, especially in rural areas and for culturally specific providers.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Medical Assistance
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page gives an overview of Medical Assistance, Minnesota's name for the federal Medicaid program. Medical Assistance eligibility is the base for the disability waivers, which add services on top of it. The page is dated 2010, so current eligibility details are on the Department of Human Services Medical Assistance pages.
requires: Medical Assistance is funded jointly with state and federal dollars and is administered by counties.
Eligible groups include children under 21, parents or relative caretakers of dependent children, people age 65 or older, people with a certified disability and pregnant women.
To qualify as a person with a disability, a person must meet the Social Security Administration disability definition or be certified by the State Medical Review Team.
Medical Assistance is generally the payer of last resort, so vendors bill other coverage first.
The county human services agency must renew Medical Assistance eligibility every year.
equityCheck: Check whether people are losing waiver services because an annual Medical Assistance renewal was missed; renewal notices should reach people in their language and format.
Help people who need a State Medical Review Team disability certification gather records; delays here delay the waiver.
Watch for groups with lower enrollment despite likely eligibility, such as immigrants and people without a fixed address.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Medical Assistance for Employed Persons with Disabilities
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes Medical Assistance for Employed Persons with Disabilities, a Minnesota Health Care Programs option that lets people with disabilities keep or get Medical Assistance while they work. People pay a premium based on income. The manual page was last reviewed in 2018; the asset limit it lists was removed on January 1, 2024.
requires: A person must be certified as disabled, be employed with Medicare and Social Security taxes withheld, and have average monthly earnings above $65.
There is no upper income limit; the person pays a monthly premium set by a sliding fee scale, with a $35 minimum and no maximum.
Since January 1, 2024 there is no asset limit for this program.
A person who loses a job through no fault of their own may stay in the program for up to four months while looking for another job.
Applications use the Minnesota Health Care Programs Application for Certain Populations (form 3876); online sign-up is not available.
equityCheck: Tell every working-age person on a waiver about this program, so fear of losing Medical Assistance does not keep people from working.
Check that premium and application information is available in the person's language and that the paper-only application is not a barrier.
Look at who uses the program by region and group to find communities where it is under-used.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Mental health services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes Minnesota's publicly funded mental health system as it relates to people served through disability programs. Lead agencies deliver or arrange mental health services under Department of Human Services supervision, and providers must meet Minnesota Health Care Programs standards.
requires: The publicly funded mental health system is administered by lead agencies (counties, Tribal Nations and managed care organizations) and supervised by the Department of Human Services.
In many parts of the state, lead agencies contract with providers to deliver mental health services.
Mental health providers must meet the eligibility criteria in the Minnesota Health Care Programs Provider Manual.
The legal authority cited is the Minnesota Comprehensive Adult Mental Health Act and the Minnesota Comprehensive Children's Mental Health Act.
equityCheck: For a person with both a disability and a mental health need, check that waiver and mental health services are coordinated rather than one system deferring to the other.
Ask whether culturally specific and language-matched mental health providers are available in the person's area.
Review crisis and hospitalization data by group to see where mental health needs are being met late.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Metro Crisis Coordination Program
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes the Metro Crisis Coordination Program, a crisis safety-net service run together by the seven metropolitan counties for people with developmental disabilities and related conditions. Its services are mostly paid for through the home and community-based services waivers.
requires: The program is a collaboration among the seven metropolitan counties and aims to prevent crises and reduce hospitalizations and civil commitments.
To take part, a person must live in one of the seven metro counties and have an open case with a county developmental disabilities unit, or be in the process of opening one.
Services include 24-hour phone support, on-site crisis and support planning, and referrals to more specialized services.
Services are primarily funded through the home and community-based services waivers.
equityCheck: People outside the seven-county metro area do not have this program; check what crisis response exists in your area and whether it is available around the clock.
Make sure crisis phone support can be reached by people who use relay services or need an interpreter.
Look at who uses crisis services and who ends up in hospital or commitment instead, by group and by county.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Minnesota Intensive Therapeutic Homes
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes Minnesota Intensive Therapeutic Homes, a state-operated program for children and young adults under 21 with serious psychiatric or intellectual disability needs. Services are provided in family foster homes as an add-on to regular foster care and are funded through the home and community-based services waivers.
requires: The program operates under Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D within the state's Community-Based Services.

A person must be under 21, medically stable, have severe psychosocial impairment from a psychiatric illness or intellectual disability, need 24-hour structure and active treatment, and be unable to be served in a less restrictive setting.
Services are set out in the person's coordinated service and support plan with a program addendum, and include 24/7 phone access to an on-call professional, training and regular team meetings.
The program cannot provide hospital level of care for a medical condition or psychiatric illness.
Referrals go through the program's supervising mental health professional, and services are funded through waiver funding.
equityCheck: Check whether a young person was offered this community option before a more restrictive residential placement, regardless of county.
Ask whether foster homes are available that match the young person's culture and language.
Track referrals and admissions by region and group to see who gets access.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Minnesota Life Bridge
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes Minnesota Life Bridge, a state-operated residential treatment program for adults with developmental disabilities whose extreme behavior presents a risk to public safety. The program grew out of the Jensen Settlement Agreement and is meant to be short-term.
requires: Minnesota Life Bridge homes are licensed community residential settings in Minnesota communities and are not secured facilities.
A person may be admitted only when the program is the most integrated setting that can safely meet the person's needs.
Treatment is meant to be short-term; there is no set length of stay that applies to everyone.
The program is not licensed to serve children, and it does not provide hospital level of care for medical conditions or psychiatric illness.
Referrals use the online Community-Based Services Program Referral Form (form 3912).
equityCheck: Confirm the transition plan back to the community starts at admission and names the supports and providers that will be in place.
Check that the person understands their rights and has access to an advocate and the Office of Ombudsman for Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities.
Review who is referred to the program by county and group, and whether community supports were tried first.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Minnesota Medical Assistance managed care programs
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes the managed care programs through which many people get Medical Assistance. For people with disabilities the main option is Special Needs BasicCare, a voluntary managed care program. The page helps lead agencies understand which services a health plan covers and which stay with the Department of Human Services.
requires: Special Needs BasicCare is a voluntary managed care program for people ages 18 to 64 who have a certified disability and Medical Assistance.
To enroll, a person must be certified as disabled by the Social Security Administration or the State Medical Review Team.
Special Needs BasicCare has no health plan premiums, deductibles or co-payments.
Certain home and community-based services stay covered by Department of Human Services fee-for-service and are not covered by the managed care organization.
equityCheck: Explain the choice between managed care and fee-for-service in plain language and in the person's language, so enrollment is a real choice.
Check that the person knows which services the health plan covers and which the lead agency authorizes, so no one falls between the two.
Look at disenrollment and complaint data by group to see whether some communities have more trouble with a plan.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Minnesota State-Operated Community Services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes Minnesota State-Operated Community Services, the state-run residential and vocational services for people with complex behavioral needs that private providers cannot meet. The page explains what the program offers and how referrals are made.
requires: The program includes both residential services and vocational and life enrichment services.
Residential services are provided in about 100 foster care homes across Minnesota, with up to four beds in each home.
Vocational services include employment and customized employment, day training and habilitation, and work through Vocational Rehabilitation Services, in programs in 17 communities.
The program cannot provide hospital level of care for medical conditions or psychiatric illness.
Residential and crisis referrals go through a unified online referral process; vocational referrals go to the service site.
equityCheck: Check that a state-operated placement is chosen because it fits the person's needs and preferences, not because private providers in the area declined the person.
Ask whether the person can stay near family, community and culture, since homes are spread across the state.
Look at transition data: how many people move from state-operated homes to less restrictive settings, and from which regions.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: MnCHOICES
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains MnCHOICES, which is both the computer application lead agencies use for long-term services and supports assessments, support plans and health risk assessments, and the assessment used to decide eligibility. It describes what the assessment and support plan do, what they replaced, what MnCHOICES does not decide, and the lead agency's duties for staff, technology, data privacy and timelines.
requires: Lead agencies (counties, Tribal Nations and managed care organizations) use MnCHOICES to complete assessments for the waivers and for personal care assistance and Community First Services and Supports, health risk assessments and support plans; the application applies rules the same way for everyone and produces data required by federal and state law.

Certified assessors use the MnCHOICES assessment to decide eligibility for the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion, Developmental Disabilities and Elderly waivers, Alternative Care, personal care assistance and Community First Services and Supports, and the Consumer Support Grant, and to help the person identify other programs to explore.
Managed care organization care coordinators use the health risk assessment; it cannot be used to decide eligibility for waiver programs or personal care assistance.

The MnCHOICES assessment does not determine diagnoses, financial eligibility for Minnesota Health Care Programs, mental health targeted case management, Family Support Grant eligibility or Rule 185 case management eligibility; a lead agency's qualified developmental disabilities professional decides developmental disability eligibility through the diagnostic determination process.

The MnCHOICES support plan documents the person's goals, strengths, needs and preferences, collects person-centered planning data, calculates rates for certain services and creates service agreements.

Lead agencies must keep a team of qualified case managers and certified assessors, meet the technical specifications for the application, make sure all users complete annual data privacy courses, complete all required assessments and meet timelines.
equityCheck: Ask how the standard rules in MnCHOICES affect people from different communities, and whether assessors can record cultural needs that the rules do not capture.
Check that assessment materials and summaries were given in the person's language.
Compare assessment timeliness across lead agencies using the public data the Department of Human Services publishes.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: MnCHOICES assessment process
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page, posted June 22, 2026, guides certified assessors through the MnCHOICES assessment. It says which lead agency must do the assessment, who takes part, how providers give input, what the assessor does before, during and after the assessment, and the 60-day deadline for the assessment summary and support plan.
requires: Lead agencies must provide MnCHOICES assessments to all people regardless of their eligibility for Minnesota Health Care Programs; for people seeking a disability waiver or Rule 185 case management and people under 65, the county where the person is located at the time of the request is responsible, and an eligible person may choose to have a Tribal Nation complete the assessment.

For people 65 or older not seeking a disability waiver, the county where the person is located is responsible unless the person is enrolled in Minnesota Senior Health Options or Minnesota Senior Care Plus, in which case the managed care organization is responsible; the managed care organization refers the person to the county or Tribal Nation when the person wants to return to a disability waiver or explore developmental disabilities services.

The assessment interview always includes the person, their legal representative if any, the certified assessor and other people the person designates; participants may not have a financial interest in the services except family members, and the person's case manager generally should not attend unless the person asks.

Providers should not attend the assessment but should give written reports; for the four disability waivers the current provider must submit the report at least 60 days before the end of the service agreement, and the assessor must review provider information before finalizing the assessment.

At the assessment the assessor must use person-centered practices, review what is and is not working in the current plan, complete the assessment summary worksheet and give the person a copy at initial assessments, review the program acknowledgement and obtain signatures, complete preadmission screening activities, and give the person the home choices resource for the disability waivers.

After the assessment the assessor completes the assessment summary in MnCHOICES, sends it to the person, completes the support plan, enters the screening document and any personal care assistance or Community First Services and Supports service agreement, and sends the communication forms to the case manager and eligibility worker.
Counties and Tribal Nations must send the assessment summary, and the support plan when the person will use services, within 60 days of the assessment activity date.
equityCheck: Check that the person was given time alone with the assessor to speak privately, with an interpreter if needed.
Ask whether people who are eligible to choose a Tribal Nation assessment were told about that choice.
Compare 60-day timeliness across counties and Tribal Nations and by the language the person speaks.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: MnCHOICES certified assessors
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page sets the role, qualifications, certification and recertification of MnCHOICES certified assessors, the lead agency staff who assess people who request long-term services and supports. From July 1, 2026 the education requirement changed from a bachelor's degree to an associate's degree in human services or nursing, or a registered nurse license.
requires: Certified assessors must give the person an estimated timeline for completing the assessment, complete conversation-based interviews within statutory timelines, help the person make an informed choice, provide information about competitive employment with or without supports, and give the person a person-centered assessment summary with support options and agreed next steps.

To be certified a person must be employed by a lead agency or a hospital under contract with a lead agency, meet the education and experience requirements in Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0911, subdivision 13, and complete the certification training.

Before July 1, 2026 candidates needed a bachelor's degree in social work or a closely related field, a bachelor's degree in nursing with a public health certificate, or a registered nurse license; effective July 1, 2026 an associate's degree in human services or a closely related field, an associate's degree in nursing with a public health certificate, or a registered nurse license is required.
Candidates must pass each of the three MnCHOICES Certified Assessor Training steps with 80 percent or higher; step 3 is available only to lead agency assessor candidates through lead agency mentors.
All lead agency staff who complete MnCHOICES assessments must be certified and must recertify every three years by logging continued learning units; lead agencies must facilitate certification.
equityCheck: Ask whether the 2026 change to associate's degree qualifications is widening the assessor workforce in rural areas and in communities of color.
Check that assessors have training on working with interpreters and on culturally responsive interviewing.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: My Move Plan Summary
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains the My Move Plan Summary (Department of Human Services form 3936), a transition plan the case manager or care coordinator must complete with a person who is moving from one residence to another and does not plan to return. The requirement comes from the Person-Centered, Informed Choice and Transition Protocol. The page lists who is responsible, what the case manager must do with the form, the allowed reasons for not completing it, and the required training course.
requires: When a person moves to a new residence and does not intend to return, the Person-Centered, Informed Choice and Transition Protocol (transition requirement 3.D) requires the case manager or care coordinator to work with the person to create a summary of the move plan on form 3936.

Responsible professionals include waiver and Alternative Care case managers and care coordinators, Rule 185 case managers, vulnerable adult and developmental disabilities targeted case managers and relocation service coordination targeted case managers.

The case manager or care coordinator must complete the form with the person, share it with the person and their paid and unpaid supports, discuss the move and record support plan changes, refer to and update the form during the move, document in the support plan when the move does not reach the person's preferred setting, and sign and keep a copy in the person's file.

If the form is not completed, the case manager must use the form to record the reason: the person is confident in their plan or moving with family or friends and needs no added support, the person already moved without the case manager knowing, or the person does not want to complete it.

The online course Supporting my move: A case manager's role is available to disability waiver case managers through TrainLink; the Lead Agency Review training attestation lists it as a required training.
equityCheck: Check that the move plan records what is important to the person, in their words, and not only logistics.
Track how often moves do not reach the person's preferred setting and why, by county and by population.

programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes night supervision, which is overnight help and supervision from staff in the person's own home when the person has an assessed need in a covered area. It gives provider and enrollment requirements and says how rates are set.
requires: The person must live in their own home and have an assessed need in one of the covered service areas.
The lead agency may not authorize night supervision when it duplicates other state plan or waiver services the person already receives.
Night supervision is a Department of Human Services enrollment-required service, and providers must have a background study.
Providers licensed under chapter 245D must report controlled procedures, emergency manual restraint and prohibited procedures to the Department of Human Services using form form 5148.
Night supervision is a framework service; the lead agency uses the rate management system to set the rate.
equityCheck: Check whether overnight staffing is available in the person's area before a residential setting is proposed instead.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Notice of action
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page tells counties and Tribal Nations when and how to send a notice of action, the document that tells a person about a decision on their services and their right to appeal. A notice is required after every assessment and whenever services are denied, ended or reduced. Managed care organizations use their own forms.
requires: A notice of action must state the reason and legal basis for the decision, the timeline for the action, and how to appeal, including the person's right to ask that services continue during an appeal.

The certified assessor must complete the MnCHOICES assessment summary, which includes the notice of action and appeal rights, after every assessment, reassessment or functional needs update, and must explain any changes and answer the person's questions.

The case manager must send the Notice of Action: Explanation of Changes to Your Support Plan whenever the support plan denies, ends or reduces a service, a requested item or service is denied, the person chooses to reduce or stop a service, the person loses eligibility for a service such as consumer-directed community supports, budgets are cut, program changes remove a service, Alternative Care fees change, the person declines an offered service, or the person receives a consumer-directed community supports budget.

When services, eligibility or level of care are denied, reduced or ended, or free choice of provider is restricted, the notice must be sent at least 10 days before the effective date; when a person no longer meets nursing facility level of care, at least 30 days before; more than 10 days is a best practice for residential services.

Legislative changes that affect services do not require a notice of action because appeal rights do not apply to them; routine changes such as schedule or a provider change with no change in amount do not require a notice.

Each denial, termination or reduction must include an effective date, a reason, a plain-language explanation with budget effects, a legal citation and appeal rights; paper forms 2828A and 2828B are used only when the assessment and support plan are not in MnCHOICES.
equityCheck: Check that notices are sent in the person's language and that the explanation is plain enough for the person to act on.
Track appeal rates and outcomes by race, language, disability type and lead agency.
Ask whether people were told they can keep services during an appeal.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Oral and enteral nutritional products
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains when waiver programs can pay for nutritional products beyond what the Medical Assistance state plan covers. It defines enteral products, given through a feeding tube, and oral products, taken by mouth, and sets different rules for the disability waivers and the aging programs.
requires: When a person's need for enteral products exceeds the state plan limits, the lead agency can authorize extra units through specialized equipment and supplies.
Under Alternative Care and the Elderly Waiver, oral products can be approved only under certain conditions; foods, special diet items, organ extracts and over-the-counter supplements are excluded.
The Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waivers exclude oral nutritional products such as commercial nutrition drinks and electrolyte products.
The support plan must document the need for products beyond state plan coverage, and the service agreement must authorize them.
equityCheck: Check that the person first received the state plan benefit before the waiver was used, so the waiver budget is not spent on a covered item.
Ask whether dietary needs tied to culture or religion were considered when documenting nutritional need.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Paying relatives and legally responsible individuals
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page says when relatives, legally responsible individuals and non-professional guardians or conservators may be paid to provide waiver services. It lists the conditions that must be met, the services relatives cannot be paid for, and the limits on spouses and parents of minors.
requires: Relatives are parents, children, siblings, nieces or nephews, grandparents, and aunts or uncles; legally responsible individuals are parents of a minor child and court-appointed guardians and conservators.

A relative or non-professional guardian may be paid only if they are related to or the guardian of one person or one family of siblings, are not otherwise responsible for the care, are qualified, are employed by a qualified provider (not required for consumer-directed community supports), and are not enrolled as a Medical Assistance provider for that service.
Professional guardians and conservators may not be paid for any waiver service.
Spouses and parents of minors may be paid only for consumer-directed community supports personal assistance.

Relatives may not be paid for caregiver living expenses, case management or individualized home supports with family training; primary caregivers may not be paid for chore, homemaker or respite meant to relieve themselves.
A county may certify a relative exempt from licensure to provide adult foster care to a related person on the Elderly Waiver.
equityCheck: Check that families who want to hire a relative know about consumer-directed community supports, where more relatives may be paid.
Ask whether the rules were explained in the family's language before a relative was turned down as a paid worker.
Watch for families in areas with few providers who rely on relatives and need the employment path explained.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Person-centered practices
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page states the Department of Human Services policy that people who receive supports and services have the same rights and responsibilities as other people, including control over their lives, making their own choices and contributing to the community. It tells lead agencies which protocol to use in support planning and tells home and community-based services providers how services must be delivered.
requires: Lead agencies must use the Person-Centered, Informed Choice and Transition Protocol (Department of Human Services form 3825) to put person-centered practices into support planning.
Home and community-based services providers must deliver services in response to the person's identified needs, interests, preferences and desired outcomes as written in the person's plan.
Providers must deliver services in a way that follows person-centered service planning and delivery, self-determination, the most integrated environment and inclusive service delivery options.

Providers must use positive supports in place of restrictive interventions, build person-centered principles into their services, and evaluate with the person whether the services support the person's preferences, daily needs, activities and desired outcomes.

The page lists the sources that require person-centered services: Minnesota's Olmstead Plan, the Jensen Settlement, the federal home and community-based services settings rule, chapter 245D licensing standards and the Positive Supports Rule.

Legal authority listed on the page: 42 CFR 441.725, Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D, Minnesota Rules chapter 9544, Minnesota Statutes sections 256B.092, 256B.49, 256B.0913, 256B.0924 and 256B.0621, chapter 256S, and Minnesota Rules 9525.0004 to 9525.0036.
equityCheck: Ask whether the person's plan was built from what is important to the person, in their own words and language, rather than from what a provider offers.
Check that the person was told about the most integrated setting options, including a home not controlled by a provider, before a provider-controlled setting was proposed.
Look for patterns by race, language, disability type or region in whose plans are written in plain language and whose are not.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Personal emergency response systems
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page covers personal emergency response systems, an electronic device such as a pendant or bracelet with an alert button the person presses in a fall or other emergency, plus installation and monitoring. Under the aging programs the service is part of specialized equipment and supplies; under the four disability waivers it is part of 24-hour emergency assistance. The page sets yearly limits, what is not covered, customized living rules, the person-centered assessment and the support plan content.
requires: Three parts each have a yearly limit per service agreement year: equipment purchase including training ($1,500 maximum), installation, setup and testing ($500 maximum) and monthly monitoring ($110 a month maximum), for a total of up to $3,000 a year.

Not covered: equipment used to deliver other Medical Assistance or waiver services, sensing or monitoring systems the person does not activate (covered by the monitoring technology policy), supervision of daily activities that belongs to another service, telehealth and biometric devices, and video equipment.

A 24-hour customized living provider may use the equipment as part of its supervision plan but may not bill extra for it; a person on the Brain Injury or Community Access for Disability Inclusion waiver in 24-hour customized living cannot receive the service separately, and a person on the Elderly Waiver in 24-hour customized living may receive it separately only for use outside the setting and from a different provider.

The lead agency must use a person-centered approach, assessing the person's ability to recognize the need for help and use the device, preferences about privacy and data access, and risk factors such as falls, and must offer a choice among all qualified providers, considering equipment features and how data is collected, shared and stored.

The support plan (or a provider purchase and use agreement with the same content) must record the equipment, how it meets the assessed need, a backup during power outages or malfunctions, training for the person and caregivers, the call list and response times, privacy safeguards for the data and the fees.
The service is an approval-option purchased-item service; eligible providers include the lead agency, state medical equipment providers and other providers listed on the page.
equityCheck: Check that the person understands who receives their alert data and agreed to it.
Ask whether people without landline or reliable cellular service can use the device where they live.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Positive supports
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains the Department of Human Services requirement that providers licensed under Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D use positive supports and stop using punitive practices such as seclusion and restraint. It defines positive supports, lists prohibited procedures, sets provider duties including positive support transition plans and reporting, and explains how a lead agency can pay for extraordinary needs and positive supports consultation.
requires: Positive supports are strategies that increase quality of life and decrease challenging behavior by teaching new skills and changing a person's environment; providers must use them instead of aversive or punishing procedures.

Minnesota law prohibits chemical restraint, mechanical restraint, programmatic use of manual restraint, seclusion, time out, prone restraint and any other aversive or deprivation procedure; the page lists examples such as denying access to assistive devices, requiring a person to earn goods or services, ridicule, threats and painful techniques.

On and after January 1, 2014, providers licensed under chapter 245D may not use prohibited procedures and must base service planning and delivery on positive support strategies and on person-centered planning, integrated settings, inclusive service delivery and self-determination.

Providers must develop a Positive Support Transition Plan (Department of Human Services form 6810) for people who need intervention to stay safe when their known behavior poses an immediate risk of physical harm to themselves or others.

Providers must report the emergency use of manual restraint and any procedure in a positive support transition plan to the Department of Human Services and the Office of the Ombudsman for Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities using the Behavior Intervention Report Form (form 5148).

When a Disability Waiver Rate System rate cannot meet an extraordinary need, the lead agency may request a rate exception or a disability waiver budget adjustment; positive supports consultation from a chapter 245D provider can be paid through positive supports consultation, positive support services, specialist services, person-centered planning consultation or family training and counseling.

The Department of Human Services may grant limited approval for emergency use of otherwise prohibited procedures only to protect a person from imminent risk of serious injury from self-injurious behavior, on a request submitted on form 6810D by the provider's designated coordinator or manager with the person's expanded support team.
equityCheck: Review behavior intervention reports for patterns by race, disability type, age or setting, and ask what positive support help the provider received before restraint was used.
Check that the person and their chosen supporters took part in building any positive support transition plan and that it was explained in their language.
Ask whether people in rural areas and people served by small providers have the same access to positive supports consultation.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Prevocational services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
intermediate care facilities for persons with developmental disabilities
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines prevocational services, work-skills training and support in provider-controlled facilities and businesses that move people toward competitively paid community jobs. People new to the service on or after January 11, 2021 may receive it for three years, with one-year extensions in listed situations. The service is not a prerequisite for the waiver employment services, and the lead agency must document that the same services are not available through vocational rehabilitation or special education.
requires: A person must be eligible for the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion or Developmental Disabilities waiver or live in an intermediate care facility, and have prevocational services as an assessed need in their support plan.

Covered services teach following work instructions and schedules, workplace skills such as communication, problem-solving, relationships, self-care and social skills, work skills such as attendance, attention, production, quality, safety and time management, work-related education, and worksite transportation, mobility and street-safety skills.

People who received prevocational services or day training and habilitation before January 11, 2021 may continue; people new to the service on or after that date may receive it for 36 months, with an additional 12 months allowed for a continued need to resolve work-skill or conduct problems that could cost a community job, a disruptive life event including a provider change, or a health condition that disrupted services.

Not covered: transportation between home and the service site, and services available under section 110 of the Rehabilitation Act or the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act; the lead agency must document in the person's file that those programs are not available; waiver funds may not be used as capital for provider businesses or to supplement wages, and wages must follow federal and state law.

Services are delivered in provider-controlled facilities and businesses; the lead agency cannot authorize the service for a person living in a setting adjoined to or on the same property as a hospital, nursing facility, intermediate care facility or institution for mental disease, and may authorize services in only one of a provider's settings on the same property, with exceptions tied to the 2017 and 2018 settings attestation process.

Providers must be enrolled, hold a chapter 245D intensive support services license, have background studies and report restraint and controlled procedures on form 5148; the service is a framework service paid through the Rate Management System and may be delivered through remote support.
equityCheck: Track how many people move from prevocational services to competitive employment and how long they stay in prevocational services, by race, disability type and region.
Check that wage and hour data on the Rates Management System worksheet is complete for each person in prevocational services.
Confirm the person was offered employment exploration or development services rather than prevocational services as a first step.

programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver

requires: All rate limits are stored in the Medicaid Management Information System reference file, and the full set of rates and maximums is published on the Department of Human Services long-term services and supports rate changes page; for home care state plan services lead agencies use the published reference rate file limits.

Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System codes identify each good or service and its unit type, such as 15 minutes, daily, monthly, per item, per meal, one-way trip, mileage or per waiver year; providers bill with the same codes.
When the Legislature changes rates, the Department publishes the new rates with instructions for lead agencies.
In a leap year, lead agencies must count February 29 when entering units for services with units shorter than a month; monthly and semi-monthly codes use the contracted rate.
equityCheck: Check that rate changes are applied on time for every person, not only for those whose service agreements happen to renew.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Remote support
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page sets the policy for remote support, a way of delivering a covered service by staff or a caregiver at another location through enabling technology with live, two-way communication. Remote support is not a service of its own. The person must choose it, may refuse or stop it at any time, and the support plan must say how in-person and remote support will be combined to keep the person safe.
requires: Remote support is covered only when the person (or guardian) chooses and prefers it, it meets the person's assessed needs, it is within the scope of the service, and it is written in the support plan; the person may refuse, stop or suspend it at any time.

The page lists which services allow remote support under the four disability waivers (including day support, employment services, individualized home supports, integrated community supports, positive support services and in-home respite), under Alternative Care and the Elderly Waiver, under consumer-directed community supports, and under Essential Community Supports.

The support plan must state the assessed needs and goals remote support will meet, how it supports the most integrated setting, which needs must be met in person, that remote support will not replace in-person support as a core service function, the plan for health and safety, whether the person agrees to cameras, and the amount, frequency and duration.

A person may get in-person and remote support on the same day, but a person receiving residential or day services cannot get both at the same time; individual community living supports is limited to 12 hours a day with at least one in-person visit each week.

Remote support does not fund the technology itself; assistive technology, environmental accessibility adaptations, specialized equipment and supplies or consumer-directed community supports home modifications may pay for it, and cameras in bathrooms are prohibited.

Providers must protect privacy, follow the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act and the Minnesota Health Care Programs provider agreement, keep electronic messages retrievable, and use separate service agreement lines for in-person and remote delivery where the page lists them; units are paid at the same rate whether in person or remote.
equityCheck: Confirm the person has the device, internet access and skills needed, and that these costs were planned for and not left to the person.
Check that the choice of remote support was the person's own and documented, and that the person knows they can stop it.
Look at who is offered remote support and who is not, by region, language and disability type.

policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page sets the conditions a setting must meet to count as a person's own home for waiver services. The purpose is to keep the person or their family in control of the home. If the conditions are not met, the setting is treated as a licensed residential program, an integrated community supports setting or an assisted living setting instead.
requires: All of the own home requirements on the page must be met for a setting to be considered the person's own home.
The requirements apply to each person individually, as documented in the person's support plan.
Services in a person's own home must be individualized and delivered individually.
If the requirements are not met, the setting falls under a residential program license, an integrated community supports capacity report or an assisted living license.
equityCheck: Check that the person holds the lease or title and controls who lives with them and who provides services.
Ask whether the person understands the difference between their own home and a provider-controlled setting, in their language.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Resource: Guidance for employment services authorization
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual resource page, updated March 9, 2026, tells lead agencies and case managers how waiver employment services fit with Vocational Rehabilitation Services, State Services for the Blind and special education services under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act. Federal Medicaid rules do not allow waiver employment services that are available under the Rehabilitation Act or special education, so the case manager must check availability before authorizing. Two tables show which service may be authorized for students and for people not in school.
requires: Before authorizing waiver employment services, lead agencies must make sure Vocational Rehabilitation Services, State Services for the Blind or special education services are not available to the person, because the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services does not allow waiver employment services that those programs provide.

For a person in grade 9 through age 22 who is enrolled in high school or a school transition program, the case manager may not authorize employment exploration or either phase of employment development, and may authorize employment support services only for hours outside school.

For a person not enrolled in school, the case manager may authorize employment exploration and the plan phase of employment development; the find phase may be authorized only when Vocational Rehabilitation Services or State Services for the Blind found the person ineligible or not in an open priority category, or closed the case because the person can no longer benefit from job placement services.

When the find phase is authorized for one of those reasons, the case manager must record the reason in the service notes of the authorization and keep the ineligibility, closed priority category or closure letter in the person's file.
Employment support services may be authorized for a person not in school once Vocational Rehabilitation Services determines the person is stable in a job.

The page explains that the Department of Human Services, the Department of Education and the Department of Employment and Economic Development work together as the E1MN partnership, that special education employment support is generally limited to school hours and the school year and to goals in the individual education program, and that pre-employment transition services are available to students with disabilities age 14 to 21.
equityCheck: Check whether people placed on a Vocational Rehabilitation Services waitlist are left without any employment service, and how long they wait.
Ask whether students with disabilities and their families are told about pre-employment transition services in their language.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Resource: Guide for emergency backup planning
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual resource page, posted April 26, 2022, gives case managers and care coordinators guidance on helping people build and document backup plans for staffing emergencies caused by the direct care workforce shortage. It applies to people who need a support plan under the waivers, Alternative Care, Essential Community Supports, personal care assistance and Rule 185 case management, and says the backup plan must reflect the person's own needs, desires and preferences.
requires: Case managers and care coordinators must inform the person and their legal representative of service and support options, including what the options are if the first choice becomes unavailable.

They must discuss and document the emergency backup plan with the person as part of finalizing the written support plan, keep monitoring the person's needs and the adequacy of the plan, and review provider emergency backup plans when the person uses home care, lives in a provider-controlled setting or receives other essential services.

The backup plan must focus on the person's needs, desires and preferences; it may rely on assistive technology, family, friends, community organizations or other informal supports, not only paid services.

The discussion must cover short-term staffing emergencies (late or absent staff), long-term emergencies (staff resign, a caregiver cannot continue, a provider ends services or a residential site closes), who the person wants support from, what support they need and want, and when it will happen.

The plan is recorded in the emergency and backup plan section of the support plan and updated as needed; the page links to self-directed options, remote support, assistive technology guides, the Direct Support Connect job board and the residential service termination guide as resources.
equityCheck: Check that the backup plan does not assume unpaid family members will fill every gap, especially in communities already carrying more unpaid care.
Ask whether people in rural areas have real backup options when the only provider in the area has no staff.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Respite
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines respite, short-term care for a person when their primary caregiver is absent or needs relief. It sets who counts as a primary caregiver under the aging programs and under the four disability waivers, what respite covers, which services cannot be combined with it, the settings and licenses allowed for in-home and out-of-home respite, and emergency rules during a community disaster.
requires: A person is eligible when their primary caregiver is absent or needs relief; under the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion and Developmental Disabilities waivers the caregiver must be principally responsible for the person's care, live at the same address and own or lease the home; under Alternative Care and the Elderly Waiver the caregiver may live elsewhere and must be unpaid or paid only for part of the care.

Respite covers the supervision and care needed for health and safety, and room and board only when respite is in a licensed setting; it does not cover training or habilitation, room and board in the person's home or an unlicensed setting, or a short-term nursing facility stay under the Developmental Disabilities Waiver.

Respite cannot be authorized for a person who receives adult foster care, community residential services, customized living, family residential services with shift staffing or integrated community supports, except during a community emergency or disaster.
In-home respite in 15-minute units may be delivered through remote support; out-of-home respite and respite in community settings away from the person's home may not.

In-home respite providers need a chapter 245D basic support license or a chapter 144A license with a home and community-based services designation; out-of-home respite may be provided in a hospital, nursing facility (not for the Developmental Disabilities Waiver), residential hospice for people 21 and younger, assisted living facility for people 65 and older on the aging programs, adult family foster care, community residential setting, child foster care or an intermediate care facility, each with the setting and service licenses listed on the page.

Adult foster care and community residential settings used for respite may not serve more than four people including respite users under the disability waivers unless a fifth bed license or variance is approved; during a community emergency or disaster the Department of Human Services may approve out-of-home respite, waive service limits and approve unlicensed providers on a short-term basis.
equityCheck: Check whether families in rural areas and families who need culturally matched caregivers can find respite providers.
Ask whether the primary caregiver definition for the disability waivers leaves out caregivers who do not own or lease the home, and how those families get relief.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Specialized equipment and supplies
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines specialized equipment and supplies, devices (including assistive technology), controls, medical appliances or supplies written in a person's support plan that help the person communicate, perceive, control or interact with their environment, or do activities of daily living. It lists what is covered beyond the Medical Assistance state plan, what is not, the rules for electronic tablets and used equipment, and the yearly limit of $10,000 for the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waivers.
requires: Covered items include durable and non-durable medical equipment and supplies denied under the Medical Assistance state plan, add-ons to state plan items, items above state plan limits, electronic tablets used for environmental control or daily activities, assistive technology, standalone equipment such as shower chairs and portable ramps, enteral nutritional products, life support items and supplies, repairs not covered by warranty, continence care wipes, thickening agents and qualifying used equipment; training on the item is part of the purchase price.

Under Alternative Care and the Elderly Waiver the service also covers personal emergency response systems, equipment used in place of state plan items, trial rentals, need evaluations and oral nutritional products; under Essential Community Supports it is limited to personal emergency response systems.

Not covered: experimental treatments, items another payer must cover, items with no direct medical or remedial benefit, oral nutritional and electrolyte products under the three disability waivers, foods and over-the-counter supplements, medications, used equipment resold to a second family member, utilities, and any item that restrains a person or restricts their rights unless ordered by a licensed health professional for a diagnosed condition and allowed under the Positive Supports Rule.

An electronic tablet used only for augmentative communication is paid by the Medical Assistance state plan as durable medical equipment; a tablet also used to perceive, control or interact with the environment or to do daily activities is paid by the waiver or Alternative Care under this service.

Used equipment may be funded only after a specialized equipment provider, occupational therapist or physical therapist confirms it meets the assessed need, works, has a fair market value and is cost-effective compared to new equipment.

For the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waivers, waivers that begin or renew on or after January 1, 2024 allow up to $10,000 per waiver year with no exceptions (the limit was $3,909 before that date); under Alternative Care and the Elderly Waiver the limit is the case mix budget cap; assistive technology for the Developmental Disabilities Waiver is a separate service.
equityCheck: Check that the person received training on the equipment in their language and that repair and maintenance were planned.
Ask whether the $10,000 yearly limit leaves people with high equipment needs without a path to the items they need.
Compare how quickly state plan denials are turned into waiver authorizations across lead agencies.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: State and lead agency oversight responsibilities
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains how the state and lead agencies share responsibility for the health and safety of people who receive home and community-based services. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services holds each state responsible; in Minnesota's lead agency system the Department of Human Services designs standards, qualifies providers and trains people, while lead agencies plan, arrange and monitor services for each person.
requires: Federal health and safety assurances require behavioral safeguards for restraints and restrictive interventions, medication administration and management procedures, reporting of critical events and incidents, and training about abuse, neglect and exploitation.

The state must design model procedures and protocols, develop training toolkits, train people who receive services and lead agency workers, set provider qualifications and performance standards, review and approve providers, provide enrollment and compliance help, and coordinate with counties and Tribal Nations on provider quality problems.

Lead agencies must plan, provide, arrange and monitor services for eligible people; case managers encourage informed choice, oversee each person's well-being, systematically monitor provider performance and decide which provider issues must be reported to the state.
The Department of Human Services and social services lead agencies keep an active investigative capacity to resolve and report maltreatment of vulnerable people.
Providers must meet the professional, certification and licensure requirements in state and federal law to take part in Minnesota Health Care Programs.

State supports for lead agencies include regional resource specialists, the PolicyQuest policy question system, the Service Agreement and Screening Document support team and the provider resource center.
equityCheck: Ask how provider performance monitoring findings are compared across regions and populations, and what happens when a pattern of harm is found.
Check that people who receive services get training about abuse, neglect and exploitation in their language.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Support planning for long-term services and supports
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page sets the support planning process that follows a MnCHOICES assessment. The person must be at the center of the process, the certified assessor and case manager or care coordinator lead it with the person, and the lead agency records the decisions in the MnCHOICES support plan. The page sets the 60-day deadline, who must sign the plan, appeal rights, grievance contacts and case manager duties before and after the assessment.
requires: Support planning is a person-centered process that helps the person identify and get social, health, educational, vocational and other supports based on their values, strengths, goals, preferences and needs, and encourages technology and informal supports as well as paid services.

The case manager or care coordinator must give the full support plan to the person, their legal representative, and every provider responsible for services in the plan, and collect their signatures, within 60 calendar days of the assessment or initial assessment review; lead agencies must set internal timelines to meet this deadline.

Every enrolled provider of waiver, Alternative Care or Essential Community Supports services must sign the support plan and keep a copy; delivering services before signing, or returning a signed plan late, risks non-payment or takebacks; the lead agency signs when it uses the approval option.

Updated signatures are required when a plan revision changes how a service is provided, such as frequency, units, tasks or a new provider; signatures are not needed for changes that do not affect a provider's services or for cost-of-living adjustments.

Counties and Tribal Nations must give people their appeal rights at assessment and during support planning, and must give people who receive contracted developmental disabilities case management the contact information to file a grievance about the quality of case management.

Before the assessment the case manager shares changes in the person's condition, assistive technology needs and provider information with the certified assessor; after the assessment the case manager reviews the assessment summary, sets the annual budget, meets with the person, gives informed choice of services, obtains releases and signatures and makes referrals.

Providers should send written reports to inform support planning at least 60 days before the end of the service agreement; chapter 245D intensive support providers must send progress reports when requested.
equityCheck: Check that the plan was reviewed with the person in their language and format before they signed it, not only sent for a signature.
Track how often the 60-day deadline is missed and for whom.
Ask whether the person chose who took part in planning, including informal supports and culturally specific supports.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Transportation (waiver and Alternative Care)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page defines waiver transportation, rides a person needs to reach waiver services, community activities and resources, and employment, as written in their support plan. It describes the three provider types (common carrier, individual driver and special transportation), what is not covered, provider qualifications and how trips and mileage are paid.
requires: Transportation is covered when it is necessary for the person to reach waiver services, community services, activities and resources, or employment.

Not covered: trips that duplicate Medical Assistance state plan services such as rides to medical appointments (covered as nonemergency medical transportation), trips when free transportation from family, friends, neighbors or community agencies is available, trips already included in a waiver service rate, and trips where the staff member driving is also providing training support.

Common carriers (buses, taxis, light rail, commercial carriers and lead agency vehicles) are an approval-option purchased-item service; individual drivers (family, neighbors, friends, community agencies and volunteer driver programs) are an approval-option direct-delivery service; special transportation for people who cannot use a common carrier is an enrollment-required service with drivers certified by the Minnesota Department of Transportation.

All providers must meet the person's needs and preferences cost-effectively, follow state and local law, and hold a valid Minnesota driver's license and the automobile insurance required by Minnesota Statutes chapter 65B.

The lead agency authorizes one-way trips at the market rate and mileage at the mileage reimbursement rate in the Long-Term Services and Supports Service Rate Limits (form 3945); volunteer drivers are reimbursed at the federal standard mileage rate; transportation cannot be billed at the same time as another waiver service from the same provider or separately when it is part of a service rate.
For people 60 and older, lead agencies should refer to Older Americans Act transportation only when the needed amount cannot be authorized within the monthly case mix budget cap.
equityCheck: Ask how people in rural areas and areas without public transit get to work and community activities when no common carrier or volunteer driver exists.
Check that the free-transportation rule is not used to expect unpaid family driving beyond what the family can give.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Tribal administration and management of home and community-based services programs
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page describes the option that lets the Department of Human Services contract with federally recognized Tribal Nations that have a reservation in Minnesota to administer and manage home and community-based services programs as lead agencies. It lists the three Tribal Nations with contracts, the programs each administers, who they serve, the duties of overlapping counties and managed care organizations, and how a Tribal Nation may set alternative provider standards.
requires: Federally recognized Tribal Nations have the right to govern themselves; the page lists the 11 federally recognized Tribal Nations in Minnesota and says the Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe, the Red Lake Band of Chippewa Indians and the White Earth Nation currently administer and manage home and community-based services under contract.

Under a Tribal lead agency contract the Tribal Nation performs most of the long-term care consultation activities in Minnesota Statutes section 256B.0911, which defines Tribal Nations as lead agencies; Tribal leadership defines the programs covered and the populations served, which can be broader than Tribal members.

Counties and managed care organizations that overlap a Tribal service area must offer eligible people the choice of Tribal, county or managed care organization management of their services at the initial assessment and at every annual reassessment; managed care organizations must accept Tribal assessments and support plans and share provider network information.

The page lists each contract: Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe (Alternative Care, personal care assistance assessment, Consumer Support Grant, the four disability waivers, Rule 185 case management, Elderly Waiver, Essential Community Supports, long-term care consultation and relocation service coordination); Red Lake Band of Chippewa Indians (Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver, Elderly Waiver, Essential Community Supports and long-term care consultation including personal care assistance); White Earth Nation (Alternative Care, the four disability waivers, Rule 185 case management, Elderly Waiver, Essential Community Supports, long-term care consultation and relocation service coordination).

A person who is eligible for Tribal administration may transfer lead agency case management at any time; the county of financial responsibility usually stays the same, and county financial workers (except for White Earth Nation, which has its own) must communicate with the Tribal Nation using the listed forms.

Tribal Nations may enroll to provide any home and community-based service for which they qualify without a lead agency contract, and a Tribal Nation that contracts as a lead agency may develop alternative provider qualifications for waiver services under Minnesota Statutes section 256B.02, subdivision 7c, by submitting the standards to the Department with evidence they meet, exceed or are exempt from the state standards.
equityCheck: Confirm that people eligible to choose Tribal management were offered the choice at the initial assessment and at each reassessment, and that the offer was documented.
Check that transfers between county and Tribal lead agencies do not cause gaps in services or funding.
