policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Waiver and Alternative Care programs overview
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page is the overview of the waiver and Alternative Care programs. It explains that each program rests on an agreement between the Department of Human Services and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, that the Department manages the programs, lead agencies administer them and providers deliver services. It lists the conditions every waiver or Alternative Care service must meet, what is never covered, and the duties of the state, lead agencies and providers.
requires: Every service must be prior authorized by the lead agency and included in the person's support plan before it is delivered, be for the person's direct benefit, be the most cost-effective option to meet the need, protect health, safety and well-being, help the person avoid institutionalization and function more independently, meet an assessed need, be the person's choice, and follow the federally approved waiver plan or Alternative Care protocol.

Services under the four disability waivers must also be related to the person's disability and within the county or Tribal Nation budget; Alternative Care and Elderly Waiver services must be within the case mix cap.

Services are not covered when they are recreational or for comfort or convenience, duplicate other services, are available from another funding source, are educational expenses under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, substitute for parental responsibility or for informal supports that meet the need, are alternative therapies (except under consumer-directed community supports), or pay for utilities; Older Americans Act funding is not treated as another funding source.

The Department of Human Services designs programs that meet federal rules, reports to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, renews each program every five years, submits amendments for changes, sets rate methods, manages lead agency administration for statewide consistency and makes sure everyone has the right to choose and live in the most integrated setting of their choice.

Lead agencies determine financial and program eligibility, provide ongoing case management and support plan development, help the person access and evaluate services, give information for informed choice about where to live and which services to use, inform the person of the option to self-direct, monitor services and adjust them, enter screening documents and service authorizations, and follow the approval-option oversight policy.
Providers must meet the provider overview standards, follow the provider manual, follow each service page and deliver only services the lead agency authorized in the support plan.
equityCheck: Check that informed choice about where to live and the option to self-direct were offered and documented in the person's language.
Review which requests are denied as not cost-effective or as duplicating informal supports, and whether families from some communities are expected to provide more unpaid care.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Waiver and Alternative Care service provider overview
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page sets the standards every home and community-based waiver and Alternative Care provider must meet. It divides services into those that require enrollment with the Department of Human Services and those a lead agency may approve on its own, lists which services need a license or certification, which are direct-contact services requiring a background study, and the training providers must complete.
requires: All waiver and Alternative Care providers must comply with Medical Assistance and federally approved state service standards and work within their license, certification or other requirements.

Enrollment-required services must be delivered by providers enrolled with Minnesota Health Care Programs that hold a Department of Human Services or Department of Health license (for example community residential services, customized living, day support, employment services, individualized home supports, integrated community supports, respite and positive support services) or a service-specific certification (for example assistive technology assessment, home-delivered meals and specialized transportation).

Approval-option services may be delivered by enrolled providers or by qualified vendors a willing lead agency approves; direct-delivery examples are chore, homemaker cleaning, environmental adaptation installation and individual-driver transportation, and purchased-item examples are personal emergency response systems, assistive technology equipment, specialized equipment and supplies and common-carrier transportation.

Everyone who provides a direct-contact service must have a background study under Minnesota Statutes chapter 245C; the page lists the waiver services that count as direct contact, and lead agencies that approve vendors for direct-contact services must follow the Department of Human Services background study process.

Enrolled individual providers must be 18 or older except for consumer-directed community supports and chore services; most newly enrolled providers must complete the waiver and Alternative Care provider training before enrollment and the resources and billing training within six months.

Caregiver living expense providers must meet the standards of the waiver service the live-in caregiver delivers; providers and people can find enrolled providers through the MinnesotaHelp.info directory.
equityCheck: Ask whether provider enrollment and licensing requirements are a barrier for small, culturally specific or Tribal providers, and what help the Department offers them.
Check that the provider directory shows languages spoken and cultural communities served.

policies.title: Community-Based Services Manual: Waiver, Alternative Care and Essential Community Supports general processes and procedures
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page walks through how a person gets into and moves through the waiver, Alternative Care and Essential Community Supports programs: access and referral, assessment and reassessment, support planning, service authorization in the Medicaid Management Information System, limits in institutional settings, changing waiver programs, the rules at age 65 including returning to a disability waiver after 65, own-home requirements and services during temporary travel or school outside Minnesota.
requires: Anyone may apply, and lead agencies accept referrals from any source; the assessor decides eligibility through the MnCHOICES assessment and the case manager or care coordinator then builds the support plan with the person, recording their informed choices of program, providers and services.

For the four disability waivers the case manager authorizes the type and amount of services, the lead agency enters authorizations in the Medicaid Management Information System and the county of financial responsibility approves them; for the aging programs the case manager or care coordinator authorizes services within the person's annual budget.

Services may not be authorized that fail the service requirements, and a person cannot receive waiver, Alternative Care or Essential Community Supports services in a nursing facility, hospital, intermediate care facility or institution for mental disease unless a service description says otherwise; entering such a setting triggers the temporary exit and restart process.

To change waiver programs a person must meet the level of care and eligibility for the new waiver through a reassessment; a person 65 or older at initial application cannot enroll in the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care or Community Access for Disability Inclusion waiver, and at 65 a person may choose a reassessment to make an informed choice about the Elderly Waiver.

There is no maximum age to return to the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care or Community Access for Disability Inclusion waiver: a person who exited for institutional care may be reopened by the county or Tribal Nation within 180 days without Department approval, and otherwise may return with Department approval on form 7759D when the Elderly Waiver does not meet their needs; a person on the Developmental Disabilities Waiver may change waivers after 65 with Department approval through the regional resource specialist.

Waiver and Alternative Care services may be authorized outside Minnesota only for temporary travel within the United States or out-of-state post-secondary school, limited to direct-care-staff services in the support plan, with the person keeping Minnesota Medicaid enrollment and a permanent Minnesota residence and all waiver plan requirements still applying.
equityCheck: Check that people turning 65 get a real informed choice between staying on a disability waiver and moving to the Elderly Waiver, and that the differences in services and budgets are explained.
Track how many requests to return to a disability waiver after 65 are approved or denied, and for whom.

policies.title: Crisis respite
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Crisis respite is short-term support that lets a person stay in the community and avoid institutional placement during a crisis. The service is licensed as an intervention service under Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D.
requires: The person must have been assessed and found eligible for home and community-based services, and the service must let the person avoid institutional placement and remain in the community.
Crisis respite covers ongoing technical assistance for the caregiver or primary provider as they carry out the person's intervention plan.
Crisis respite can be delivered through remote support.
The lead agency cannot authorize services that duplicate other Minnesota state plan or waiver services the person already receives, including case management.
In-home and out-of-home crisis respite are intensive support services under the home and community-based services license (245D.03, subdivision 1, paragraph (c)).

policies.title: Customized living, including 24-hour customized living
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Customized living is a bundle of services delivered in a licensed assisted living setting; 24-hour customized living adds round-the-clock supervision. The Community-Based Services Manual page defines the service for the Brain Injury and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waivers and the Elderly Waiver. Minnesota Statutes 256S.20 sets provider licensing and lead agency duties, and 256B.49, subdivision 28 limits new settings for the two disability waivers.
requires: A provider must hold an assisted living facility license under chapter 144G, or a comprehensive home care license and deliver services in a setting exempt from assisted living licensure (256S.20, subdivision 1).

The lead agency must make sure a documented need exists for every authorized component service, and may authorize 24-hour customized living only when the person needs 24-hour supervision for listed reasons (256S.20, subdivisions 3 and 4).
Providers may not bill the person or family for extra units beyond the rate limits or the lead agency-approved plan (256S.20, subdivision 5).

For the Brain Injury and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waivers, the Department of Human Services may not enroll new customized living settings serving four or fewer people in a single-family home, except for ownership changes at the same address; for newer settings the authorizing lead agency is financially responsible (256B.49, subdivision 28).

Settings operational on or after January 11, 2021 may serve only people age 55 or older on the two disability waivers; settings operational between May 1, 2001 and January 10, 2021 may serve up to four people under 55 who are not related to the principal care provider, with a size-limit exception form (form 7759B) for larger licensed settings (form 6189X).

Customized living may not be provided in a setting adjoined to or on the same property as an institution with a financial interest in the setting, or to people living in integrated community supports settings (form 6189X).
equityCheck: Check that the person was offered independent living and non-provider-controlled options before customized living, as Minnesota Statutes 256B.4905 requires.
Check that the setting's staff can communicate in the person's language and that culturally familiar food and routines are possible.

policies.title: Day support services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Day support services help a person build and keep daily living, social and community skills during the day, outside the home. The service replaced day training and habilitation as a waiver service during the rolling implementation of Waiver Reimagine streamlined services (the day training and habilitation page was deleted effective January 1, 2022). It is licensed under Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D and paid under the Disability Waiver Rate System.
requires: Day support services are an intensive support service under the home and community-based services license (245D.03, subdivision 1, paragraph (c), clause (4)).

Rates use the Disability Waiver Rate System day program formula with staffing ratios; at least 45 percent of revenue for these rates must go to direct care staff compensation (256B.4914, subdivisions 7 and 10d).
Day support services have an eight-hour daily billing limit starting in 2027 (256B.4914, subdivision 7).
Day support services can be delivered through remote support.
Each working-age waiver recipient must be offered the chance to work and earn a competitive wage before being offered only day services (256B.4905, subdivision 5a).
Day services may not be provided by the person's residential provider unless the person is offered a choice of providers and agrees in writing (256B.092, subdivision 5).
equityCheck: Check that the person was offered employment exploration or supported employment first, and that the offer is written in the plan.
Check transportation: people in rural areas and people without family drivers may be unable to reach a day program.
Check that the program's activities reflect the person's culture, language and interests.

policies.title: Developmental Disabilities Waiver
policies.summary: The Developmental Disabilities Waiver funds home and community-based services for children and adults with a developmental disability or related condition who need the level of care given in an intermediate care facility for persons with developmental disabilities, as an alternative to living in one. The Community-Based Services Manual page describes the program; Minnesota Statutes 256B.092 is the state law behind it.
requires: The person must need intermediate care facility level of care; case managers use the Department of Human Services guide form 4147A to make that determination.
The Department of Human Services does not pay from the waiver for a short-term admission to an intermediate care facility as respite care.

Each waiver recipient gets case management and a written person-centered support plan signed by the person and the county; the plan must cover needs, goals, services with amounts, informed choice of providers and appeal rights (256B.092, subdivisions 1a and 1b).

Case managers must make at least one face-to-face visit each year and complete annual training; a private agency with a financial interest in other services in the plan may not provide case management (256B.092, subdivision 1a).
Before a denial, reduction or termination, the county must offer to meet with the person (256B.092, subdivision 5).

Counties keep a waiting list of people who need but are not receiving services, with statewide priorities for people leaving institutions and people needing protection from abuse or neglect (256B.092, subdivisions 1f and 12).
equityCheck: Check that the waiting list category and reasonable pace standard were applied the same way for every person, and look at who waits longest by race and county.
Check that the support plan was built with the person in their language and reflects their culture.
Check that the person was offered a choice of providers and of case management.

policies.title: Developmental Disabilities Waiver waiting list guide
policies.summary: The Community-Based Services Manual guide (reviewed April 9, 2024) explains how lead agencies manage the Developmental Disabilities Waiver waiting list. It covers the legal basis, the urgency categories, and the reasonable pace standards that say how long a person can expect to wait from assessment to funding approval. Minnesota Statutes 256B.092, subdivision 12 sets the statewide priorities.
requires: Reasonable pace starts when the lead agency assesses the person and ends when the lead agency approves the person for waiver funding using the pend enter function in the Waiver Management System.
Institutional exit, immediate need and defined need each have a 45-day standard from assessment to funding approval; future need has no reasonable pace standard.
The lead agency assigns the category using the Waiting List Category Determination Tool (form 7209), based on the person's assessment.

Statewide priorities for people on the waiting list include people moving from institutions and people needing protection from abuse or neglect; the commissioner must consider the number of people waiting when allocating new enrollment resources (256B.092, subdivision 12).
The Department of Human Services tracks timely funding approvals and gives technical assistance to lead agencies to assure compliance with the reasonable pace standards.
equityCheck: Compare days from assessment to funding approval by county, race and language; a 45-day standard means little if some groups wait longer.
Check that people in the future need category are reassessed when their situation changes, and that families know how to ask.
Check that category decisions are explained to the person in writing and in their language.

policies.title: Disability-specific financial management (waiver allocations for lead agencies)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Each fiscal year the Department of Human Services gives every lead agency a budget to manage waiver authorizations: one budget for the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waivers, and a separate budget for the Developmental Disabilities Waiver. Lead agencies must keep the waivers accessible without overspending. The Community-Based Services Manual financial management pages explain the process; Minnesota Statutes 256B.49 and 256B.0916 set the county and Tribal agency duties.
requires: Lead agencies can view their resource allocations in the Waiver Management System and must authorize services within allowable rates.

County and Tribal agencies are responsible for spending above their annual allocation and must submit a corrective action plan covering the following two years (256B.49, subdivision 26; 256B.0916, subdivision 11).

County and Tribal agencies must spend their annual allocation; an agency that spends less than 97 percent while keeping a waiting list must submit a corrective plan, and if it does not, the commissioner must ensure access within that agency's allocation (256B.49, subdivision 27; 256B.0916, subdivision 12).

The commissioner posts financial and waiting list information online, updates financial data for each county and Tribal agency at least monthly, and compiles a report each December 1 (256B.0916, subdivision 8).
The statutes note that these allocation subdivisions are repealed upon federal approval of a new waiver structure; the Revisor pages do not say whether that approval has occurred.
equityCheck: Compare spending and waiting lists across county and Tribal agencies; underspending with a waiting list is a sign people are being left out.
Check whether allocation pressure leads to lower authorizations for people with the same needs in some counties.
Use the monthly posted data to look at access by region.

policies.title: Elderly Waiver
policies.summary: The Elderly Waiver funds home and community-based services for people age 65 and older who are eligible for Medical Assistance and need nursing home level of care but choose to live in the community. The Community-Based Services Manual page (updated June 30, 2025) describes the program; Minnesota Statutes chapter 256S sets eligibility and administration. Counties, Tribal entities and managed care organizations administer it.
requires: A person must be 65 or older, eligible for Medical Assistance, and have a MnCHOICES assessment under Minnesota Statutes 256B.0911 that results in a nursing facility level of care determination (256S.05, subdivisions 1 and 2).
A person enrolled in a managed care organization cannot receive county-administered fee-for-service Elderly Waiver services (256S.05, subdivision 5).
Spousal impoverishment rules apply, with a maintenance needs allowance for participants at or below the special income standard (256S.05, subdivisions 3 and 4).
Customized living under the waiver must be delivered by a provider licensed as an assisted living facility or under an exempt home care arrangement (256S.20).
Service definitions and standards follow the federally approved Elderly Waiver plan unless a statute says otherwise.
equityCheck: Check that older adults with limited English get the MnCHOICES assessment with an interpreter and understand the choice between nursing home and community care.
Check that rural older adults can find enrolled providers for the services in their plan.
Check that Tribal elders are told about services administered by Tribal entities.

policies.title: Guidelines for Positive Supports in Settings Licensed by the Department of Human Services (form 6810C)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: A resource manual (version 1.0, April 2016) written by the Disability Services Division for providers licensed by the Department of Human Services. It explains duties under Minnesota Rules, chapter 9544 (the Positive Supports Rule) and Minnesota Statutes, chapter 245D, and gives guidance on person-centered planning, understanding behavior, positive support strategies and positive support transition plans.
requires: The Positive Supports Rule covers license holders serving a person with a developmental disability or any person receiving a service licensed under Minnesota Statutes, chapter 245D, and requires positive support strategies for every person covered.

The rule prohibits many physical and behavioral interventions; Minnesota Statutes 245D.06, subdivision 5 and Minnesota Rules 9544.0060 prohibit chemical, mechanical and manual restraint except the emergency use of manual restraint under Minnesota Statutes 245D.061.

A positive support transition plan is required when emergency manual restraint is used three or more times in 90 days or four or more times in 180 days, to eliminate aversive procedures and avoid further restraint.

License holders must build person-centered principles into services: what is important to and for the person, respect for history, dignity and cultural background, self-determination, civil and legal rights, and the most integrated setting with a balance of risk and opportunity.

License holders must evaluate with the person at least every six months whether services support the person's preferences, daily needs, activities and goals, under Minnesota Statutes 245D.07, subdivision 1a, and 42 CFR 441.725.
The manual points lead agency staff to the Person-Centered, Informed Choice and Transition Protocol for Department of Human Services expectations on person-centered planning.
equityCheck: Check that behavior is understood in the context of the person's culture, language, trauma history and communication method before any intervention is planned.
Check that people who do not speak or who have guardians still drive their own planning and that strategies reflect what is important to them.
Check restraint and emergency-use data by setting and by group to see whether some people or settings carry a disproportionate share.
Check that the person and family received the manual's information in an accessible format or language they understand.

Service definitions and standards are in the Community-Based Services Manual.
requires: A provider must be enrolled in Minnesota Health Care Programs, keep its license or other proof of qualifications, and get a Department of Human Services-approved service authorization before serving a person.
Providers report the services they plan to offer on the Home and Community-Based Services Programs Service Request Form (form 6638) and must register for a MN-ITS account.
Providers must verify each person's waiver eligibility every month by phone or through MN-ITS.
Minnesota Health Care Programs pays only for services on the service authorization, and an approved authorization is not a guarantee of payment.
The page includes a service-by-waiver table and links each service to its Community-Based Services Manual page.
equityCheck: Check that enrollment steps and forms are not a barrier for small, rural or culturally specific providers that people want to use.
When a claim is denied because eligibility lapsed, find out whether the person lost Medical Assistance for a reason that could have been prevented.

policies.title: Paying relatives and legally responsible individuals
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Community-Based Services Manual page explains when a relative, guardian, conservator, spouse or parent may be paid to provide a waiver service. It follows the federally approved waiver plans for the Brain Injury Waiver, Community Alternative Care Waiver, Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver, Developmental Disabilities Waiver and Elderly Waiver. It sets out which services relatives can and cannot be paid for.
requires: A relative or non-professional guardian of an adult may be paid only if they are related to or guardian for one person (or a family of siblings), are qualified to provide the service, and are not otherwise responsible for that care.
The relative must be employed by a qualified provider; they cannot be enrolled themselves as the Medical Assistance provider for that service. Consumer-Directed Community Supports is the exception.
Relatives cannot be paid for caregiver living expenses, case management, or individualized home supports with family training.
A primary caregiver cannot be paid for chore, homemaker or respite services that are meant to relieve or support that same caregiver.
Professional guardians and conservators cannot be paid for any waiver service.

Spouses and parents of minors can be paid only for Consumer-Directed Community Supports personal assistance, not for other waiver services. A parent is a legally responsible individual only for a minor child.
Under Minnesota Statutes 256B.0919, subdivision 3, a county may certify an exempt relative to provide Elderly Waiver adult foster care.
equityCheck: Check whether families who rely on relatives as caregivers, including families whose first language is not English, have been told in plain terms which services a relative can be paid for and how the relative can be hired through a qualified provider.

Ask whether the person was offered Consumer-Directed Community Supports as a real choice when a spouse or parent of a minor is the preferred caregiver, since that is the only route that allows paying them.

In rural areas and in communities with few enrolled providers, check that the one-person limit for paid relatives is applied the same way for every family and that no one is refused without the policy being explained.
Review who is being approved and denied as a paid relative across the lead agency's caseload and look for patterns by race, language or geography.

policies.title: Positive support services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Positive support services help a person reduce behaviors that put the person or others at risk by using positive, person-centered strategies instead of restrictive ones. The Community-Based Services Manual page cites Minnesota Rules chapter 9544 and Minnesota Statutes 245D.091 and links to the positive support transition plan forms. The service may be delivered remotely if it meets the manual's remote support requirements.
requires: Providers must use positive support strategies, document them in the person's plans and evaluate them with the person at least every six months (Minnesota Rules 9544.0030).
A functional behavior assessment is required before a qualified professional develops or changes a written intervention for a target behavior (9544.0040).
Prohibited procedures include prone restraint, chemical and mechanical restraint and punishment; manual restraint is allowed only in emergencies (9544.0060 and 9544.0070).

A positive support transition plan is required after three emergency manual restraints within 90 days or four within 180 days; the forms are the Positive Support Transition Plan (form 6810) and its review (form 6810A).
Staff need eight hours of core training before taking on duties and four hours of refresher training each year (9544.0090).
A positive support professional, analyst or specialist must meet the credentials and supervision rules in Minnesota Statutes 245D.091.
equityCheck: Check that the person leads the planning process and that the plan reflects the person's culture, language and history, not only the provider's routines.
Review restraint and incident reports by race, disability type and setting to spot patterns.
Check that rural providers can reach qualified positive support professionals, including by remote support.

policies.title: Waiver, Alternative Care and Essential Community Supports case management
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Case management gives a person access to assessment, person-centered planning, referral, support plan monitoring, coordination and advocacy. The Community-Based Services Manual page says case managers must use the Person-Centered, Informed Choice and Transition Protocol (form 3825) and the My Move Plan Summary, and that each person has a choice of case management. Minnesota Statutes 256B.49, 256B.092 and 256B.4905 set the duties.
requires: Each waiver recipient must get case management from a qualified vendor; duties include finalizing the person-centered support plan, explaining service options, finding providers, helping with appeals and monitoring services, with at least one face-to-face visit each year (256B.49, subdivision 13; 256B.092, subdivision 1a).
Case managers may delegate some tasks but not those needing professional judgment, such as finalizing or changing the support plan (256B.49, subdivision 13).

A private agency with a financial interest in other services in the plan may not provide case management; case managers must complete at least 20 hours of training each year (256B.49, subdivision 13).
Lead agencies must give complete, accurate, culturally and linguistically appropriate information so people can make informed choices (256B.4905, subdivision 2a).

For members of a federally recognized Tribal Nation in Minnesota, informed choice includes the right to services administered or provided by their Tribal Nation; lead agencies must tell people about those services and coordinate directly with the Tribal human services agency (256B.4905, subdivision 2a).
County procurement of case management must consider culturally responsive services (256B.49, subdivision 13).
equityCheck: Check that the person was offered a choice of case management and that the choice is documented.
Check that Tribal members were told about services from their Tribal Nation, as the statute requires.
Check that the yearly face-to-face visit happened for people in rural areas and people who move often.

programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: On December 31, 2024, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services approved a package of amendments to the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion and Developmental Disabilities waiver plans. Positive support analyst and specialist qualifications and MnCHOICES assessor qualifications were updated; environmental adaptations that violate the Positive Supports Rule are not covered; respite 'home' means a setting the person or family owns or leases.

requires: The waiver is authorized under section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act; the federal entry shows status Approved, first approval April 1, 1985, current effective date 2023-04-01 and expiration 2028-03-31.

The federal entry links to the approved application and a waiver description fact sheet, both dated April 6, 2026.

policies.title: 2025 legislative changes to Early Intensive Developmental and Behavioral Intervention
programs: Early Intensive Developmental and Behavioral Intervention
policies.summary: The 2025 Legislature changed the Early Intensive Developmental and Behavioral Intervention benefit in Laws 2025, First Special Session, chapter 9, article 6. The Disability Services Division summarized the changes on July 1, 2025, with translations added July 24, 2025: provisional licensing, comprehensive licensing standards to come, licensing-led maltreatment investigations, removed treatment modalities, employee status for providers and provider qualifications.
requires: All enrolled agencies must apply for provisional licensure once the application is available; the Department of Human Services planned to begin issuing provisional licenses in early 2026, and existing agencies may keep serving people under Minnesota Statutes 256B.0949 while they wait.
The Department must propose comprehensive licensure standards to the Legislature by January 2027.

Effective July 1, 2025, the Department's licensing function is the lead investigative agency for alleged maltreatment in these programs; reports for people under 18 go to Licensing and for ages 18 to 21 to the Minnesota Adult Abuse Reporting Center.

Effective July 1, 2025, the Play Project and Early Social Interaction are no longer approved treatment modalities, and no new modality may be approved without legislative approval; providers must stop using them and update plans.
Effective immediately, all Level I, II and III providers must be agency employees, not independent contractors, and former provider shortage exceptions are now official provider qualifications.
equityCheck: Removing modalities and contractor status can shrink the provider pool; check which regions and language communities lose providers and how families are told.
The announcement was translated into Spanish, Somali and Hmong; make sure families who speak other languages also receive the information.
Track provisional licensing outcomes for small and culturally specific agencies.

policies.title: 2025 legislative changes to the MnCHOICES assessment process
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: On August 26, 2025, the Aging and Adult Services and Disability Services divisions summarized eight changes the 2025 Legislature made to Minnesota Statutes 256B.0911 that affect MnCHOICES assessments. Several need federal approval before they start; others set new duties for the Department of Human Services with dates.
requires: Certified assessor education requirement changes from a bachelor's degree to an associate degree (needs federal approval).

Lead agencies may contract with licensed hospitals to perform MnCHOICES assessments; hospital assessors must be qualified, may not do other waiver tasks, and the lead agency stays responsible for oversight (needs federal approval).
The lead agency must give the person an estimated timeline for completing their assessment, while still meeting the 20-day assessment requirement.

Allowable consecutive remote reassessments rise from two to four for the four disability waivers; verbal attestation or another communication method may replace signatures at reassessment; a person age 22 to 64 on a disability waiver or Community First Services and Supports may attest to no change in needs for up to two consecutive reassessments (each needs federal approval).
Effective January 1, 2026, the Department must publish a dashboard of MnCHOICES assessment completions and update it at least twice a year.
The Department must propose a long-term care consultation payment method that does not rely on a time study, due to the Legislature by October 1, 2026.
equityCheck: Hospital-based assessments can speed discharge; check that the person still gets a full conversation about community options, not only a quick placement.
Attesting to 'no change' saves time but can hide growing needs; make sure people who are isolated or have no advocate are still asked real questions.
Use the new assessment completion dashboard to compare timeliness across counties and Tribal Nations.

policies.title: 2026 Disability Waiver Rate System component values, tiered rates and rate remediation for start dates on or after January 1, 2026
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: The Legislature required updated Disability Waiver Rate System component values effective January 1, 2026, or upon federal approval, along with tiered rates for family residential services and a split of night supervision into awake and asleep services. Because federal approval of the 2025 waiver amendments had not arrived, the Disability Services Division told lead agencies on February 10, 2026 that rates for framework services with start dates on or after January 1, 2026 must be remediated once approval and instructions come. The amended 2026 frameworks for January through March start dates are posted on the Department of Human Services rate frameworks page.
requires: Updated component values apply to Disability Waiver Rate System framework services effective January 1, 2026 or upon approval by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, whichever applies.
Family residential services (adult, child and life sharing) become a tiered-rate service, and night supervision splits into awake and asleep night supervision with separate frameworks.

Lead agencies must remediate rates for adult day, day support, prevocational, employment, individualized home supports, night supervision, positive supports, community residential, family residential and individualized community supports services with start dates on or after January 1, 2026.
Adult day bath, customized living and 24-hour customized living do not need remediation because their component values did not change.

Until instructions arrive, lead agencies keep using MnCHOICES with the 2025 frameworks and authorize the full waiver span; the Department will give the percentage change for each service and how to document the change.
equityCheck: Make a list of every person whose rate must be remediated so no one in a small or rural lead agency is missed when the instructions come.
Tell providers and people plainly why 2026 increases are delayed; small and culturally specific providers have the least cushion to wait.
Check that tiered family residential rates do not reduce support for families caring for people with the highest needs.

requires: Married Alternative Care applicants are not required to have a financial worker asset assessment from October 1, 2024; assessments started before that date must still be finished.

policies.title: Change to the MnCHOICES remote reassessment policy for disability waivers (effective January 1, 2026)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Effective January 1, 2026, the Disability Services Division changed the remote reassessment policy for people on the four disability waivers. Remote reassessments by video or telephone may now replace in-person reassessments for four years in a row, followed by an in-person reassessment in the fifth year. The change follows a 2025 amendment to Minnesota Statutes 256B.0911, subdivision 24.
requires: For annual reassessments on or after January 1, 2026 on the Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion and Developmental Disabilities waivers, four consecutive remote reassessments (including the 65th birthday reassessment) may substitute for in-person ones, with an in-person reassessment in the fifth year.
After January 1, 2026, lead agencies must review past assessments to decide whether a person qualifies for a remote reassessment next time.
The new rule replaces the earlier two-consecutive-years rule for disability waivers.

It does not apply to Alternative Care, Essential Community Supports or the Elderly Waiver (remote every other year) or to Community First Services and Supports (two consecutive years), which keep their current rules.
The person must still receive informed choice and give informed consent for a remote reassessment, as described on the manual page on assessment applicability and timelines.
equityCheck: Treat remote reassessment as the person's choice: check that people with hearing, memory or language needs are told the advantages of an in-person visit and can pick it.
Track which people are offered remote versus in-person reassessments by race, language and region so remote visits are not used mainly to save staff travel in rural areas.
If the assessor cannot observe the home or complete screening tools remotely, schedule an in-person reassessment.

policies.title: Community First Services and Supports replaces personal care assistance and the Consumer Support Grant (from October 1, 2024)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Community First Services and Supports is a Minnesota Health Care Programs service that replaces personal care assistance and the Consumer Support Grant. Starting October 1, 2024, people using those programs move to Community First Services and Supports at their next assessment. The Aging and Adult Services and Disability Services divisions published the final policy manual on August 27, 2024 and the transition steps on October 1, 2024.
requires: From October 1, 2024, a person using personal care assistance or the Consumer Support Grant begins the transition at their next assessment; eligibility is the same as for personal care assistance.

If the person is eligible and chooses Community First Services and Supports, the lead agency gives them the list of consultation services providers and the information sheet (available in English, Hmong, Karen, Somali and Spanish); the person picks a consultation services provider.
The lead agency authorizes consultation services and three months of personal care assistance or Consumer Support Grant to avoid a gap, following the unit determination rules.
The person writes their service delivery plan, with help from the consultation services provider if they want it; the lead agency approves the plan and authorizes services.

Lead agencies and providers had to review the final policy manual before October 1, 2024 and update internal procedures; consultation providers, agencies and financial management services providers, not lead agencies, give people the rights and responsibilities form form 6893R.
Waiver participants may receive extended Community First Services and Supports under the four disability waivers, with rates set by the approved state plan method.
equityCheck: Check that the information sheet in the person's language was given and that interpreters are offered when choosing a consultation provider.
Watch for service gaps during the three-month bridge, especially for people whose workers must enroll under new rules.
Review whether consultation services providers are available in every region and in languages people speak.

policies.title: Department of Human Services Equity Policy
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: The Equity Policy requires every Department of Human Services employee to look at policies, practices, procedures, rules, budgets and decisions through an equity lens, using the Department of Human Services Equity Analysis Toolkit, with the goal of reducing disparities and improving access for the communities the department serves. It first took effect February 27, 2017, was revised December 31, 2022, and was reissued effective August 4, 2023. It applies to all employees; vendors, contractors, grantees and volunteers may have the same duties through their agreements.
requires: A formal equity analysis is required for all actions with prolonged or long-term impact that go to a supervisor, manager, director, assistant or deputy commissioner or the commissioner for approval; the action must be accompanied by the Equity Analysis or Equity Scan from the toolkit, or a customized tool developed with an equity director.

The toolkit must be used in policy development and revisions, legislative proposals, budgets, strategic planning, leadership decisions, training, contracting and procurement, community engagement, service delivery and other listed areas.
Employees must attend annual learning on the policy, use the toolkit in their work, and each year acknowledge and sign the staff commitment for advancing equity and the agreement to use the toolkit.

Each administration or area must keep an Equity Committee led or supported by its equity director, pursue workforce development, review contracts and procurement through an equity lens, do ongoing community engagement, and apply the National Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services standards.
Managers must promote equity in strategic planning and encourage staff to apply an equity lens; human resources must support workforce equity.
Failure to comply may lead to discipline up to termination or the end of a contractor or volunteer relationship.
equityCheck: Before you approve or propose a change, ask the four toolkit questions: which groups are affected, does it reduce a disparity, what are the positive and negative impacts, and can it be sustained.
Check that representatives of the affected communities were consulted, not just informed.
Record the equity analysis with the decision so others can see it.

policies.title: Department of Human Services letter to legislative committee chairs: intent to issue a temporary 245D licensing moratorium
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: On December 1, 2025, the Department of Human Services told legislative committee chairs that it would put a temporary moratorium on new licenses for home and community-based services under Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D. The moratorium starts January 1, 2026 and is expected to last 24 months. The letter cites Minnesota Statutes section 245A.03, subdivision 7a and Executive Order 25-10 as authority.
requires: Starting January 1, 2026, the Department of Human Services stops issuing new 245D licenses, stops accepting new 245D license applications, stops adding new services to existing 245D licenses, and cancels pending applications.
Application fee refunds are available to affected applicants until December 31, 2026.
The moratorium is expected to end December 31, 2027.

An exception process is available based on requests from the county, Tribal Nation or managed care organization responsible for a person's waiver case management; a provider approved through an exception still goes through the standard license review.

During the moratorium the department will focus on reviewing providers not evaluated in more than three years, to meet the federal waiver plan commitment to review each 245D provider at least once every three years.

Watch for groups whose preferred providers (for example, culturally specific or language-matched agencies) cannot enter the system during the moratorium.
Keep data on exception requests by county and Tribal Nation so gaps in access are visible.

policies.title: Disability waiver amendment approval and implementation timelines (2025 legislation)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: On January 23, 2026, the Disability Services Division replaced two earlier notices and explained where the 2025 amendments to the Community Alternative Care, Community Access for Disability Inclusion and Developmental Disabilities waivers and the Brain Injury Waiver renewal stood with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. It told lead agencies how to set rates while approval was pending and summarized the proposed changes.
requires: The Department of Human Services held 30-day public comment periods in October and November 2025 and submitted the amendments in December 2025; it cannot implement them until federal approval, and the federal agency has up to 90 days, paused by formal requests for information.

For Disability Waiver Rate System framework services and family residential services with effective dates on or after January 1, 2026, lead agencies must keep using MnCHOICES, which applies the 2025 rate frameworks, and authorize the full waiver span at that rate.

Proposed MnCHOICES changes: assessor qualifications aligned to state law, an estimated assessment timeline for the person, hospital social workers allowed to assess, and attestation of no change in needs for reassessments.

Proposed service changes: swim lessons for some children under consumer directed community supports, water safety lessons, updated positive support provider qualifications and updated rules for respite in unlicensed settings.

Proposed rate changes: inflation adjustment of component values, tiered rates for family residential services, hour limits on individualized home supports with training and with family training, and a service agreement review process.
Implementation was delayed by the 2025 special session, changes during drafting, a late start to public comment and delayed federal submission and approval.

policies.title: Disability Waiver Rate System compensation thresholds for direct care staff (delayed to January 1, 2029)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: The 2023 Legislature required providers paid under the Disability Waiver Rate System to spend a minimum share of their rate revenue on direct care staff compensation: 66 percent for residential services, 45 percent for day services and 60 percent for unit-based services, under Minnesota Statutes 256B.4914, subdivision 10d. The requirement was first set for January 1, 2025; the 2025 Legislature delayed it to January 1, 2029, with compliance tracked through cost reporting beginning in the 2030 reporting period.
requires: Residential services: at least 66 percent of Disability Waiver Rate System revenue must go to direct care staff compensation; day services: 45 percent; unit-based services: 60 percent.
Compensation includes wages, taxes, workers' compensation and benefits as listed in the statute.

The 2025 Legislature (Laws 2025, First Special Session, chapter 9, article 2, section 63) delayed the requirement to January 1, 2029; the Department of Human Services will check compliance using cost report data from the 2030 cost reporting period.
The requirement applies to all organizations that provide Disability Waiver Rate System services except assisted living facilities that provide customized living and 24-hour customized living.
Over the next four years the Department will work with community partners on the program and advise the Legislature on the policy.

policies.title: Disability Waiver Rate System cost reporting: provider selection, submission and audit (Minnesota Statutes 256B.4914, subdivision 10a)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Minnesota Statutes 256B.4914, subdivision 10a, requires the Department of Human Services to collect cost data from randomly selected providers paid under the Disability Waiver Rate System and to audit selected reports for validity and completeness. The Disability Services Division selects providers each cycle, sets a submission deadline and, since 2024, reviews every submitted report for data validation.
requires: Selected providers must submit and attest to 12 months of business costs, with the period ending no more than 18 months before submission; the report covers staff wages, facility, client and program support, transportation and administrative costs.
Providers selected in the 2024 cycle (chosen March 27, 2024) had to submit by August 31, 2024; failing to submit by the deadline can result in stopped payments for services.
The Department reviews all submitted cost reports during a reporting period; a report that fails validation is unsubmitted and the provider must fix and resubmit it promptly.
The data is used to give the Legislature cost-based advice on payment rates and, from the 2030 reporting period, to check compensation threshold compliance.
In late 2025 the Department asked providers who reported between 2021 and 2025 for feedback on improving the cost reporting system.
equityCheck: Small, rural and culturally specific providers have the least capacity for cost reporting; check that they get help before a missed deadline stops their payments.

From January 1, 2026, the qualified supervising professional must give at least one hour of clinical supervision for every 16 hours of direct treatment, and the agency must observe and direct services for each person at least monthly. The Disability Services Division updated the policy manual and the treatment plan form.
requires: Effective January 1, 2026, at least one hour of clinical supervision by the qualified supervising professional for every 16 hours of direct treatment, unless the person's treatment plan (form 7109) states otherwise.

Effective January 1, 2026, the agency (qualified supervising professional, Level I or Level II provider) must provide observation and direction at least once a month for each person and may not do so by telehealth for more than two consecutive months.

Agencies must use the updated Individual Treatment Plan and Progress Monitoring Form, form 7109, and complete the new clinical supervision frequency section for plans with 2026 service dates, with an option to request a different supervision plan when clinically necessary.
Agencies must review the manual page on clinical supervision and the form instructions.

policies.title: Electronic visit verification provider training (Department of Human Services slide deck)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: A Department of Human Services training deck for providers that explains what electronic visit verification is, which services it applies to, how Minnesota's open model works and how a provider enrolls. It does not cover how to use a system, billing, or compliance enforcement.
requires: Electronic visit verification is required by section 12006(a) of the 21st Century Cures Act and Minnesota Statutes, section 256B.073, for certain personal care, home health and waiver services; providers are responsible for knowing which of their services require it.
Each visit record must verify the type of service, the person receiving it, the date, the location, the worker, and the start and end times.

Minnesota uses an open model: a provider may use the state-selected system (HHAeXchange, at no cost) or a third-party system that connects to the state data aggregator and meets Department of Human Services requirements; the same policy applies either way.
Live-in caregivers are not exempt; they have an exception that lets them enter the required data at least once per day instead of in real time.
For Safe at Home participants, telephony is the only allowed verification method and the Safe at Home post office box is used as the location for every visit.

Providers enroll with HHAeXchange after receiving their National Provider Identifier or Unique Minnesota Provider Identifier, receive a monthly compliance report, and are expected to train their caregivers and the people they serve on the system they choose.
equityCheck: Check that people who receive services at home or in the community are not pushed toward fewer settings because of verification: the policy says it does not create a barrier to where services are provided.
Check that small providers, culturally specific providers and rural providers have the training, devices and connectivity they need, since third-party system costs fall on the provider.
Check that caregivers and people served get plain-language instructions in their own language and format, and that Safe at Home participants' addresses stay confidential.
Check that live-in caregiver families know about the once-per-day exception so they are not wrongly marked noncompliant.

source.title: Electronic visit verification provider training, Department of Human Services electronic visit verification team

requires: All disability waiver case managers had to complete the employment training by August 1, 2024.

As of June 4, 2024, 1,606 case managers had enrolled, 1,139 had completed the course and 565 had received credit.

policies.title: Home and Community-Based Services Lead Agency Review frequently asked questions (updated August 1, 2026)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: The Department of Human Services question-and-answer document for lead agencies about the Round 5 Lead Agency Review. It explains who is reviewed and how often, how case files are sampled and what reviewers look for in support plans, the survey and training attestations, and how remediation and corrective action plans work.
requires: Every lead agency (county or Tribal Nation) that administers home and community-based services waiver programs is reviewed about every three to four years; Round 5 began in spring 2024, agencies get 60 to 90 days' notice, and since October 1, 2024 reviews are remote.

Case files are sampled at random: 10 percent of cases by program, 10 cases, or all cases if fewer than 10, whichever is largest; reviewers look at the previous 18 months of case notes, the current assessment and the matching support plan.

The Round 5 survey includes a training attestation covering four trainings for all disability waiver case managers, including contracted ones: Supporting my move, Getting to work, Informed choice, and the annual 20-hour requirement; gaps must be remediated within 60 days.

From April 2, 2026 the emergency backup plan is a required part of the support plan with four sections (backup for provider no-shows or staff shortages, community-wide disaster, plan in an emergency, and evacuation help); 'not needed' or 'N/A' does not meet compliance.

The support plan must be developed and sent within 60 days of the assessment, eligibility update or initial assessment review; from August 1, 2026 all providers responsible for services under the plan must sign it within 60 days, and the lead agency signs as provider when it uses a service approval option.

Support plans are reviewed for plain language, a future-oriented dream statement from the person's own perspective, specific strengths, rituals and routines, a monitoring statement, and identified needs; remediation of individual files is due within 60 days and a corrective action plan within 10 days of the final report.
equityCheck: Check that dream statements, strengths and routines are written from the person's perspective even when a guardian or family member answers, and in the person's own words where possible.
Check that plain-language and people-first standards are met for people who read in languages other than English and for people who use alternative communication.
Check that backup and disaster plans are realistic for people who live alone, in rural areas, or without natural supports.
Check that contracted case management agencies, including culturally specific ones, meet the same training and timeliness standards as county staff.

policies.title: Housing Stabilization Services program ended October 31, 2025
policies.summary: Housing Stabilization Services, a Medical Assistance benefit that began in 2020 to help older adults and people with disabilities find and keep housing, ended October 31, 2025. The Department of Human Services sought to end it because of widespread fraud, submitted a state plan amendment, took public comment and received final federal approval. No new eligibility requests were accepted after October 10, 2025.
requires: October 31, 2025 was the last day Housing Stabilization Services could be delivered; no new eligibility requests were reviewed after October 10, 2025.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services gave final approval to the termination; the approval letter and the public comment summary are posted.
The Department received more than 200 public comments in a 30-day period, most opposing the end because of effects on participants, and published a summary with responses.

The Department worked with counties, Tribes, Urban Indian organizations and managed care organizations to identify other housing resources, each with its own eligibility rules, and said these do not replace the services that ended.
The Department said it remains open to a redesigned program with stronger integrity tools.
equityCheck: People who lost this service are at risk of housing loss; check that every former participant on a waiver was connected to a case manager and to the posted housing resources.
Make sure the end-of-program information and the resources page reached people in their own languages and through trusted community organizations.
Record who lost services by race, disability and region so the effect of the termination is visible.

policies.title: Instructions for consumer directed community supports budget changes in the revised MnCHOICES application
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: On October 8, 2024, the Disability Services Division gave lead agencies steps to follow when a person's consumer directed community supports budget changes after a reassessment in the revised MnCHOICES application. The Department of Human Services is comparing budgets with the earlier MnCHOICES version and expected some changes because it clarified assessor guidance.
requires: When a consumer directed community supports budget changes for a person on a disability waiver, the lead agency must review changes in the person's needs since the last assessment, check past and current assessments for errors, and check that the Medicaid Management Information System entry matches the screening document.

If the reviews do not explain the change, the lead agency should ask the Department for an assessment review through the MnCHOICES Help Desk Contact Form, form 6979; a policy expert will explain the change so the lead agency can share it with the person.

The person has the right to appeal their assessment results; if the new budget does not meet their needs the lead agency can check eligibility for an enhanced budget or an exception to the budget methodology.
The Department will keep monitoring budgets for trends as more people are reassessed in the revised application.
equityCheck: Explain any budget decrease to the person in their language and in writing, with appeal rights, before the new budget starts.
Track budget decreases by race, language, county and Tribal Nation to see whether assessor practice differs across groups.
Offer the enhanced budget and exception options proactively to people who cannot advocate for themselves.

policies.title: Minnesota Employment First Policy
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: The Olmstead Subcabinet adopted the Minnesota Employment First Policy on September 29, 2014. It says that all working-age Minnesotans with disabilities can work and should be offered the chance to work for a competitive wage before other supports and services are offered. It directs the Departments of Human Services, Education, and Employment and Economic Development to build the policy into their programs.
requires: Competitive, integrated employment is the first and expected service option, and employment is a priority outcome of services and supports.
Employment and support services must be grounded in informed choice, including community-based experiences, information about how work affects benefits, and support to understand options.
The three agencies must define and document a person-centered, informed choice process that is free of conflicts of interest or bias against work.
If a person chooses not to work after an informed choice process, the agency must document the reasons and regularly review the decision with the person, who may change their mind at any time.
The agencies must align programs, funding and policies, and must develop uniform data collection and public reporting on implementation and outcomes.
equityCheck: Check that every working-age person on a waiver has had an informed choice conversation about work, including people with the most significant disabilities and people whose families expect them not to work.

Look at competitive employment rates by race, language, disability type and county; the 2026 Olmstead Plan reports that in state fiscal year 2025, 39 percent of people who got both waiver services and vocational rehabilitation services had competitive integrated employment.
Make sure benefits counseling is offered in the person's language so fear of losing benefits does not decide the outcome.

policies.title: People who receive waiver services must be assigned an individual case manager
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: On July 19, 2022, the Aging and Adult Services and Disability Services divisions clarified that every person who receives waiver services, or Rule 185 case management, must be assigned their own individual case manager. A team approach without a named case manager is not allowed. The policy took effect immediately.
requires: Each person must have an individually assigned case manager, and the case manager's name and contact information must be given to the person so they can reach them directly.
Lead agencies may use temporary or time-limited coverage, peer consultation and case aides for support, but not as a substitute for an assigned case manager.
Lead agencies must monitor case management practice and compliance, provide support and fix noncompliance.
A lead agency or contracted provider using a team approach must correct it immediately by assigning a case manager to each person and telling the person who it is.
The requirement comes from state statute and the federally approved waiver plans, including the 1915(b) case management waiver.
equityCheck: Check that people with limited English or communication disabilities have the case manager's contact information in a form they can use.
Where workforce shortages are used to justify team coverage, ask which communities are affected and consult the state before changing practice.
Ask people directly whether they know their case manager's name; low awareness is a warning sign.

policies.title: Person-Centered, Informed Choice and Transition Protocol
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This Department of Human Services protocol (document form 3825) sets the Department's expectations for person-centered support planning by its lead agency partners. Part One covers person-centered planning and informed choice for everyone who gets long-term services and supports. Part Two adds requirements when a person moves from one living arrangement to another. It is tied to Minnesota's Olmstead Plan.
requires: Every support plan written by a lead agency support planner must be based on person-centered principles, and the person keeps control of the plan and the information in it.

Part One is required practice for people on the disability waivers, people with Rule 185 case management or relocation services, people with mental health targeted case management, and older adults on the Elderly Waiver, Alternative Care or Essential Community Supports.

Part Two must also be followed when any of these people move from one residence to another; it covers options and informed choice, coordination and transfer of responsibilities, and a quality review of the move.

Waiver and Alternative Care case managers, care coordinators, and adult and children's mental health targeted case managers are required to write plans that follow the protocol; Rule 185 and vulnerable adult case managers are listed at a lower accountability level; MnCHOICES certified assessors, relocation services coordinators and Moving Home Minnesota case managers contribute.

Planning must look for providers who can give culturally specific services that fit the person's needs, strengths and preferences, and a person who knows what they want may opt out of extensive planning.

The protocol covers the full service cycle: discovery and learning, support and action planning, implementation, and quality review. It cites Minnesota Statutes 256B.0911 and does not override existing statutes, rules or federal regulations.
equityCheck: Check that the plan records what is important to the person in their own words and reflects their culture, ethnicity, language and community, not just a list of services.
When a person is moving, confirm they were shown real options, including living on their own or with family, in a language and format they understand, and that the choice was theirs.
Ask whether providers who offer culturally specific services were searched for and offered, especially outside the metro area where the list is short.
Review whether people with guardians, people with limited English and people in segregated settings get the same depth of discovery and follow-up as everyone else.

policies.title: Residential support service criteria for community residential services and customized living (effective July 1, 2025)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Since July 1, 2025, a person on a disability waiver can get community residential services, or customized living on the Brain Injury or Community Access for Disability Inclusion waivers, only if they have complex medical or complex behavioral health needs and the planning team has found that no other available residential option meets their needs. The criteria come from Minnesota Statutes 256B.49, subdivision 29 and 256B.092, subdivision 11, with federal approval received December 31, 2024.
requires: The assessor decides at every assessment after July 1, 2025 whether the person has complex medical or complex behavioral health needs and sends the person the result.

Before authorizing community residential services or customized living, the case manager must present all available least-restrictive and own-home options first, run an informed decision-making process and document the person's informed choice in case notes and the support plan signature sheet.
If the person does not meet the criteria, the case manager cannot authorize the service, must send a notice of action and must support the person through an appeal if they choose one.

People with an active service agreement for these services on July 1, 2025 and continual authorization are exempt, even if they later try a less restrictive option and return; the criteria do not apply to family residential services, integrated community supports, the Elderly Waiver or Alternative Care.
Providers must confirm an active service agreement before starting service, document the scope of services in the service delivery plan, and consider models that increase independent living.
The policy supports Minnesota Statutes 256B.4905 (informed choice and community and independent living first) and the Olmstead Plan.
equityCheck: Check that 'complex behavioral health needs' is applied consistently and not more readily to people of color or people with communication differences.
Make sure own-home options are real in the person's area; if no own-home providers exist locally, document that gap rather than treating it as the person's choice.
Review denials and notices of action by race, language, disability and county, and confirm people were told how to appeal.

policies.title: 42 CFR 440.180, Home or community-based services
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This federal Medicaid rule defines home or community-based services that a state may offer under a section 1915(c) waiver instead of care in an institution. It lists the services a waiver may include and the conditions the state must meet. Minnesota's four disability waivers are approved under this authority.
requires: Home or community-based services are services not otherwise covered under the state Medicaid plan, provided under a waiver approved under 42 CFR part 441, subpart G, and must meet the health and welfare assurances in 441.302(a).

Services may include case management, homemaker, home health aide, personal care, adult day health, habilitation, respite care, day treatment and other services for people with chronic mental illness, plus other services the state requests and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services approves as cost-effective and needed to avoid institutional care.

Expanded habilitation services, in effect since October 1, 1997, include prevocational, educational and supported employment services, but not special education available through a school district or vocational rehabilitation available under the Rehabilitation Act.
Waivers may not cover people age 22 through 64 who would otherwise be in an institution for mental diseases.
equityCheck: When a service is denied as 'not a waiver service', check whether it fits one of the listed categories or the 'other services' category before saying no.
Supported employment is a listed service; check that people with high support needs are offered it, not only day programs.
Watch for people excluded by the institution for mental diseases rule and make sure they are connected to other programs.

policies.title: 42 CFR 441.301(c), Person-centered service plans and home and community-based settings requirements
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This federal Medicaid rule sets what every section 1915(c) waiver must contain. Paragraph (c) requires a person-centered planning process led by the person, a written person-centered service plan, yearly plan reviews, and qualities every home and community-based setting must have. The 2024 amendments added minimum reassessment performance and a grievance system.
requires: The planning process must be led by the person, include people they choose, happen at convenient times and places, use plain language and be accessible to people with disabilities and limited English proficiency, reflect cultural considerations, and keep case management separate from service delivery except where the state proves no other qualified provider exists.

The plan must reflect the setting the person chose, their strengths and preferences, assessed needs, goals, paid and unpaid supports, risks and backup plans, and must be written in plain language, signed with informed consent and shared with everyone involved.

The plan must be reviewed at least every 12 months, when needs change or at the person's request; beginning three years after July 9, 2024, at least 90 percent of people enrolled a full year must get a yearly functional reassessment and plan review.

Settings must be integrated in the community, chosen by the person from options including non-disability-specific settings and a private unit, protect privacy and dignity, be free from coercion and restraint, and allow choice of services and providers.

Provider-owned residential settings must give a lease or similar protection, lockable doors, choice of roommate, control over schedule and food, visitors at any time and physical accessibility; any modification must be documented in the plan with assessed need, positive supports tried first, time limits and informed consent.

Nursing facilities, institutions for mental diseases, intermediate care facilities and hospitals are not home and community-based settings; settings on institutional grounds or that isolate people are presumed institutional unless heightened scrutiny shows otherwise.

Beginning two years after July 9, 2024, the state must run a grievance system that accepts oral or written grievances, resolves them within 90 days, offers free language help and protects people from retaliation.
equityCheck: Check that the planning meeting was held in the person's language, with an interpreter if needed, and that the written plan is in a format they can read or have read to them.
Ask whether the person was offered a non-disability-specific setting and a private unit, and record the options they turned down.
Review modifications to the residential rules (locked doors, food access, visitors) by provider and by the person's race and disability to spot over-use of restrictions.
Make sure grievance information is given in plain language and the person knows they will not lose services for complaining.

programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: The official summary of the federal Access rule, published May 10, 2024 and effective July 9, 2024. The rule adds oversight, reporting, grievance and payment requirements for Medicaid home and community-based services in both fee-for-service and managed care.
requires: States must strengthen oversight of person-centered service planning and adopt nationwide incident management system standards for home and community-based services programs.
States must set up a grievance system for home and community-based services delivered through fee-for-service.

Within six years, at least 80 percent of Medicaid payments for homemaker, home health aide and personal care services must go to direct care worker compensation, with a hardship exemption and a separate level for small providers; Indian Health Service and Tribal health programs subject to 25 U.S.C. 1641 are exempt.
States report readiness to collect direct care worker compensation data in three years and the actual percentages in four years.

States must report on section 1915(c) waiver waiting lists, how quickly personal care, homemaker, home health aide and habilitation services start, and a standard set of home and community-based services quality measures.
States must publicly report home and community-based services quality, performance and compliance measures.

Check how the 80 percent compensation rule affects small, rural and culturally specific providers and whether the small-provider level or hardship exemption is being applied fairly.
Check that incident management covers people in self-directed services and in all settings, not only licensed residential settings.
