policies.title: Home and community-based settings final rule (CMS-2249-F and CMS-2296-F), 79 FR 2948
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: The federal rule published January 16, 2014 and effective March 17, 2014 that defines what counts as a home and community-based setting for Medicaid waiver and state plan services. It also sets person-centered planning rules, limits who may do case management, and required each state to file a transition plan.
requires: A home and community-based setting must be integrated in the community, chosen by the person from options that include a non-disability-specific setting, protect privacy, dignity and freedom from coercion and restraint, support individual choice and autonomy, and let the person choose services and providers (42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)).

In provider-owned or controlled residential settings the person must also have a lease or similar agreement with eviction protections, a lockable door, choice of roommates, freedom to furnish and decorate, control of schedule and access to food at any time, visitors at any time, and a physically accessible setting; any change to these conditions must be documented in the person-centered plan with an assessed need, less intrusive methods tried, review dates and the person's consent.

Nursing facilities, institutions for mental diseases, intermediate care facilities for individuals with intellectual disabilities and hospitals are not home and community-based settings; settings in or next to an institution, or that isolate people, are presumed institutional unless they pass heightened scrutiny (42 CFR 441.301(c)(5)).

The person-centered planning process must be led by the person, held at times and places convenient to the person, reflect cultural considerations, use plain language, be accessible to people with disabilities and limited English proficiency, and offer informed choice of services and providers (42 CFR 441.301(c)(1)).

Providers of a person's home and community-based services, or those with a financial interest in a provider, may not develop the plan or do case management, except where no other willing qualified entity exists and the state has approved conflict protections.

The plan must be reviewed at least every 12 months, when circumstances change, or at the person's request; states with existing waivers had to submit a transition plan with 30 days of public comment (42 CFR 441.301(c)(3) and (6)).
Changes to section 1915(c) waivers must follow a public input process that includes consultation with federally recognized Tribes (42 CFR 441.304(f)(4)).
equityCheck: Check that the settings offered to a person include options outside disability-specific housing in the person's own community, not only the settings with open beds.
Check that planning meetings use the person's language and communication method and are held at times and places the person can reach.
Check that any restriction on a person's rights in a provider-controlled setting is in the plan with the required safeguards and is not applied to everyone in the setting.
Check who does the person's case management and whether that agency also provides their services.

policies.title: Medicaid Program; Ensuring Access to Medicaid Services (final rule)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This federal rule from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services sets new requirements for home and community-based services paid by Medicaid. It covers how much of the payment must reach direct care workers, quality reporting, incident management, grievance systems and advisory groups that include people who use services. It was published in the Federal Register on May 10, 2024 and took effect July 9, 2024, with compliance dates spread over several years.
requires: Within six years of the effective date, states must generally ensure at least 80 percent of Medicaid payments for homemaker, home health aide and personal care services go to compensation for direct care workers; states may set a hardship exemption and a separate level for small providers, and Indian Health Service and Tribal health programs are exempt.
Within three years, states must report on their readiness to collect data on the share of payments spent on direct care worker compensation for these services and for habilitation.

The rule adds requirements for incident management systems, grievance systems for people in fee-for-service home and community-based services, and reporting on person-centered service plans and reassessments.
States must report on waiting lists and access measures and publish payment rates.
States must have a Medicaid Advisory Committee and a Beneficiary Advisory Council that include people who use Medicaid services.

policies.title: 2023 Annual Report on Olmstead Plan Implementation
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This report from the Minnesota Olmstead Subcabinet, dated November 27, 2023 and accepted January 17, 2024, reports progress on the 40 measurable goals in the April 2022 Olmstead Plan. The goals cover moving people from segregated to integrated settings, timeliness of waiver funding, quality of life, person-centered planning, housing, employment, education, transportation, health, positive supports, crisis services and preventing abuse. Data runs through October 31, 2023.
requires: Of 40 goals, 8 were met, 4 were on track, 15 were not met, 1 was not on track and 12 were in process; for each goal not met the report says how agencies will improve.

In fiscal year 2023, 470 of 858 people assessed for the Developmental Disabilities Waiver (55 percent) had funding approved within 45 days of assessment, down 7 percent from the prior year; the goal is funding at a reasonable pace by urgency category.

In fiscal year 2022, 106 people moved from intermediate care facilities, 799 from nursing facilities (under 65, more than 90 days) and 2,127 from other segregated housing to more integrated settings, each meeting the annual goal.

The eight required elements of person-centered planning were present at a combined 96.3 percent in fiscal year 2023, and 838 more people lived in the most integrated housing of their choice, meeting the goal of 635.
In fiscal year 2023, 406 people experienced a restrictive procedure, 18 more than the previous year.
equityCheck: When reviewing waiver funding timeliness, break the 45-day data down by county, Tribal Nation, race and urgency category to see who waits longest.
Use the positive supports numbers to ask which providers and which groups of people experience restrictive procedures most.
Check that quality of life survey results are reported for people who communicate without words or in languages other than English.

policies.summary: This December 2025 report from the Aging and Adult Services and Disability Services divisions gives calendar year 2024 data on six MnCHOICES performance measures that Minnesota Statutes 256B.0911 requires the Department of Human Services to develop with lead agencies. The measures track how many people are assessed, how fast paperwork is sent, how often eligibility takes more than 60 days, interview length, repeat assessments and waits for financial eligibility.
requires: In calendar year 2024, 28,174 people had initial MnCHOICES assessments and 77,724 had reassessments statewide; counts rose in the second half of the year when managed care organization assessments were added.

Average days from assessment to mailing the assessment summary were about 20 to 21 days for initial assessments and 12 to 13 days for reassessments in quarters two through four; lead agencies have 60 days by statute.

On average 9 percent of people with an initial assessment in 2024 had an eligibility determination take longer than 60 days (7 percent in quarter one rising to 12 percent in quarter four); use of eligibility updates varied from none to about 30 percent of cases by lead agency.
Common causes of delay were backlogs in Medical Assistance long-term care eligibility at the lead agency and waits for a State Medical Review Team disability determination.
The reporting requirement changed in 2023 from an annual legislative report to an annual data report.

programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: A published Round 5 Lead Agency Review report on a county lead agency, based on a September 2024 review and issued June 2025. It explains how the Department of Human Services reviews lead agencies and records the county's strengths, suggested improvements, corrective actions and case file remediation.
requires: The Department of Human Services develops and monitors home and community-based services waiver policy; lead agencies (counties, Tribal Nations and managed care organizations) administer the programs.

The review covers six programs: Alternative Care, Brain Injury Waiver, Community Alternative Care Waiver, Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver, Developmental Disabilities Waiver and Elderly Waiver.

Methods are a case file review, a lead agency survey, supervisor and leadership interviews, and assessor and case manager focus groups; results are used to document compliance and remediation to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

A corrective action is issued when a pattern of noncompliance with a program requirement is found; the lead agency must submit a corrective action plan that shows how it will bring every item into full compliance.
Case files missing required items must be remediated after the review; the report records how many files needed remediation and that it was completed.
This review found no corrective actions; 64 of 191 case files reviewed needed remediation, which was completed before publication.

Suggested improvements were to keep building person-centered skills in the revised MnCHOICES system, including for non-speaking people and when a parent or guardian answers, and to grow assessment capacity as intake rises.
equityCheck: Check the report's demographic snapshot: who the lead agency serves by race, age and language, and whether that matches the county's population.
Check interpreter access: both reports note that in-person interpreters for some languages are hard to find and that families sometimes interpret sensitive topics.
Check timeliness measures by program: delays between assessment and support plan fall hardest on people waiting for services to start.
Check employment, self-directed services and living-at-home rates against the cohort and statewide figures to see which groups are being offered fewer options.

source.title: Home and Community-Based Services Lead Agency Review, Olmsted County, form 8488AX

policies.title: Home and Community-Based Services Lead Agency Review report, Washington County, form 8488BX (January 2026)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: A published Round 5 Lead Agency Review report on a county lead agency, based on a September 2025 review and issued January 2026. It explains the review process and records the county's strengths, suggested improvements, two corrective actions and case file remediation.
requires: The Department of Human Services develops and monitors home and community-based services waiver policy; lead agencies (counties, Tribal Nations and managed care organizations) administer the programs.

The review covers six programs: Alternative Care, Brain Injury Waiver, Community Alternative Care Waiver, Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver, Developmental Disabilities Waiver and Elderly Waiver.

Methods are a case file review, a lead agency survey, supervisor and leadership interviews, and assessor and case manager focus groups; results are used to document compliance and remediation to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

A corrective action is issued when a pattern of noncompliance with a program requirement is found; the lead agency must submit a corrective action plan that shows how it will bring every item into full compliance.
Case files missing required items must be remediated after the review; the report records how many files needed remediation and that it was completed.

Corrective action 1: 14 percent of case files lacked documentation that face-to-face visits happened within required timelines (Developmental Disabilities Waiver under Minnesota Rules 9525.0024; Elderly Waiver and Alternative Care under Minnesota Statutes 256B.0911 and 256B.0915; Brain Injury, Community Alternative Care and Community Access for Disability Inclusion waivers under the waiver plan).

Corrective action 2: 45 percent of case files missed the requirement in Minnesota Statutes 256B.0911, subdivision 29 that the assessment summary and support plan be completed no more than 60 calendar days after the assessment visit.
107 of 301 case files reviewed needed remediation, which was completed before publication; the county was asked to extend its internal file review to contracted case management agencies.

policies.title: House Research Department bill summary, H.F. 4338 first engrossment (Department of Human Services finance bill), April 21, 2026
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: A plain-language summary by the Minnesota House Research Department of the House version of the 2026 Department of Human Services finance bill. Article 6, Aging and Disability Services, describes the disability provisions as they stood before conference committee, so section numbers and details differ from the final act, Laws of Minnesota 2026, chapter 121.
requires: Moratoria effective January 1, 2027 on new integrated community supports licenses and settings (Minnesota Statutes 245D.12 and 256B.492) and on new customized living and 24-hour customized living settings and provider enrollment (Minnesota Statutes 256S.20), with exceptions the commissioner may approve and priority for regions short on capacity.

Electronic visit verification rewritten in Minnesota Statutes 256B.073: new definitions, provider duties, a no-cost state system, third-party system rules, data and manual-visit requirements, and commissioner authority to phase in services or waive requirements.

Billing limits effective January 1, 2027 for listed disability waiver services (adult companion, chore, homemaker, day support, family training and counseling, independent living skills, individualized home supports, home-delivered meals, personal emergency response, respite, overnight supervision, transportation) and for early intensive developmental and behavioral intervention from July 1, 2027.

MnCHOICES changes: the commissioner employs certified assessors to conduct assessments on behalf of lead agencies, providers get limited role-based access to a person's support plan, and a MnCHOICES redesign working group reports by September 1, 2027 on shifting assessments to the state.

Residential support services providers under the Disability Waiver Rate System and the Elderly Waiver must document direct staffing hours per person for services on or after January 1, 2029, keep records six years and submit them yearly, with audits and annual aggregate reports.

Studies and groups: a market rate study of waiver payment rates with a report due February 15, 2027; a waiver case management advisory working group reporting September 1, 2027; a waiver case management rate evaluation due December 15, 2028; and an integrated community supports reform study due September 1, 2027; informed choice in technology and remote supports provisions in Minnesota Statutes 256B.4905 are expanded.
equityCheck: Check how moratoria on integrated community supports and customized living affect people in regions that already have few settings, and whether exceptions are prioritized by documented regional need.
Check whether billing limits and the exception process are explained to families in plain language and whether people with higher needs can still get what they are assessed to need.
Check that the market rate study and staffing documentation look at rural, small and culturally specific providers, not only statewide averages.
Check that the working groups on case management and MnCHOICES redesign include people receiving services, Tribal Nations and lead agencies of different sizes.

source.title: Bill Summary, H.F. 4338 First engrossment, Department of Human Services Finance Bill, Minnesota House Research Department

policies.title: Minnesota Housing report on Olmstead Plan activities
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This February 13, 2026 report from Minnesota Housing to legislative committees describes the agency's Olmstead Plan work on affordable and accessible housing for people with disabilities. It was required by Laws of Minnesota 2025, chapter 32, article 3, section 15. It reports results on the shared housing goal with the Department of Human Services and describes the proposed goals for the 2027 to 2032 plan.
requires: The existing Olmstead housing goal counts people with disabilities who move to integrated rental housing of their choice with financial support for rent; over 2021 to 2023 the goal was 1,802 and 2,352 people moved (the goal was met in 2021 and 2023 and not met in 2022).
The goal is shared between Minnesota Housing and the Department of Human Services.

The updated Olmstead Plan will be a five-year plan for 2027 to 2032, developed with paid Inclusion Consultants who have lived experience of disability, community conversations, surveys and a public comment period.

Minnesota Housing's proposed goals are to expand accessible, affordable rental units and permanent supportive housing, increase financing for home accessibility and homeownership, and work with other agencies to help people move from segregated settings into integrated housing.
equityCheck: Ask whether the people moving into integrated housing reflect the people on waivers in your area by race, language and disability type.
Check that people in segregated settings know about rental assistance and supportive housing options and have help applying.
Watch for regions with few accessible units, where the housing goal cannot be reached without new development.

policies.title: Minnesota's Olmstead Plan, 2026 (Putting the Promise of Olmstead into Practice)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: Minnesota's Olmstead Plan is the state's commitment to serve people with disabilities in the most integrated setting of their choice, as required by the United States Supreme Court's Olmstead v. L.C. decision. The 2026 plan is the first comprehensive update since 2015. It sets measurable five-year goals for 13 state entities in eight topic areas and was co-created with people with lived experience of disability.
requires: The plan's vision is that people with disabilities are living, learning, working and enjoying life in the most integrated setting and community of their choice.

Goals cover eight topics: crisis services, education, employment, health and safety, housing, preventing abuse and neglect, transportation and transit, and transition; agencies report publicly on progress at least quarterly and the plan is updated each year.

Transition goals for the Department of Human Services cover people leaving intermediate care facilities, people under 65 in nursing facilities, other segregated settings and people receiving home and community-based services.

Employment goal 1B: by December 31, 2027, 41 percent of people who receive both Medicaid waiver services and vocational rehabilitation or State Services for the Blind services will have competitive integrated employment, up from 39 percent in state fiscal year 2025.
The plan calls for a Disability Systems Change Workgroup to design transformative changes that go beyond the five-year goals.

The Olmstead Subcabinet exists under Executive Order 19-13; the Leadership Forum reviewed the revised draft in August 2026 and the Subcabinet voted to accept the plan in September 2026, with versions in English, Spanish, Hmong and Somali to follow.
equityCheck: Use the plan's goals as a checklist when reviewing a person's plan: is the person in the most integrated setting, working if they want to, and safe from abuse and neglect?

The plan was written with Inclusion Consultants from many communities; check that your local input processes also reach people of color, Indigenous people, people in Greater Minnesota and people in segregated settings.
Quarterly progress reports are public; compare statewide progress with what you see in your county or region.

source.title: Minnesota's Olmstead Plan, September 2026

policies.title: Olmstead Subcabinet (Executive Order 19-13, Minnesota Olmstead Plan)
policies.summary: Executive Order 19-13, signed March 29, 2019, continues the Olmstead Subcabinet that implements Minnesota's Olmstead Plan. The plan responds to the Olmstead v. L.C. decision and Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act, which require services in the most integrated setting. The Subcabinet is made up of state agency leaders, the Ombudsman for Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities and the executive director of the Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities.
requires: Members are the Ombudsman for Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities, the executive director of the Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities, and the leaders or designees of the Departments of Human Services, Employment and Economic Development, Transportation, Corrections, Health, Human Rights, Education, Veterans Affairs and Public Safety, the Housing Finance Agency and the Metropolitan Council.
The Subcabinet must identify and address barriers to services and opportunities in the most integrated settings, and areas of disparity in where people with disabilities live, work and engage.
It must engage communities with the greatest disparities in health outcomes for people with disabilities and work to address barriers to equitable health outcomes.
It oversees and monitors the Olmstead Plan, recommends amendments, holds public meetings, engages people with disabilities, and continues the Quality of Life survey.
The Olmstead Implementation Office provides staffing and carries out duties assigned by the Subcabinet; the order rescinds Executive Order 15-03.
equityCheck: When reviewing a program, ask how it supports the Olmstead Plan goals of integrated living, work and community participation.
Use the order's list of protected characteristics, which includes race, ethnicity, language, geography and economic status, as a checklist for who may be left out.
Look at Quality of Life survey results and Olmstead Plan reports for your region.

source.title: Executive Order 19-13, Rescinding Executive Order 15-03, Supporting Freedom of Choice and Opportunity to Live, Work, and Participate in the Most Inclusive Setting for Individuals with Disabilities through the Implementation of Minnesota's Olmstead Plan

policies.title: Overview of Medicaid Home- and Community-Based Waiver Services (Minnesota House Research Department, September 2025)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This short nonpartisan report from the Minnesota House Research Department explains Minnesota's five home and community-based waivers, who is eligible, who administers them, how many people use them and what they cost. It also describes the Waiver Reimagine plan to move from four disability waivers to two starting January 1, 2027.
requires: The Department of Human Services oversees the waivers and distributes funding; counties administer the programs and develop individual service plans.
A person must be eligible for Medical Assistance, choose community services, meet the waiver's level of care and have an assessed need beyond the state plan.

An estimated 114,019 people received waiver services in 2025: Developmental Disabilities 26,377; Community Alternative Care 888; Community Access for Disability Inclusion 52,195; Brain Injury 969; Elderly Waiver 33,590 (managed care only).
Estimated 2025 spending was about $6.86 billion, with average cost per person ranging from about $22,458 (Elderly Waiver, managed care) to $127,913 (Brain Injury Waiver).
Phase one of Waiver Reimagine, a common service menu, began in January 2021; the two-waiver system and individual budget method are to be phased in beginning January 1, 2027.
equityCheck: Use the enrollment and cost figures as a baseline, then ask for the same data by race, language, county and Tribal Nation.
Note that the Elderly Waiver counts exclude fee-for-service, so totals understate older adults served.
Ask how the 2027 individual budget method will be tested for fairness across regions and populations.

source.title: Overview of Medicaid Home- and Community-Based Waiver Services, Minnesota House Research Department

policies.title: Waiver Reimagine Advisory Committee report to the Legislature and the Legislative Task Force on Waiver Reimagine
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This September 2025 report from the tri-chairs of the Waiver Reimagine Advisory Committee goes to the Minnesota Legislature and the Legislative Task Force on Waiver Reimagine. The committee was set up in 2021 to advise the Department of Human Services on Waiver Reimagine and was dissolved in June 2025 when the task force was created. The report records what the committee agreed on and the concerns its members raised.
requires: The committee met every two months from March 2022 through June 2025 and named the two proposed waivers: the Individual Support Waiver and the Residential Support Waiver.

Members with lived experience were strongly opposed to a two-waiver model based on where a person lives, which came from the 2018 transition report and 2019 legislation and was not open for discussion.
Members overwhelmingly opposed individual budgets tied to living setting, noting proposed budgets for corporate foster care were more than 100 percent higher than for family or independent settings.
Members said the validity of the MnCHOICES 2.0 assessment must be independently confirmed because of reports of unexplained budget reductions.

Consensus positions: Consumer-Directed Community Supports should stay available under both waivers; all services should be available on both waivers regardless of setting; case management practice should be standardized across counties.
The report asks the task force to use authentic partnership practices and to reconsider waiver structures that may restrict choice, equity and community integration.
equityCheck: When applying Waiver Reimagine changes, check whether budgets or service menus differ by where a person lives and whether that pushes people toward licensed settings instead of family or independent living.
Confirm people and families, not only agencies, had a real say in design decisions and that feedback was gathered in community languages and formats.
Watch for assessment-driven budget reductions and track them by race, language, disability type and county so patterns can be seen and explained.
Check that self-directed options such as Consumer-Directed Community Supports are offered equally in every county and every living setting.

source.title: Waiver Reimagine Advisory Committee Report, September 2025

policies.title: Waiver Reimagine update: what 2026 legislative changes mean for the new Disability Waiver Program (July 6, 2026)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: On July 6, 2026, the Department of Human Services posted a quarterly Waiver Reimagine update. It repeats that the new Disability Waiver Program cannot launch by January 1, 2027 and that no new date has been set. It says the program will launch in a rolling, phased way only after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services approves new waiver plans and after people receive an assigned support range and budget range through a MnCHOICES assessment at least 12 months before launch. It lists the work under way and how people can give input.
requires: The new Disability Waiver Program will not launch by January 1, 2027; the Department of Human Services has not set a new launch date.

Launch will be rolling and phased, and will happen only after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services approves the new waiver plans and after people have received an assigned support range and budget range through a MnCHOICES assessment at least 12 months before launch, for planning purposes only.

Under the 2026 legislative changes, before asking for federal approval the commissioner must consult with the Olmstead Implementation Office so the new program aligns with Olmstead goals for inclusive living.

Activities planned for 2026, such as sharing information about budgeted services and releasing the updated federal waiver application for public comment, are being retimed and some may happen later than expected.

Current work includes a budget exception process, the updated federal waiver application and public review materials, technology systems and business processes, an accessible online information portal for informed choice, and community engagement through the Expert Panel and the Advisory Task Force on Waiver Reimagine.

The stated goal is a waiver program that is simpler, more equitable and sustainable; the Disability Waiver Program website is the central source for updates, and people can join the Virtual Insight Panel or Professional Insight Panel or use the public feedback form.
equityCheck: Check that people and families, not only professionals, get plain-language updates in their languages about what the delay means for them.
Ask how support ranges and budget ranges will be tested for bias by race, disability type, language and region before they are assigned.

source.title: Department of Human Services, Waiver Reimagine update: What 2026 legislative changes mean for Minnesota's new Disability Waiver Program (July 6, 2026)

policies.title: Waiver Reimagine: Phase 1 Service Streamline and Phase 2 Recommendations for Reshaping Waivers and Individualized Budgets (legislative report form 7841B)
programs: Community Access for Disability Inclusion Waiver
policies.summary: This January 2021 report from the Disability Services Division of the Department of Human Services to the Legislature describes the two phases of Waiver Reimagine. Phase 1 simplified the waiver service menu and built an online service-planning tool. Phase 2 proposes combining the four disability waivers into two waivers based on living setting and moving to individual budgets based on assessed need.
requires: The 2017 Legislature required two studies of the four disability waivers; the 2019 Legislature (Minnesota Laws 2019, chapter 9, article 5) authorized a two-phase set of changes.
Phase 1, the streamlined service menu, was set to take effect January 1, 2021, or on federal approval, whichever came later.

Phase 2 proposes an Individual Support Waiver for people who live independently or with family and a Residential Support Waiver for people in group or shared living, keeping current level-of-care and eligibility rules.
Phase 2 proposes individual budgets set by assessed support need through MnCHOICES, replacing county-based budget methods, with a budget exception process to be developed.

The report proposed a one-year rolling implementation at each person's annual reassessment, with new waivers submitted to the federal government in 2022 and the four existing waivers sunsetting December 31, 2023 (later delayed).

The report gives fiscal year 2019 data: the Developmental Disabilities Waiver was 82 percent white and 16 percent Black, Indigenous or people of color, while the other three waivers were 70 percent white and 29 percent Black, Indigenous or people of color, against a state population of 79.1 percent white; it says moving diagnosis into the background is meant to reduce this gap.
equityCheck: Track waiver enrollment by race, ethnicity, language and county before and after any Waiver Reimagine change, using the fiscal year 2019 figures in this report as a baseline.
Check that diagnosis-based bias, including under-diagnosis of Black children with developmental disabilities, does not carry into the new eligibility or budget process.
Confirm that outreach for feedback reaches people of color, people with culturally specific needs, parents of school-age children and every region of the state, as the report describes.
Make sure self-directed options and employment-first and independent-living-first choices are explained and available in both waivers and every county.

source.title: Legislative Report: Waiver Reimagine, Phase 1 Service Streamline and Phase 2 Recommendations (form 7841B, January 2021)
